Researchers have discovered that a typical two-layer neural network can accurately approximate the eigenvalues of the Schrödinger equation in one-dimensional spaces with high precision, overcoming the limitations of classical methods in such complex multi-dimensional environments. However, there are concerns about generalizing these findings, especially in 2D and 3D scenarios where the computational demands are significantly greater. Our study investigates these concerns by analyzing a neural network's initial error pattern in approximating Schrödinger eigenvalues. Our analysis explains how non-smooth changes in potential values at the grid intersections cause abrupt changes in the associated Hamiltonian matrices. Consequently, we observe a disordered distribution of eigenvalues, including near-zero and highly oscillating values. Our findings also reveal a strong, negative linear correlation between the order of eigenvalue discrepancies and the corresponding grid point errors. Furthermore, we identified specific trends in approximating errors for systems characterized by real and complex eigenvalues. Our analysis provides insights that can inform the development of more accurate approximations of Schrödinger eigenvalues in multi-dimensional spaces. It is worth noting that the errors outlined may not necessarily hinder the overall performance of a neural network in approximating Schrödinger eigenvalues; however, they may impact the reliability of approximations in areas requiring high precision. Our analysis also demonstrates that a neural network is capable of producing reliable results in certain scenarios by ignoring areas with minimal approximation errors while focusing on critical regions. Furthermore, we found that a neural network is able to produce reliable results in certain scenarios by incorporating the errors into the weight adjustment process of the network. In accordance with our theoretical observations, we successfully obtained highly accurate approximations of 2D and 3D Schrödinger eigenvalue problems using a neural network. Interestingly, our results also reveal that a neural network is capable of producing the same level of precision as a finite element method that utilizes a Korn-Södderström scheme for solving the linear eigenvalue problem. The spatial distribution of deadwood in forests follows a distinctive pattern, often forming, and being contained within, circular shapes. Previous research has demonstrated that the stationary vertex number of certain probability distributions, including the Gaussian and Cauchy distributions, can be constrained by the radius of a sphere under specific conditions. By leveraging regional limit theorems, we have expanded upon this finding to cover a broader range of probability distributions, including generalized multi-dimensional Cauchy distributions. Furthermore, we have confirmed that our findings apply to forests of various dimensions and types of deadwood patterns. The patterns of deadwood's spatial distribution are also illustrated through the use of Monte Carlo simulations. The theoretical conclusions derived from our research have also led to a new probability problem concerning the distribution of points within a closed hypersphere. The problem states that when points are randomly and uniformly distributed within a sphere, the expected value of any polynomial function of the distance between points should be zero. This expectation holds true for most cases, except when points are concentrated in areas close to the hypersphere's surface, at which point the expectation transitions from negative to positive. Consequently, a probability measure, referred to as the 'vacant volume polynomial,' and associated 'vacant volume conjecture' have been introduced to describe this transition. The evidence and methods for proving this conjecture will be discussed in detail. The research presented here and methods for proving the conjecture imply a range of open problems that link probability distributions, regional limit theorems, and the properties of algebraic geometry. Specifically, a number of open questions and challenges have been identified in the accompanying note, regional-vacant-conjecture-nov-2020.pdf. This paper proves that any finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebra over a given field possesses a solvable solvability index. Building upon the classification of finite-dimensional solvable non-associative algebras over a closed field, it further shows that any finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebra is constructible in nature. A specific example is given to illustrate a solvable Zinbiel algebra of solvability index 3. The proof involves examining various subalgebras, including nilpotent and solvable subalgebras, and establishing the solvability of the original algebra through induction, while utilizing the representation theory of the general linear group to achieve this. The solvability of the algebra allows the creation of a natural gradient, used in conjunction with the power of the non-associative algebra, to derive a chain of ideals within the original algebra. The solvability of the original algebra is thus determined by the longest length of such chains. A method for determining the exact length of solvability is also proposed. The remainder of the paper discusses the determination of the solvability index of specific types of Zinbiel algebras under particular constraints. For instance, it is shown that a solvable unitary algebra can have a maximum solvability index of 2, while providing an example of a solvable tridimensional Zinbiel algebra with a 2-dimensional solvable subalgebra and a one-dimensional nilpotent subalgebra. In addition, the paper proves that a solvable filiform Zinbiel algebra is necessarily commutative. The determination of the solvability index is also relatively straightforward in the cases of solvable algebras with a degree of linear transformation less than or equal to 3. However, an example of a four-dimensional solvable algebra over a finite field is given, illustrating that the solvability index can be arbitrarily large. The primary objective of this study is to examine how migration impacts the spread of infectious diseases across interconnected populations. To achieve this, we have developed a comprehensive framework that combines intracommunity transmission and intercommunity transmission. Focusing on the latter, we have obtained a discrete-time intercommunity transmission model, which we have found to be analogous to a continuous-time process. We have further demonstrated that this model exhibits two distinct equilibrium states and exhibited both stable and unstable behavior. Furthermore, we have established the existence of a metastable region in this model, which we used to develop an approximation for the long-term asymptotic behavior of the model. In addition, we have studied the effects of migration on the transmission process by means of Monte Carlo simulations and partial differential equations modeling. The results of these simulations revealed that the metastable region can be divided into two distinct metastable regions, one of which is highly resistant to change and persists over extended periods of time. We have also observed that the model's behavior may undergo a phase transition from stability to instability under specific conditions, facilitated by the action of migration. This study has contributed significant insights into the complex relationships between migration, transmission, and disease spread through theoretical modeling and numerical simulations. These findings have the potential to inform public health policy for the prevention and/or mitigation of COVID-19 outbreaks. Ultimately, we have established two metastable regions in the model; one is highly stable, while the other is highly unstable. We intend to extend this research by exploring metastable regions in models featuring multiple diseases and multiple populations. We are particularly interested in discovering whether the concept of metastable regions is applicable to the Bellman-Harris chain model, which we suspect may exhibit a level of stability similar to that of a single disease spreading across multiple populations. We also aim to investigate the application of learning algorithms, such as reinforcement learning, to models featuring migration and transmission, as well as the metastable region model. In this context, we have discovered that the Bellman-Harris chain model is capable of learning the optimal strategy of a Trolley Problem, where the model's target is to avoid running over people with the trolley while still preventing death on the tracks. This research has the potential to significantly expand the scope of the applied mathematical modeling of transmission and migration processes. We look forward to embedding our models within the context of machine learning, the philosophy of artificial intelligence, and the ethics of public health policy. Exoplanetary systems with near 3:2 orbital resonances are relatively rare, and identifying systems in the final stages of resonance progression is challenging due to the noisy data from space missions. Further complicating the process is the fact that most numerical integration techniques can't replicate the observed orbital configurations without exceeding computational limits, for low mass ratio systems. However, researchers have developed a novel approach by numerically integrating various Newtonian variations to track the hypothetical host star's motion and its impact on the evolving orbital configurations of its planets. Applying this methodology to the K2-138 system allowed scientists to reconstruct its full resonance sequence and confirm that it follows a specific 3:2 resonance chain: $k:m$. Moreover, they discovered new findings that could explain a discrepancy in astronomical observations by showing that the planets actually lie at slightly different distances than previously thought. These results were obtained using various Newtonian variations to verify the sequence. When they used their algorithm without modifications, the results suggested a possible period shift of less than 0.1%, which could potentially explain the observed disparity. However, when they ran the model with artificially enhanced noise levels mimicking space mission conditions, the results showed that precision of less than 0.2% is required to reproduce the observed period ratio of the planets. Finally, they ran several numerical integrations with each possible $k:m$ resonance chain, and determined that the most likely sequence for K2-138 is 3:2, 3:4, 2:7, and 1:7. However, the model couldn't confidently exclude other possible combinations such as 2:3, 4:2, and it couldn't reproduce the observed planetary motion when in the $k=m+1$ resonance chain. Therefore, while the model significantly enhances our understanding of the K2-138 system, it still has some limitations that need to be addressed. Furthermore, the researcher notes that the model produced the expected results when run with the correct numerical integration approach, and suggests its applicability to similar cases. One such system that it can be applied to is K2-251, which is at the final stages of its resonance progression with the second planet. However, when it was run with the correct Newtonian variation, it produced the expected results showing that the planets at near 3:2 resonance typically follow a specific $k:m$ chain. However, when it was run with the correct Newtonian variation for the $k=m+1$ resonance chain, it failed to reproduce the observed planetary motion

Different knowledge representation approaches often vary in their effectiveness and suitability for specific tasks, yet there's a lack of systematic research evaluating various declarative knowledge graphs in terms of their text understanding capabilities. In this paper, we systematically assess and compare the textual comprehension abilities of 7 widely-used declarative knowledge graphs in English question-answering tasks. To do so, we built an recall-based framework that leverages these knowledge graphs to generate answers for synthetic English questions drawn from a diverse set of texts. Our analysis reveals a clear disparity in the comprehension capabilities of these declarative graphs, with WIKIDATA and YAGO being relatively proficient, but DBP15K, TSVK, DBpedia, TDM, and Wikitags struggling to accurately answer the questions. Based on our findings, we provide recommendations and propose an alternative graphical structure to enhance the text comprehension abilities of these declarative knowledge graphs. In addition to evaluating the understanding capabilities of these graphs, we also investigated the role of graphical query expansion in the answers generated by the recall-based framework. Querying a declarative knowledge graph can be resource-intensive due to its inherent complexity, but by incorporating relevant words from the query into the graph, we can mitigate the query processing time. Our results demonstrate that incorporating an unsupervised distance-based query expansion technique can significantly improve the text comprehension capabilities of less proficient declarative graphs, while also yielding better answers for the questions. Overall, our paper contributes to the development of systematic methods to assess and improve the text comprehension capabilities of large-scale declarative knowledge graphs, ultimately contributing to their construction and maintenance. In terms of potential applications, our paper could benefit researchers working with declarative knowledge graphs in information retrieval tasks, while its code is publicly available on the GitHub repository 'Textual-Declarative-GRFs'. Lastly, our analysis reveals a notable disparity between graph query construction and actual question-answering tasks in terms of complexity, a gap that could potentially lead to efficient automatic question-answering methods. In light of this distinction, we make another major contribution by introducing a novel automatic question-answering framework known as the AutoQAFramework, designed to bridge this complexity gap. By leveraging the text comprehension capabilities of declarative graphs, the AutoQAFramework aims to automatically rephrase questions drawn from various text types and generate more informative versions that improve the answers obtained. For the utmost protection of life and equipment during abnormal conditions in power systems, precise detection of hidden failures in two-core transformers is vital. To enhance detection efficiency, researchers have explored using diverse features from magnetic sensors or flux sensors. Through a numerical investigation into transient phenomena in failed and healthy transformers, this study rigorously evaluates features extracted via the Fourier Transform, Magneto-Resistive Effect, Power System Protection, and Categorization methods. As a result, this study advises against employing certain Fourier Transform features and instead offers a tailored approach to categorize transients – identifying failed or healthy states of the transformer – with adapted magnetic sensor characteristics. Furthermore, this work develops and proposes an optimized configuration of two-core transformers for the most effective detection of their transients. To validate this approach, this study conducts a realistic test on a small power system equipped with a two-core transformer. To numerical simulations, this study adds an element of unpredictability, using the Finite Element Method to model real-world materials as realistically as possible. Ultimately, the results of this study categorize transients from manufacturing and electrical imbalances. To confirm the practical value of this work, the study conducts experiments on a prototype of its proposed setup, demonstrating the practicality and effectiveness of this approach in real-world scenarios. However, this system is vulnerable to interference from adjacent groups sharing the same sub-carriers. In an attempt to prevent these interference effects, each transmitter is restricted from using certain groups of carriers. The task of maximizing network downlink capacity can be redefined as an optimization problem within a shared spectrum environment, where the goal is to allocate frequency blocks and group assignments to minimize interference while ensuring groups assigned to the same transmitter use compatible carrier sets. This optimization problem can be efficiently solved by first finding potential group assignments for each transmitter, then distributing these groups across the spectrum to minimize interference, with both steps being sub-problems of a shared variable BIP-TWAP problem. The dynamics of the beam are governed by a partial differential equation, and we're using two methods - one based on the multiplier operator, and one on the issue of inverse MHD-type boundary conditions - to investigate its behavior. The analysis takes into account a capillary force and no control or external disturbance in the internal node, leading to the derivation of a matrix-related spectrum and associated eigenfunctions. The results show that the beam's stability depends on specific relationships between its spatial parameters, and we're able to derive bounds for the exponential stability. The findings are substantiated using numerical examples. The methods we've employed could be adapted for investigating the behavior of other linear diffusion models in graph geometry. The presented principles could be applied more broadly to the study of various linear diffusion models in graph geometry with consideration of outer solutions. For the elements created within the r-process, accurate nuclear weights are essential for studying their abundance and nuclear reaction pathways. Unfortunately, nuclear weights are influenced by various nuclear decay processes including beta and alpha decay, as well as electron capture and internal pair decay. In the realm of atomic physics, calculating nuclear weights for elements up to zinc using experimental data and theoretical predictions is relatively feasible. However, this task becomes increasingly difficult for the elements beyond zinc. To address this challenge, we employed AI-driven methods to forecast the relative isotopic abundances of elements in the r-process range, utilizing a combination of experimental data and the mass models of Suleimanov, SMM. These models were based on the mass relationships of neighboring nuclei as well as experimental data for the most stable isotopes. By testing the predicted nuclear weights using two approaches - a weighted average of beta and alpha decay probabilities and the inverse of the electron capture-to-beta decay ratio - we found that the models achieved a high accuracy, with a average relative uncertainty of about 0.03 percent. This level of accuracy is sufficient for investigations of the r-process, allowing us to incorporate the predicted nuclear weights into r-process network simulations. Therefore, this study demonstrates the effectiveness of machine learning in addressing intractable nuclear data challenges. Future work will focus on calculating the decay properties of highly unstable nuclei using the tensor finite elements method. Furthermore, we plan to improve the accuracy of the predicted nuclear weights by incorporating more data using the moving finite parts method. This approach will enable us to establish data connections between highly unstable neighboring nuclei across the nuclear chart. In doing so, we aim to achieve a level of accuracy comparable to that required for investigations of the r and p-processes. A new version of the nuclear weights forecasting code, initially developed for studying beta decay, has been established within the new PyURCAP framework, a Python-based urban cell model for radioactive decay processes that can be employed in the wider nuclear physics community. This work is part of a larger effort to systematically address the data challenges in nuclear physics and physics of stars through advanced machine learning techniques. A new version of the nuclear weights forecasting code has been established within the URQCAP framework to support a range of calculations including beta and alpha decay, electron capture, internal pair decay, etc. This contribution is part of a larger effort to use machine learning to address the data challenges in nuclear physics and stars through data completion and predictive modeling. The dissipation factor of sapphire was measured at the level of billionths for the first time by using two distinct approaches. By examining the q-factor of a superconducting resonator made from sapphire, researchers were able to determine the dissipation factor. In one method, the temperature was quickly varied between 4.2 and 300 Kelvin to measure the dissipation factor. An even higher level of sensitivity was achieved by using stimulation at twice the resonance frequency and varying the temperature while making precise measurements. Both techniques yielded dissipation factors that were consistent with previously published studies, to a level of precision of around 50 parts-per-billion. This research showcased the potential for accurate measurement of the dissipation factors of materials using superconducting resonators. It could also contribute to developing strategies for overcoming current boundaries in measurement sensitivity. Such advancements could have significant implications for the further development of superconducting devices serving various purposes including quantum computing, spectroscopy and sensing. Furthermore, the research's outcome, specifically the highly sensitive and precise measurement of the dissipation factor, has the potential to expand existing knowledge to a significantly smaller length scale. In particular, the question of the origin of the dissipation loss can be explored and understood by examining the dissipation factors at various lengths ranging from micrometers to nanometers. Ultimately, the research's results can contribute to developing strategies for overcoming current limitations in the measurement of the dissipation factors. It may lead to a significant enhancement in the current sensitivity limit that is typically in the order of 10^-3. By achieving such a breakthrough, researchers can develop more precise and sensitive experiments including electrical transport and mechanical measurements, potentially yielding significant findings. Moreover, the current boundary in the measurement of the dissipation factor limits researchers from performing device evaluations that depend on the material properties and hinders scientific understanding of the dissipation mechanism at various length scales. Therefore, the exploration of the dissipation factor can lead to a more profound understanding of the underlying mechanisms. Moreover, the superconducting resonators can be used to evaluate and develop quantum devices such as Displacement Sensing, the Kittel dipole and the Quantum Electrodynamics devices, where the dissipation factor plays a decisive role. By achieving parts-per-billion sensitivity to the dissipation factor, researchers will be able to develop highly sensitive devices in this regime, thereby increasing the current boundary by an order of magnitude. Consequently, future research can leverage this technological breakthrough to develop extremely precise experiments in this field. Such advancements could have far-reaching implications for the future of the science

The theoretical framework of Electromagnetics has a fundamental concept called pull or anti-push, which is peculiar in optics and is often associated with weights rather than forces. This article will explore the optical pull through the lens of a minimal, classical two-level system by examining its underlying dynamics. By using a basic framework with coherent and incoherent light interactions, we can determine conditions that lead to significant optical pull effects in scenarios involving incoherent light pull and reveal an intriguing possibility of pull without forces. Our work primarily focuses on principles rather than technical applications. Despite being grounded in a classical approach, our findings may also offer insights relevant to quantum optical contexts. One of the key relationships we identify in this paper - $-{\bf F}_p\propto{\bf F}_l $ - could potentially hold valuable applications in light engineering. This relationship suggests that linear momentum forces are related to spin or angular momentum pull forces, which is an intriguing similarity that existing momentum conservation laws do not fully utilize. Moreover, we can derive the pull force coefficients $F_{\alpha}$ by combining principles of pull forces with that of momentum coupling, an approach that is an extension of Minkowski's co-energy and power relations. This is an original contribution of this study. Pull force coefficients provide access to various effect measurements, e.g. optical magnetoelectric effect, and are essential for understanding within and extrinsic properties. This is another key finding of our work. Our work further extends beyond even push-pull optics by enabling measurement of coherent state effects that go beyond the reach of magnetoelectric measurements due to potential non-coherent effects. Finally, we can use our model to determine unidirectional effects that are absent from magnetoelectric measurements, thus further expanding the frontiers of pull optics. This is an additional key finding of our work. Our work is thus an advancement beyond existing knowledge in magnetoelectric physics and optics that bridges coherent and incoherent optics with magnetoelectric physics. This is an accompanying article to a recent publication in the journal New Journal of Physics. In this article, we have further developed and extended our model of optical pull to include path-averaging average momentum pull effects that are also explored in the companion article. Moreover, we have further extended our model to include electron pull effects. This article complements our work in the companion article by delving into electron pull effects. One of the key findings of this article is the possibility of achieving coherent effects that correspond to significant optical pull effects even in incoherent light conditions.

This work addresses a real-world optimization challenge characterized by uncertainty in its decision variables, necessitating a high degree of robustness and protection against potential losses. In response to these risks, we formulate an approach known as two-stage resilient optimization, which minimizes expected costs while safeguarding against adverse outcomes. Our focus is specifically on varible binary problems involving flows, for which we have developed an exact Lagrangian dual-based algorithm with computational efficiency improvements. Building upon this foundation, we have created a hierarchical algorithm for solving more complex problems with multiple layers of resilience. Empirical evidence demonstrates that our methods not only produce high-quality solutions but also outperform established optimization techniques in terms of computational speed. Furthermore, we have applied our approach to tackle real-world network problems, leveraging small-scale examples to effectively model supply chain operations. With the ability to easily adapt our model to various industries, we have also explored its potential in contexts such as wireless networks and power grids. Ultimately, our research aims to promote the use of varible binary models for tackling real-world optimization challenges, for which we have obtained promising results in practice. As the world's most populous megacity, Beijing is a major economic hub with a huge impact on the environment. Resolving the capital's numerous societal problems necessitates a deeper understanding of its diverse population, the resources and natural environment, as well as the complex relationships between these factors. To achieve this, researchers are developing various artificial intelligence (AI) based analytical systems. However, these systems require extensive training data that accurately represents the intricacies of this complex system, which has posed significant data preparation challenges. To address this challenge, we have developed the H4M dataset, an extensive collection of data related to Beijing's socioeconomic analysis. Comprising four essential components, the H4M dataset is a unique resource that includes demographic information, a wide range of environmental data, geographical maps of the city, and detailed images capturing the diverse essence of Beijing. Comprising 120 distinct datasets and containing over 300GB of data, the H4M dataset is one of the largest and most comprehensive datasets of its kind. Committed to promoting data-driven research and development in this field, the H4M dataset can be accessed through an online platform at http://data.bjsdat.com/. Future research aims to expand the dataset through the incorporation of additional sources, such as educational, cultural, and other essential datasets, which will be announced on the dataset website. By leveraging various methodological approaches, we have initially demonstrated the effectiveness of the H4M dataset through a series of competitive challenges and research trials. Notably, the dataset has already facilitated numerous research trials and competitions, as well as several real-world applications and collaborative projects. Subsequent research is expected to utilize the H4M dataset to develop more sophisticated AI models capable of analyzing and managing the complex and diverse data within the dataset. As such, the H4M dataset is expected to play a vital role in driving research and development in this field in the years to come. The online platform for the H4M dataset is accessible at http://data.bjsdat.com/. The associated GitHub repository for the H4M dataset can be found at https://github.com/bjsgisdata/H4M-Dataset. The contact information for the research team can be obtained at https://www.nuancebj.com/. We welcome researchers and practitioners to join us in leveraging the H4M dataset to tackle some of the most critical socioeconomic challenges facing megacities like Beijing worldwide. To analyze complex data sets, visitors can engage with the Data Template Gallery (DTG) https://dtg.gse.asu.edu/. This tool allows for digital exploration of the analyzed data set by allocating a digital area for each data component. Users can select templates to represent various data segments, such as spatial or temporal subsets, and customize their appearances for easier comparison. Additionally, the DTG includes interactive visualizations to expedite the discovery of interesting patterns. Our research showcases the application of the DTG in three domains: (a) detecting crime patterns in police surveillance data; (b) visualizing street conditions for urban improvement initiatives; and (c) analyzing gene expression to find potential treatments for cancer through collaborative and intuitive analysis methods. We argue that the DTG represents an effective visual method for investigating extensive data sets and to facilitate team-based analysis. It incorporates elements: (i) uncovering dominant patterns with low-frequency visual comparisons, (ii) identifying rare events with visual ID classification, and (iii) group-related content with visual categorization. A concise proof demonstrates that for any n, the number of sets that can contain at most one common element in all sets is equal to the number of subsets of a set containing n distinct elements (2^(n-1) elements). This basic result has significant implications for data streaming, particularly for problems such as determining set cardinality and finding frequent elements. A specific example illustrates how this theorem can be utilized to improve the space efficiency of these problems when the size of the sets is known in advance. Evaluations on synthetic and real-world datasets such as the Stanford Track Montage dataset confirm the improved performance of this novel approach. A brief exploration into potential future applications, particularly in computing the sum of elements in data streams, is also included. Additionally, we extend our findings to general two-dimensional systems and discuss the distinction between classical and quantum Hall effects. This model partners with a speech enhancement network, allowing them to learn in tandem through an end-to-end training process. Our study indicates that incorporating ITRSE can effectively overcome the limitations of traditional methods when faced with pandemic-driven breathing pattern variations. Due to the inherent complexity of the learning problem, the process of adjusting a neural network's parameters through supervised learning involves modification transmission from the local to global level. This transmission takes place through simultaneous updates across all layers and iterations of the backpropagation process. However, because each iteration considers the previous layer's errors, sending modifications through supervised learning is a multi-step process involving error propagation. Furthermore, the learning process itself can be seen as an evolving modification transmission pathway, where the objective is to optimize target output. Interestingly, the initial and final points of this pathway coincide, implying that supervised learning is capable of modifying neural networks in a self-referential manner. This concept is formalized through the lens notation, where the learning process can be represented as the composition of small, high-level modifications, known as delta lenses. By combining these lenses, the learning process becomes a straightforward modification transmission. This formulation offers a fresh perspective on the learning process and paves the way for the creation of more tailored and domain-specific training methods. To illustrate this idea, we introduce a fundamental set of delta lenses that can learn the optimal positioning of convolutional neural network (CNN) activation codes for a given dataset. By incorporating a domain-specific univalent lens, the optimal codes can be determined simultaneously. This setup has practical implications, as illustrated by our example demonstrating how the orientation of images within a dataset can be optimized. This research marks the first time that the learning process has been reinterpreted as a unified modification transmission, the foundations of which rely on the notion of lenses. Additionally, the concept of delta lenses enables the creation of tailored and domain-specific training methods, potentially paving the way for the development of machine-learning algorithms tailored to specific computational domains. These events fall into three main categories: 186 with high energies above 1 TeV, 128 with moderate energies between 100 GeV to 1 TeV, and 52 with lower energies below 100 GeV. To better understand these events with high arrival directions and varying energy levels, we proposed a novel method for grouping them. This approach allows us to determine the role of each type of particle within these groupings more effectively. After applying this method to the experimental data, we were able to pinpoint six main groupings, where two types of groupings consist of quark-based particles alone, and the remaining four involve a combination of quark and neutrino-based particles. A closer look at the data revealed that the observed energies of the groupings do not align with the predicted energy levels obtained from existing particle acceleration studies. However, we were able to demonstrate that the energies of the groupings can be generated by accelerating nuclei with masses similar to iron, resulting in the simultaneous emission of both quark and neutrino-based particles. If such a phenomenon of multi-modal grouping of this type is of extraterrestrial origin, it could potentially provide valuable information regarding particle acceleration methods used by cosmic sources. Inspired by a desire to protect user privacy, we have developed a novel, lightweight form of stealthy content generation. By applying a specific type of recurrent neural network, known as the Long Short Term-Hidden Markov model, we have successfully produced LSTMs that distribute the same input in multiple discrete segments. Building on this foundation, we have effectively integrated the capabilities of LSTMs within the Bohai Steganography Framework, a state-of-the-art steganographic content generation approach based on Gauvin-Van Gool Channel, a variational autoencoder, and Generative Adversarial Networks. On selected images from the ImageNet database, our method consistently outperforms the existing best approach, presenting a breakthrough in the field of Artificial Adversarial Networks. We also examine the inherent complexities of LSTMs, including their capacity limitation and the dangers of cycles, which significantly impede their potential application. By contributing these findings, we aim to facilitate further research that could eventually lead to more advanced and stable models, like the one based on Transformer. Currently, our code is publicly accessible on the repository https://github.com/silicas/stealthy-Generative-Artificial-Networks. 

Compared to existing work, our approach presents a significant advancement as high-capacity models, particularly those built upon variational autoencoders and Generative Adversarial Networks, fail to produce stealthy content consistently, often resulting in noticeable errors or artifacts. We have also identified that existing reports of LSTMs, including those of vanhatakhurin2017semi and gondy2018semi, are misleading as they misrepresent the capabilities of LSTMs, claiming them to be as effective as Generative Adversarial Networks when in fact they are incapable of producing images on selected databases. Our work addresses these shortcomings, making a substantial contribution to the field.

Nevertheless, conventional drone fleets often struggle with operational deployments due to TFS's restrictive licensing terms. This issue renders commercial operations unfeasible, as individual drones require individual licenses, which are expensively priced. Furthermore, our study showcases the applicability and versatility of RepeatNet in real-world scenarios, exemplified by its successful deployment in a toy delivery application. With RepeatNet, drone manufacturers are empowered to eliminate the financial burden of TFS licenses, thereby accelerating their path towards commercial success. Yamgou originally established a foundational theorem for normal subgroups within the B-type Coxeter groups, which were of finite rank. Our theorem broadens the scope of this earlier result by removing the rank constraint and also extends it to include an 'almost normal' subgroup classification. Additionally, we prove an application related to the generation of groups. Specifically, we present a description of the smallest normal subgroup that can be formed from any finite B-type Coxeter group, which is generated by a single element. This investigation was inspired by an earlier challenge issued by Y. Guo. Our approach to solving this problem also allows us to challenge the continuation of a trend identified by Yamgou. Yamgou had noted that for an individual finite rank group, the normal subgroups can be effectively characterized through both logical and algebraic means. Our theorem reveals that in the broader context (of infinite rank groups), the characterization relies solely on algebraic means. Finally, we have also developed a related but independent result related to generating sets within group theory. Specifically, we have shown that for the special linear group SL(n, k) (where k represents a field, which in this case is finite)) the process of selecting a maximal set of elements with relatively prime lengths to form a generating set yields a relatively small normal subgroup, which is generated by this set of elements. This element-generated normal subgroup turns out to be the smallest possible one among all normal subgroups that can be generated by a single element. Ultimately, the calculation shows the order of this smallest normal subgroup generated by a single element to be very close to the order of the group as a whole. Specifically, we have shown that this smallest normal subgroup generated by a single element is such that its order is no more than n times the order of the group as a whole. Our theorem holds the potential of being extended to more general precision characteristics defined in terms of generators over fields with a finite characteristic. However, the other theorem related to generating sets that we have developed does not seem to be extendable in this direction since the other identity was established using a relatively simple calculation in a relatively small field, which was necessary for proving our other theorem. In order to prove our other identity, we had to employ a more sophisticated calculation in relatively high-dimensional fields, which was found to be highly non-regular. In other words, our other identity did not seem to be extendable because the other proof had clearly excluded the collection of fields with a finite characteristic from its scope of operation. We introduce a novel application of the exactly solvable at-least-one integer partition problem, the Set-Union Rucksack Issue. By adopting a model of connected covers, the original AIP is equivalently represented as a parallel machine problem, known as the Set-Union Machine Schedule (SUMS), to derive a formally well-defined version of the at-most-one integer partition problem. For previously indeterminate instances of the AIP, such as the famous "coin machines," we demonstrate the creation of corresponding SUMS instances with optimal solutions. Furthermore, our proposed algorithm, the Efficient Local Search for the Set-Union Rucksack (ELSS), is an improvement of the previous Best-First Search (BFS) solution, leveraging organizational and exploratory mechanisms to enhance performance. Elliptic curves are utilized to accelerate ELSS by efficiently calculating distances. We show that ELSS yields a substantial 202.9 times improvement in runtime over BFS, while producing equivalent or superior results in experiments. We also derive a new theoretical bound of approximation ratio of 0.4208 for the general (m, k)-partum AIP and its applications, including SUMS and BMCC, by analyzing the ELSS algorithm. We further derive a generic reduction from SUMS to BMCC with a factor of O(m/ k). Consequently, by applying the ELSS algorithm, we obtain a substantial 202.9 times improvement in runtime over the previous greedy algorithm, while achieving a superior approximation ratio of at least 0.4208 in BMCC solutions. The ELSS algorithm is distinguished from other local search methods by its efficient and effective mechanisms. In particular, we show that no algorithm can achieve a better approximation ratio than 0.5 for the (m, k)-partum AIP under the PTAS framework. Therefore, the existing theoretical bounds and approximations of the AIP imply that ELSS achieves the best-known results for both quality and efficiency in solving SUMS and its characteristic applications. This study proposes a motion planning strategy that accounts for both static and moving obstacles. A polygon-based algorithm is introduced to represent the spatial environment, which is divided into compact areas with uniformly defined safety margins. A robot path planner is developed to identify optimal routes within these regions, considering the varying obstacle environment. A predictive control system is designed to guide the robot through its planned route, maintaining a safe distance from moving obstacles. This approach leverages control barrier functions and is applicable to diverse robotic systems. Its effectiveness is demonstrated through simulation tests involving various robotic platforms, even when one of two onboard GPS devices fails. It's noteworthy that relying on two GPS devices isn't necessary for the method's implementation, as it's designed to be adaptive to any mapping or localization approach. Moreover, this framework is capable of withstanding unexpected events occurring either on the robot or due to environmental changes. The presented method successfully passes a robustness check, outperforming existing research in this area. The source code for this approach is publicly available at https://github.com/jayjayjay/safe_controlmbf. Its implementation is intended to inspire future research in environmental mapping, particularly in the areas of perception and sensor fusion. Despite the lack of a formal evaluation in this study, we plan to adapt our approach to more challenging environments, such as dense forests, in the future. A future work is outlined in Section 7 of this research. The presented research is an expansion of the authors' prior work (Bera et al., 2021) published in CDC 2021. The key variation between this study and the prior work is the method's ability to account for non-convex polyhedral environments, in contrast to the previous results which were confined to only convex geometries. In this paper, we establish the encompassing numbers of certain isomorphic classes of rings, including local rings with maximally commutative maximal ideals. We also determine the encompassing numbers of local rings with commutativity greater than 2. These findings lead to inequalities involving the ranks of such rings. We further apply our approach to examine the encompassing numbers of infinite rings, using the concept of 'n-divisibility' to analyze properties of arbitrary rings with well-defined encompassing numbers. These concerns have prompted the creation of open-source ITA systems to promote transparency. While open-source systems protect against stolen model exploitation, they still make data accessible to unverified users, subjecting it to potential interception by malicious actors. This paper examines current ITA systems, discussing their source status, user access, and data handling. By delving into these topics, we aim to stimulate discussion and guidance for open-source ITA communities on the practical implementation of organic resilience to protect their valuable contributions in the field of ITAs. We define a new class of links, called horizon saddle links, and investigate their properties. Specifically, we show that any horizon saddle link can be embedded in a dilation surface with four distinct components and possessing at least two Morse-Smale dynamics. Conversely, we find that any dilation surface with four parts and Morse-Smale dynamics is homeomorphic to a horizon saddle link. This equivalence establishes that horizon saddle links and a particular subclass of dilation surfaces are equivalent under homeomorphism. As additional context, we establish that hyperbolic horizon saddle links can be embedded within complement regions of knots in 3-space. Additionally, we demonstrate that horizon saddle links can take on up to four distinct colors under a classification system and utilize this fact to show that no horizon saddle links exist with two colors. Finally, by combining this discovery with a previously established equivalence between dilation surfaces and tricolorable links, we are able to conclude that no tricolorable links exist with two colors. To further organize these findings, we introduce a novel classification system for dilation surfaces and horizon saddle links within this text. Future predictions in human motion prediction, motion forecasting, and spatiotemporal learning involve generating a sequence of future frames detailing the subject's movement. Many current approaches suffer from two significant flaws: their failure to use the initial frames' full motion and relying too heavily on static features like camera views, which aren't indicative of a subject's true motion. We introduce a novel model called Motion Detail Capture using RNNs (MoDeRNN) that addresses these issues by incurring minimal additional computational costs. We discover that recent neural network-based systems lack sufficient temporal context and suggest integrating the subject's velocity and the last few captured motion frames to enhance the model's performance. We also introduce Capture Loss (C-Loss), which differentiates static and moving features to improve detailed prediction precision. Two benchmark tests using H3.6m and Amc2 datasets show that MoDeRNN outperforms the leading methods. Detailed results and analysis reveal that MoDeRNN significantly enhances model accuracy with minor additional computational costs by incorporating both initial frames' motion and a feature capture loss. We also demonstrate the effectiveness of velocity's role and the capture loss in our model design. We visually illustrate that the capture loss can distinguish beneficial and useless features, especially initial frames' features, which are crucial for the model's success. We also illustrate the subject's velocity's contribution to capture motion details. We hope the details in our paper and supplementary materials will facilitate further detailed prediction research. However, verifying the results of quantum algorithms is too laborious due to the enormous number of possible outcomes. To address this limitation, researchers have turned to the study of linear duration problems, which are a broad category of problems that can take varying times to solve on different computers. This requirements is known as efficiency and is a well-established concept in computer science. To bridge this gap, researchers have been exploring ways to validate quantum calculations based on this efficiency concept. In the field of computational biology, preserving the details of periodic structures is crucial for accurate representation. Typically, approaches relying on implicit neural representations (INRs) achieve state-of-the-art results in shape reconstruction, but they neglect the inherent periodicity present in many biological structures like cell membranes. We introduce Period-IOR, an INR model that integrates a periodic representation function to capture the distinct characteristics of periodic shapes like cells. We conduct numerous experiments, comparing Period-IOR to standard INRs and revealing significant improvements, particularly in modeling periodic cell shapes, through a combination of real-world cell image datasets and simulated scenarios. Our results indicate that Period-IOR achieves superior results and suggests its potential applicability to other domains featuring periodic patterns. Our study offers the first detailed, multi-wavelength snapshot of galaxies that are highly luminous in the infrared but relatively faint at optically brighter wavelengths. We employed a comprehensive dataset, including MIRI, NIRCam, and NICMOS observations from JWST, along with archival data from the Herschel Space Observatory and the Sloan Digital Sky Survey. By thoroughly analyzing the spectral energy distributions and determining infrared luminosities, we probed the depth and depth properties of this galaxy population. We discovered that highly obscured galaxies that are highly luminous in the infrared are predominantly dense, star-forming galaxies with extremely high dust content. We also found that galaxies with lower optical brightness but higher infrared luminosity generally have greater mass, dust content, and star formation rates compared to typical galaxies. As the largest Herschel survey, our use of prior data provided a deeper, top-down view of this galaxy population in the local universe, helping to reveal a critical piece of evidence for cosmic star formation history. We also had the opportunity to estimate a critical galaxy property: gas-to-dust ratios. Our research provides valuable insights into the diverse behaviors of interstellar dust at varying IR luminosity levels and optical depths. We actively contribute to current discussions about dust properties, astrophysical uncertainties, and their implications for understanding cosmic star formation rates. Moreover, our research offers initial insights into the evolution of massive star-forming galaxies from high-density environments. We believe that ongoing and future observations will help clarify key aspects of this galaxy formation process. This study identifies and assesses three types of ENSO phenomena: Central Pacific, Eastern Pacific and No-No-Neutral ENSO.  Unique ENSO varieties emerge when ENSO indices are grouped rather than treated as continuous values.  Specifically, this work uses the Dietrich et al ENSO classification, a physically motivated ENSO classification that classifies ENSO phenomena into Central Pacific and Eastern Pacific.  This study takes it further by creating new varieties of ENSO phenotypes by dividing the ENSO phases into three.  Initially, this study provides a brief overview of ENSO's impact on precipitation patterns.  It specifically analyzes and compares observed and predicted precipitation in South America and Africa for two ENSO varieties - Central Pacific and No-No-Neutral ENSO - using 30 years of satellite data and 85 years of model simulations.  The findings reveal that ENSO has a profound impact on precipitation in South America but not in Africa, with differing ENSO varieties exhibiting distinct patterns.  For example, in South America, the Central Pacific ENSO variety is associated with the highest precipitation in the western Amazon, while No-No-Neutral ENSO is characterized by lower precipitation in the same region, compared to other ENSO varieties.  These comparisons highlight the complex relationships between ENSO and precipitation, with implications for understanding and predicting ENSO's impact.  The study demonstrates that ENSO's predictions improve by acknowledging its diverse phenotypes rather than viewing it as a continuous phenomenon.  It also suggests that ENSO's classification could be used to develop region-specific and variable models that capture ENSO's complexity.  Ultimately, this study emphasizes the importance of understanding ENSO's complexity in order to mitigate climate variability and change.  The accompanying data includes model outputs and code for the simulations used in this study along with descriptions of the underlying physics and methods.  This study further highlights the utility of using multiple ENSO classification systems as a strategy for addressing and reducing uncertainty in ENSO research.  Lastly, it acknowledges that ENSO's complexity cannot be reduced, only be better characterized.  As such, this research aims to promote the development of additional and more accurate ENSO classification systems.  These classifications can be used in conjunction with one another in order to improve our understanding of ENSO's diverse range of phenomena and its many climate and geographical applications. Our research examines the kinetic dynamics of expanding polymer networks that undergo strain-hardening with light scattering. The kinetic model by Morse et al. was used to generate specific scenarios, which our experiment cannot produce solely based on light scattering measurements alone. To overcome this limitation, we combined the Morse model with the energy framework and conducted novel simulations of photopolymerization and light scattering during kinetic effects. The outcomes reveal that simple scattering measurements can distinguish affine and non-affine models due to their distinct behavior in the Tanada-Morse parameter space. Therefore, we propose that the affine model is insufficient and that the non-affine model provides a more accurate representation of the kinetic dynamics. Nevertheless, we acknowledge the presence of affine kinetic effects and propose the utilization of supplementary methods, such as fluorescence, to dissect the two types of behavior. Ultimately, this approach enables a more detailed understanding of the underlying mechanisms in complex polymer systems. In the field of computer vision, researchers often tackle a problem known as concept expansion, which involves encoding a broad label into a more detailed set of narrower terms to improve classification accuracy. This paper presents an innovative method called HyperExpan for concept expansion based on extended vector representation learning. Unlike traditional approaches that employ taxonomies, our proposal leverages the efficient structure of hyperbolic space. Furthermore, we incorporate a new depictions learning mechanism using a simple sample-dependent approach, which enhances concept expansion in this space. Through rigorous testing on challenging datasets from diverse fields, including medical, web, and product categories, our results demonstrate the superior performance of HyperExpan over existing state-of-the-art solutions. The repulsive nature of electric fields can make it challenging to accurately calculate the interaction energies of associated dimers, which interacts through non-covalent forces. This problem becomes more pronounced in dimers held together by van der Waals and hydrogen bonding, due to larger deformations. To tackle this challenge, researchers applied the counterpoise correction plus polarization model, which takes into account the effects of induced charges on the monomers and the interaction energy of the ground state. This approach corrected the interaction energies of the dimers in the S66 set, which includes 20 dimers that are sensitive to electric fields. Upon correction, the CP-C6 and CP-C12 components of the S66 dispersion coefficients were found to converge at high electric field strengths. Furthermore, the repulsive energies were successfully modelled using the Yukawa potential, which when combined with the CP-C6 component, provided an accurate description of the interaction energies across the S66 dataset. From the fitted Y-C6 parameters, the scaled electric field scale of the monomers was determined and found to correlate with experimental data. Additionally, the model was able to predict the energy barriers that need to be overcome for the rotation of amide groups in peptides. Upon deconvolving the energy components, it was found that dispersion played a dominant role in the interaction energies of the S66 set. Furthermore, the model was able to correctly predict the relative interaction energies of the dimers in the APTS2 test set. From the results, it was clear that the CP-C6 component dominated the interaction energies of the S66 set and APTS2 data. However, the inclusion of higher frequency induced polarisation terms via the DFT-D3 model significantly improved the accuracy and precision of the predicted interaction energies. Upon including DFT-D3, the prediction of the interaction energies of the APTS2 dataset showed negligible frequency dependence. To further demonstrate the effectiveness of the model, it was used to calculate the influence of water on molecular interactions by creating a model water-molecule interaction, which was similar to the model dimer interaction. Upon applying a counterpoise correction plus polarization model to the water-molecule interaction, the model was able to correctly predict the experimental dispersion coefficients within a 5% margin of error. From the results, it was clear that the high frequency induced polarisation terms played a crucial role in modelling molecular interactions. The emergence of cyber-physical systems has granted access to previously unobtainable data, enabling more precise scheduling and resource allocation. Despite this, the unpredictability of certain factors, such as random machine breakdowns or unpredictable worker absence, complicates efforts to fully schedule production and services. Various methods have been employed to model uncertainty, including probabilistic and fuzzy logic approaches, with the latter gaining prominence due to its ease of use and computational efficiency. However, the fuzzy logic method only accounts for one type of uncertainty, whereas industrial settings typically encounter multiple forms of uncertainty. Therefore, this paper aims to represent multiple types of uncertainty within the cyber-physical manufacturing framework. By utilizing a fuzzy logic approach to assign uncertainty levels to variables and operations, the uncertainty type is no longer assumed but instead is dynamically determined and displayed in an uncertainty matrix. This matrix, along with a modified version for five-fold symmetry, can be obtained from the system designer or planner, ensuring no additional computational burden on the cyber-physical system. The paper also illustrates this concept through integration with Industry 4.0 scheduling systems, showcasing a real-world example of a fuzzy-based uncertainty scheduling approach for a multi-product, multi-machine environment. The results show promising outcomes in terms of computational efficiency and quality of service delivery. The proposed framework is compatible with existing Industry 4.0 scheduling software and cyber-physical systems, providing a valuable tool for industrial applications. Lastly, the paper discusses the fields of application for this concept, including diverse non-deterministic ambiguity models and practical implications for scheduling in the presence of multiple types of uncertainty within cyber-physical manufacturing. A novel approach is developed to derive and analyze discrete versions of a nonlinear diffusion equation that operates on extensive Riemannian manifolds. Specifically, a semi-discrete approximation is developed for the nonlinear diffusion equation that uses a fully explicit method, and then a fully discrete version is developed for the equation's spatial and temporal resolution, utilizing tensor product constructions and finite difference schemes. Subsequently, a thorough analysis is conducted to establish the local and global existence of the solutions to these discrete equations, and to verify their convergence in various $L^p$ spaces. Moreover, it is demonstrated that the proposed schemes are stable in a specific context. To validate the theoretical findings, numerical experiments are performed and presented. Our methods' applicability is illustrated through an application to a nonlinear diffusion equation that solves the minimal surface problem, and to a model for tissue growth and repair, specifically the Eells-Simon diffusion equation and a growth model with boundary constraints. Our numerical results are found to be in line with the analytical solutions to these problems. Minus the minor discrepancies resulting from the approximation, The numerical findings are considered to be complete and accurate. Additional numerical experiments are performed and presented for the Eells-Simon diffusion equation and the growth model to showcase their properties and behavior over time. Moreover, a gradient restoration approach is developed and is effective in enhancing the image quality in various types of maps. In particular, a novel approach is developed for restoring gradients in vector fields, and a combination of this approach and nonlinear diffusion is found to be highly effective in improving image quality in various types of scalar-valued images. In conclusion, a comprehensive body of results is found to support the derivation and analysis of discrete nonlinear diffusion equations that operate on extensive manifolds. The approaches and findings are found to be versatile and applicable to a wide variety of equations and domains. The proposed algorithms are found to be simple, efficient, and accurate, and are suitable for use in a variety of practical applications. The numerical phase is found to be concluded successfully. Additional numerical experiments are performed and presented to demonstrate the properties and behavior of various minimal surface-based models. In particular, a combination of mean curvature flow and curvature prescription is found to be effective in generating complex and realistic minimal surface profiles. In another set of experiments, a growth model is found to be effective in modeling growth and morphogenesis processes in plants. In a separate phase, the derivation and analysis of discrete nonlinear diffusion equations that operate on higher-dimensional lattices are found to be concluded successfully. Radio sources come in various sizes, and certain observations benefit from distinguishing between subarcsecond and arcsecond resolution as the sources intersect with 21 cm hydrogen maps differently. In this study, we separate sources based on their angular extent and examine properties like radio luminosity and redshift, which indicate how luminous a source appears at a particular distance. We use two datasets with high-resolution observations, Future Radio Sky and an analysis dataset, and stack sources while accounting for scattering. The distinction between faint sources that are large or small in size holds across both datasets, and within each size group, the luminosity shows minimal correlation with redshift. In contrast, we observe a significant correlation between redshift and source size, as larger sources appear more luminous due to the scattering effect that is prevalent at greater distances. In a companion paper, we will investigate the size distribution of radio sources. These studies contribute to a thorough understanding of radio galaxies by acknowledging that source size and appearance depend not only on astrophysical factors, but also on the telescope used for observation. In a broader context, we discuss the implications of distinguishing between faint sources of different angular sizes in the context of cosmic ionization and quasar connectivity within the Universe. In particular, we explore a hypothesis that some radio galaxies may originate from compact black hole openings of giant quasars, which could explain the abundance of faint large sources relative to faint small sources, in line with expectations set forth by Kassiola and Stiernfelt (2022). In addition, we highlight the need for observations of radio sources to be adjusted based on their expected sizes and for the need of separate calculations of the expected number of sources within given areas as the sources' angular sizes change. Such adjustments will facilitate the collection of valuable data from forthcoming large-scale observation projects. In a future study, we intend to utilize our findings to limit the size of compact extragalactic objects that could host our Milky Way galaxy, and in another study, we will apply similar methods to analyze properties of compact near-Earth objects. In a broader cosmic context, we will also utilize our results to establish upper limits on the expected number of cosmic sources that could indicate the presence of life within Earth's surroundings. In particular, future observations should be adjusted in order to account for the expected abundance of sources of different angular sizes in a given volume, and for the expected size distribution of sources that are relevant for the astrobiological search for life within Earth's surroundings and in a broader cosmic context. Concealed Markov Models, a type of probabilistic process, govern the sequential masking of observations in a probabilistic space. They integrate the characteristics of Markov Processes and Hidden Markov Models, with applications extending to data-independent encryption methods. The concept can be generalized to higher-dimensional probabilistic spaces. CMs have been utilized to analyze quantitative data flows, a common context in practical scenarios. This work provides a formal framework for CMs by introducing the abstract concealed Markov model (ACMM), defined as the fixed-point of an operator in the category of probabilistic monads. To illustrate the framework's value, we derive a natural language definition for ACMMs from their algebraic representation. Furthermore, we show that CMs, specifically Markov Processes and Hidden Markov Models, can be characterized as instances of ACMMs by imposing specific conditions on their fixed points. Additionally, we examine the relationship between probabilistic monads and bisimulation, resulting in a dual interpretation of these concepts. As a practical example, demonstrating the potential advantages of working with algebraic representations over natural language definitions, we show that ACMMs can be utilized to describe the Cluney Digramm, a well-known application of HMMs. This example highlights the distinct properties of CMs, specifically the Cluney Digramm, by deriving relevant results through a methodical algebraic approach. Finally, we complement the introduced algebraic representation of CMs by providing a corresponding parser in Haskell. The parser demonstrates its capabilities through a series of example illustrations. Its primary accomplishment, however, lies in its capacity to aid in the manual construction of models, especially in the creation of HMMs, where difficult to parameterize upon manual observation, due to the presence of $\mathcal{O}(p^{|Q|})$ possible configurations in the base case of their induction. Several examples of successfully crafted CMs are provided and made accessible through the included demo at https://muesch-j.github.io/ACMM/EXM-pl.html. In addition to its practical utility, the parser also helps to elucidate the underlying concepts of ACMMs and their associated fixpoint theorems. The explanation is facilitated by the incorporation of semantic visualizations to supplement the algebraic representation of the parser. Robot motion planning that takes into account time varying obstacles presents a complex problem in many real-world applications. Traditional methods such as collision avoidance and spatial planning require a map of the environment to generate feasible paths, but in situations like autonomous driving or swarm robotics, accessing real-time data on the surroundings isn't possible. For these scenarios, an alternative approach is to create temporary barriers to avoid obstacles without needing an up-to-date map. However, planning barycentric spatial regions in 2D space is an NP-hard problem and a similar issue arises in 3D space. We introduce a new method based on Reeds and Shapoio's algorithm that efficiently creates a spatial region in a 2D dynamic environment by both preventing collisions and reducing travel distance while being simple to implement. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through simulations on a physical robot and show its efficiency on a 3D simulation environment under time varying obstacles. This study contributes towards addressing a long-standing question raised by Tsurumi in 2019: under what conditions does the steady Navier-Stokes equation remain stable in the sense of well-posedness for high-frequency perturbations? The Navier-Stokes equation's critical regime is particularly challenging, featuring a cascade of chaos and a lack of meaningful energy methods, making it less amenable to analysis. Nevertheless, by leveraging the interactions between different frequency components, this work demonstrates that the steady Navier-Stokes equation becomes ill-posed in certain critical Besov spaces characterized by an index greater than or equal to 5. This result underscores the necessity of imposing sensitive initial conditions or structure in the Navier-Stokes equation to ensure it remains well-defined. The method employed here relies on a novel combination of the Fourier analytic approach and a reduced model for the Navier-Stokes equation's low-frequency behavior, offering a fresh perspective that may be applicable to other partial differential equations in turbulent regimes. The computational aspects of this work are detailed in a separate note [arXiv:2103.14694]. By numerically solving the high-temperature generalization of the two-dimensional Bloch equation, we found that the magnon's speed displays a marked increase followed by a drastic shift in frequency as the wave's amplitude grows larger. We also discovered that the magnon's speed can be made to travel far beyond the speed of sound in these materials by enhancing the interactions between the waves, which is exemplified through its application in yield forces. Moreover, we found that the magnon's propagation can be significantly altered by connecting it to a nearby normal conductor. By exploring the underlying structure of the magnon's dispersion curve, we have identified and analyzed the various types of nonlinear behavior exhibited. Our research also suggests a means of controlling the magnon's frequency through the application of a magnetic field. By envisioning the magnon as a part of a mechanical system comprising two masses, we demonstrate that the magnon's dynamic relation to the applied magnetic field can be utilized for precise control over the mechanical wave. The possibility of achieving highly stable and fast changes to the magnon's frequency off-frequency and out-of-phase with respect to the applied field position positions us well for the development of a range of diverse types of magnonic interferometry and paramagnetism. This research introduces a couple of modifications for Loidreau's code-based cryptography system, aiming to elevate its security and operational efficiency. Initially, we propose the application of random column permutations to Loidreau's code-based encryption scheme, thereby increasing the encoder's computational load and rendering it more resistant to frequent attacks. We provide theoretical evidence as well as experimental results demonstrating the augmented scheme's resilience against several common attackers. Subsequently, we introduce a dual-cyclic version of Loidreau's code-based decryption algorithm to increase the cryptosystem's security and practicality. Specifically, we introduce a decryption algorithm utilizing the properties of dual-cyclic codes, allowing the same key to be employed for multiple codewords within the same message. We evaluate the efficacy of our modifications through both theoretical and practical assessments, showcasing the improved security and performance of the modified schemes compared to Loidreau's original code-based cryptography system. In particular, we illustrate the modified schemes' capacity to meet the NIST standard's recommendation for high-security systems, thereby ensuring that the increased key sizes resulting from our modifications are in line with industry best practices. All related experiments and assessments were conducted using the open-source PyMC code-based cryptography library. The information presented can serve as a useful guideline and inspiration for developers working on code-based cryptography systems, aiming to achieve high security levels like those required by the NIST. Finally, we outline several potential avenues for further research on code-based cryptography systems, including the exploration of alternative Loidreau's system modifications, the application of parallel computing techniques, and the potential for the modified schemes' parameters to be optimized through further experimentation. The corresponding modification guidelines and associated computational results for various code-based cryptography systems have been documented in Chapter 8 of my dissertation. Additionally, the PyMC code-based cryptography library, which was utilized in our computational investigations, is publicly accessible at https://github.com/kthakur22/PyMC. A recent study has demonstrated the existence of Pragmatic Attacks in FL and revealed that teachers are vulnerable to such assaults due to their role in the federated learning process. Furthermore, the study has developed a new category of Pragmatic Attacks called 'Practical Label Assaults', which target teachers with physical-world incentives, and successfully implemented it in the education vertical. The outer surface of the black stars is bounded by the octahedron's faces, while the vertices represent the locations where the imaginary gravitational potential becomes infinite. As a result, we were able to demonstrate the similar thermodynamic behavior of the black stars in the cavity, which shares the same characteristics as black holes in an asymptotically flat spacetime. Search engine optimization is an essential component of web development, as search engines directly impact website traffic. Consequently, various techniques have been developed to enhance webpage ranking on major search engines. However, these algorithms often employ supervised learning techniques, requiring extensive labeled data. Since webpage content can be vulnerable to noise from source labels, methods to counterlabel noise in optimization have been developed. Specifically, Google's Rich Snippet technology demonstrates noisy label risk during content optimization, highlighting the need for robust search engine optimization algorithms capable of adapting to label noise. This study proposes a new algorithm for search engine optimization that utilizes bag sampling and group-based loss to retrieve reliable features from noisy labels. In turn, our approach improves the overall effectiveness of search engine optimization. Our method outperforms existing baselines in both clean and noisy settings for various search engine benchmarks. Specifically, our technique achieves greater accuracy than others in ranking optimized rich snippets on four major search engine datasets, notably Google, Bing, Yahoo, and Google Knowledge Graph. Furthermore, our algorithm enhances retrieval efficiency by reducing data storage needs, thereby accelerating training and deployment. Interestingly, our technique also achieves faster training and testing times, reaching optimal performance faster, even exceeding human-level performance in optimal cases. In summary, our approach enhances search engine optimization effectiveness, performance, and efficiency across four major search engine benchmarks. In computer vision, various machine learning models have been developed to tackle complex tasks like image classification and segmentation. Graph Neural Networks have also been employed for similar tasks, utilizing image partitioning to simplify the problem. Nonetheless, working with limited labeled data can lead to overfitting in GNNs due to their sensitive nature. To address this issue, a method called pseudo-tagging for GNNs has been introduced, which utilizes a text-image cross-dataset to generate additional labeled information. The method composes multiple text features and fine-tunes a transformer model to produce image descriptions that closely match the given labels, thereby improving the quality of generated pseudo-tags. To optimize performance, a self-supervised strategy is implemented, allowing the model to utilize pseudo-tags as self-supervised images for further training. To complement this method, a global feature aggregation strategy is designed to enhance the resistance of GNNs to overfitting. The proposed approach has been successfully tested with labeled datasets of various sizes, outperforming existing state-of-the-art techniques. Notably, experimental results have shown that pseudo-tags can be accurately understood by humans at a semantic level, providing actionable insights that could be beneficial in various practical applications.
