Developing techniques to enhance model efficiency and reduce computational complexity becomes a crucial objective in the field. Research has successfully created logic-inspired models for tasks like linear regression and neural networks. Such models often rely on bit-based operations and take advantage of specialized, low-overhead instructions for computing with integers and booleans. They typically exhibit equivalent performance to their real-number counterpart while achieving substantial speedup. Despite their potential, logic-inspired models have lacked equivalent implementations for tasks involving logistic regression. Existing high-overhead instructions for implementing the logistic function make them less suitable. We present a new efficient representation of the logistic function, named "log2," which allows for a logic-inspired model that runs the task both faster and with comparable performance to existing approaches. Our paper introduces the first practical logic-inspired model for binary classification, which achieves a 3.73x speedup on V100 GPUs and a 4.72x speedup on P100 CPUs compared to a highly-optimized CUDA model. We also provide instructions on integrating the cross-entropy loss into the log2 representation, allowing for cross-dataset generalization across datasets like CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and SVHN. We demonstrate the feasibility of running the model on the Tensor Core-enabled Jetson Xavier NX mobile GPU. The emergence of topological surface states in twisted bilayer graphene is a testament to its unique properties. Despite displaying only one topological surface state below 5 K, we find through temperature and magnetic field variations that it's capable of adapting to two different temperature ranges. At low temperatures, the topological surface state transitions into a polycrystalline topological spin liquid, comprised of multiple smaller topological states, which survive up to 8 K. This phenomenon is attributed to the breakdown of long-range molecular orbital ordering induced by the magnetic field. Moreover, beneath 5 K, the application of an in-plane magnetic field transforms the single topological surface state into an amorphous topological spin liquid, characterized by the appearance of a broad distribution of underlying underlying one-dimensional topological channels. This phase exhibits similarities with the polycrystalline topological spin liquid, hence accounting for its observed temperature-dependent behavior. Our findings unlock new avenues for manipulating topological surface states in twisted bilayer graphene, relying on the interplay between temperature and magnetic fields. They also facilitate the adaptation of theoretical models developed for chiral Weyl semimetals to describe the underlying physics of topological spin liquids. Moreover, the concept of one-dimensional topological channels reveals that even at low densities, the underlying properties of matter are profoundly influenced by their dimensional characteristics. The lack of substantial advancements in increasing the speed of large-scale radio interferometers in recent decades presents an issue, particularly when it comes to scaling in proportion to the square of the number of antennas. In order to overcome this limitation, a strategy has been implemented to treat the antennas as point sources and reconfigure the way data processing considers their spatial arrangement, effectively achieving scaling proportional to the logarithm of the number of antennas. By doing so, it becomes possible to utilize a greater number of antennas without experiencing a corresponding increase in computational complexity, thus enabling the effective use of large arrays in fields such as radio interferometry. Two potential approaches have been devised to implement these improvements: the first involves rearranging the layout of the data to minimize computational requirements during processing, and the second entails dividing the antennas into smaller groups with overlapping ranges to increase the efficiency of data collection. By implementing these strategies, it is feasible to design or optimize systems with up to 1000 or more antennas that can execute all necessary processing tasks within 10 minutes or less, even in the presence of atmospheric interference. In practice, this optimization strategy could be incorporated into a variety of systems by modifying the antenna controller software, and subsequent evaluations of an experimental system have confirmed its performance advantages under real-world conditions. The recommended implementation strategy, in which the algorithm is split into distinct components with independent processing paths, accommodates scalable parallel processing of each component but fails to improve proportionally with increasing array size when executed on a whole, effectively limiting its performance gains to about 7 orders of magnitude despite utilizing up to 100 GPU processors. In order to overcome this limitation, a more systematic approach to array construction has been implemented in which the algorithm and array are simultaneously optimized in tandem, effectively removing the dimensionality disparity and enabling the creation of a scalable infrastructure. The resulting optimization strategy has demonstrated remarkable scalability, in which every added GPU processor in proportion enables equivalent gains in array size, thereby enabling the effective creation of arrays of arbitrary large sizes. The incorporation and evaluation of this optimized processing strategy across a multitude of scientific disciplines have yielded numerous significant improvements in technological proficiency metrics and are discussed in detail throughout this series of publications. In massive machine-type communications (mMTC), granting numerous users low-power connections is facilitated by orthogonal waveforms, but these are prone to degradation under high density conditions. Conversely, non-orthogonal waveforms offer greater spectral efficiency with low interference effects, although they typically require more complex receivers. To harness the benefits of both, a novel approach involves combining orthogonal and non-orthogonal waveforms in a hybrid system. However, the major challenge lies in designing non-orthogonal patterns that can effectively distinguish between users under various channel conditions. To address this issue, a new genetic algorithm is proposed, which can efficiently derive narrowband channel characteristics and allocate non-orthogonal patterns to users with high values of the minimum mean squared error (MMSE) angle components. Our results indicate that this approach offers improved performance relative to existing methods. Moreover, a related optimization problem related to the amount of interference between users is formulated as a mixed-integer optimization problem and solved using a genetic procedure. The results of extensive simulations demonstrate that the newly-designed non-orthogonal patterns excel in terms of joint detection rate, even when incorporating orthogonal patterns for complex channels. Notably, the approach allows for the identification of compact, easy-to-interpret patterns that are largely invariant to changing environmental conditions. These patterns are also highly adaptable to different channel states and can be used to derive more efficient, non-orthogonal waveforms in various settings. A corresponding testbed implementation validates the effectiveness of the designed patterns in low-power connections. Various simulation techniques used to model water in air have distinct implications on dynamic processes, but these models often differ minimally when observing steady-state conditions. To assess their accuracy, we analyze the validity of these methods through a thermodynamic analysis, evaluating whether they adhere to established thermodynamic principles as air interacts with the sea-water interface. Upon reviewing the existing methods, we identify considerable inconsistencies and recommend developing models that effectively integrate thermodynamic changes to accurately represent air-dynamic and thermodynamic changes. Furthermore, we introduce two new methods: one that incorporates a combined thermodynamic-statistical approach and another based on the advanced micro-scale model of the water droplet surface. We simulate scenarios such as sea-surface cooling, sea-surface cooling with precipitation, and contrasting atmospheric conditions with precipitation. Results demonstrate that the methods yielding higher entropy are essential for effective humid air simulations, while models failing to coherently adhere to thermodynamic principles are not suitable for air modeling. To address the limitation of the large-scale micro-models, we develop an alternative method that combines the droplet surface with a quasi-uniform air-gas interface. This new model maintains the water droplet surface's intricate properties while allowing it to efficiently couple with external atmospheric conditions. It also opens up possibilities for using biological systems as model systems to study various physical phenomena. Networks of neurons with randomly distributed biophysical parameters can model cognitive processes and neural disorders effectively. Randomly extending the maximum axonal length in these networks replicates brain atrophy in diseases such as Alzheimer's. However, the method used to generate axon lengths significantly affects the functional properties of neural networks. We investigated the impacts of different extent distributions on the functional organization of large neuronal networks. We found that as the deviation of axon lengths from the mean increased, neural networks transitioned from an organized critical state to a disorganized high-conduction state. We observed that axon lengths beyond a certain point caused the neural codes in these networks to fail. Interestingly, axon length distributions in primate cerebral cortices, known for their efficient conduction properties, are not found in neural networks that model the frontal and parietal cortices. These findings suggest that extensive brain atrophy might be a consequence of impaired neural communication rather than brain degeneration. We propose the use of axon length distributions that maintain neuronal networks in an organized critical state for modeling cerebral cortex degeneration. Such networks can facilitate the study of the neural basis of cognition and provide insights into potential therapeutic strategies for cortical degenerative diseases. We propose the use of axon length distributions in neural networks, which maintain neuronal systems in an organized critical state, for modeling cerebral cortex degeneration. This approach enables researchers to study the neural basis of cognitive functions and failed neural codes in diseases such as Alzheimer's. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that neutral point distributions can maintain neuronal systems in an organized critical state, thus allowing for effective modeling of frontal and parietal cortex regions. We suggest that such networks, capable of efficient neural communication, might be essential for modeling the cerebral cortex successfully. Information about neural networks, generated using the software Neuron, along with related image processing, can be found at https://github.com/tunapanda/CriticalAxons. The Generalized Inverse Fisher's Confidence (GIFC) region has been a highly valued statistical region for analyzing parameter estimates and has various applications in assessing the quality of estimators. This paper develops a novel method to determine if GIFC certification is achieved. The proposed method establishes a connection between GIFC certification and the distribution of a statistical test's power. This leads to a new approach for calculating GIFC certification, referred to as the data spectrum approach. The efficacy of this method is demonstrated through theoretical analysis and practical application. The results show that the proposed method can effectively calculate GIFC certification in both simple and complex scenarios. This method is available for practical use in relevant software packages. The paper also showcases its practical application in evaluating the performance of two distinct estimators of the same parameter in a simulated scenario. The results reveal that, out of one hundred simulated data sets, conventional methods fail to achieve GIFC certification for one estimator, while the proposed data spectrum approach successfully calculates GIFC certification for both estimators. The practical application of the proposed method is further illustrated through its use in evaluating the sensitivity of parameter estimates to missing data within a simulated missing data framework. The proposed method emerges as the most effective method for determining GIFC certification. The paper concludes with suggestions for future research. The relevant software for the paper can be accessed at https://github.com/jianhuiyang/GIFCdataSpectrum. The paper's supplements can be found at https://doi.org/10.11864/jass.2022.04.001.README. We explain its foundations and present results based on 200 GeV Au+Au collisions in Ultra-Relativistic Heavy-Ion Collisions simulations, showing that 3D flow instruments' signals heavily depend on the individual's collision structure and Equation-of-State characteristics. The outbreak of COVID-19 worldwide has prompted healthcare systems to leverage the potential of machine learning models to forecast future infections based on the progression of the disease. However, the application of ML models in this context poses significant risks to individual privacy, given the availability of rare disease data. To address this concern while contributing to the global fight against COVID-19, we introduce an innovative and privacy-respecting approach to training temporal survival machine learning models. Our strategy adapts the concept of adversarial training to develop predictive models for COVID-19 patient data without compromising confidentiality. This method is particularly crucial when working with institutions that handle sensitive patient information. We have successfully tested various adversarial training techniques, both with numerical labels and using soft labels, and evaluated their effectiveness using data from two hospitals. The results suggest that using an adversarial decoder can lead to improved data proxy quality when simulating labels using an adversarial generator, and that using soft labels rather than numerical labels can further enhance performance. Ultimately, this approach enables accurate and efficient COVID-19 data simulation for healthcare institutions seeking to deploy machine learning models without compromising patient confidentiality. The simulated data are available for further research through the following link: https://github.com/kshay/covid-19_data_simulation. The code for our approach is hosted on GitHub at https://github.com/kshay/adv-ksnet. This research has been funded by the the Fulbright program, the FAPESP grant, and the Serrapilheira Foundation. A related technical report more comprehensively outlining the methodology and associated computations can be found at https://doi.org/10.5281/terng.unicamp.edu/20213. To the best of our knowledge, this work provides the first systematic analysis of the adversarial training techniques used in this context. Moreover, due to the growing prevalence of ML model deployments, where even medical data is now exposed to machine learning models, we highlight the importance of adopting a new deployment culture that prioritizes data privacy above all else. In recent years, the need for effective decision-making in complex communication systems has become more pronounced due to the numerous variables and interconnected components involved. This need is aimed at overcoming challenges such as optimal power allocation, efficient multi-user coding, and precise latency estimation. However, the complexity of these tasks is characterized by high-dimensional non-linear problems that are difficult to solve using conventional methods without compromising performance and stability. This issue is even more severe in decentralized systems where limited local information is available to individual components. To address these challenges, a novel decentralized approach using Graph Neural Networks for optimization is presented. This method leverages its deep learning capabilities to tackle various communication systems' problems by incorporating problem-specific constraints into the loss function. Several key factors are investigated in this context, such as network convergence speed, the impact of edge connections, and the feasibility of solving distinct problems using the same GNN model. This study provides a comprehensive foundation for applying deep learning techniques to communication systems, paving the way for extensive expansion into diverse wireless transmission systems. The experimental results validate the effectiveness of the proposed solutions and outperform the current standard approaches in terms of performance and stability. This research is available on arXiv. The pre-trained models and code can be accessed via repositories on GitHub. A related demo video is also provided. Furthermore, the findings and recommendations derived from this investigation have practical implications for wireless communication technology and bandwidth scarcity mitigation. In addition, the approach can be adapted for real-time problem-solving in communication systems. A related tutorial incorporating some of these concepts is also available. In contemporary society, the threat of violence poses a significant concern, and violent deaths, particularly murders, have become a major issue in many countries. Research focusing on murder rates has revealed that they are influenced by diverse factors, but the underlying dynamics remain underexplored. This study aims to identify the latent factors giving rise to murders in an insular city in central Brazil, Goias. We analyzed murder data from the state's capital, Goias, over a 13-year period spanning from 2002 to 2014, utilizing the wet score approach to discover underlying patterns. We found that murders in this city are largely consistent with Poisson distribution, and cluster analysis revealed the presence of seven clusters, some of which showed increasing or decreasing trends. We observed four distinct time-based clusters, revealing three independent latent factors, which helped identify the most violent periods and areas. We discovered that the state's murder rates were influenced by three primary factors: irregular socioeconomic conditions in slum areas, high concentrations of firearms, and inadequate law enforcement presence. We observed that the murder situation in Goias underwent a distinct transition from 2008 to 2009, characterizing three violent sub-periods. One of the factors, capturing the presence of organized crime, emerged in Goias during the period from 2005 to 2008. We found that the proposed approach can efficiently uncover complex dynamics of high murder cities and recommend its application to similar contexts. Furthermore, the developed method can be adapted for studying other social issues with geographical data, such as air pollution in cities. Nonetheless, the presence of geographical variables in the analysis did not significantly contribute to explaining murder dynamics in Goias. Current optimization methods used for training neural networks over large datasets do not take into account the quality of the samples, which can vary dependent on factors such as the label encoding and data distribution. As a result, these methods may achieve improved results in non-standard scenarios but underperform when dealing with well-known datasets such as MNIST. The current best practices involve running optimization methods in an unsupervised manner to adapt to the dataset, but an alternative approach could be to develop a sample-aware ascent method that directly responds to the variability of the dataset. The objective of this paper is to facilitate further research in this direction by providing a comprehensive analysis of the effects of sample variability on stochastic gradient ascent and proposing a novel method called Europhor that achieves accelerated gradients while also being robust to noise and adaptable to challenges. Theoretical comparisons with existing optimization methods have shown that Europhor outperforms standard techniques, while empirical results on MNIST dataset have shown that Europhor successfully achieves these robust and adaptive properties. By facilitating a thorough examination of the sun's composition and possible hidden mass, the experiment delves into the mysterious relationship between the sun's (anti-)matter and the dark matter found within the earth. We will also explore the potential implications and challenges associated with the most groundbreaking findings, particularly those related to anomalous neutrino signals, with an approach optimized for frequent discoveries. We have now taken into consideration recent scientific developments within the fields of solar physics and dark matter research as we evaluate various feasible explanations for non-fermi dark matter in the sun. We also propose an alternative to the established solar modulus as the primary dark matter component within the earth and suggest possible search areas for this particle. We have found, however, that novel'solar anomalies' with masses below geV would leave telltale signs within the earth's composition, in conflict with existing data. We investigate a recently introduced class of systems capable of producing
spike-regular patterned waveforms with complex dynamics. The recurrent
interaction of these systems, involving a combination of linear and nonlinear
mechanisms with random elements, is studied in detail. Key characteristics,
such as the existence of two equilibrium states and the occurrence of Hopf bifurcations, are investigated mathematically. In addition, we analyze how these systems can generate intricate spatiotemporal patterns, including primary and secondary limit cycles in phase space. The findings are further validated by numerical simulations, which also evaluate the effects of varied parameter settings on dynamic behavior and offer insights into experimental approaches to exploring these systems. The research showcases examples of these systems in the form of simplified neural networks. Lastly, we examine the potential for these systems to produce diverse types of spike pattern sequences. The corresponding waveforms are assessed and evaluated based on their correspondence to biological neurons. Some examples of generated waveforms are provided and made accessible online for practical applications. The corresponding source code is also available for download on GitHub. Lastly, we offer some promising avenues for further research and future investigation. The results were further tested in USA. To accelerate the development of robotic grasping skills, top-notch training data with precise ground truth is essential. Although current datasets with grasp information have helped contribute to breakthroughs, they fall short in several areas: first, they don't encompass a diverse range of objects despite the crucial role objects play in grasping techniques, second, they don't account for the intricacies of real-world environments and third, they don't offer comprehensive depth information vital for successful grasping. In response to these limitations, a new dataset called DexGraspNet has been created, distinguished by its focus on simulated objects and comprehensive depth information. Additionally, a companion tool was developed to streamline the process of expanding DexGraspNet to include various objects, allowing the dataset to be expanded through user feedback. With a potential of upscaling simulation technologies, the DexGraspNet dataset has the promising potential of becoming a valuable resource in robotic grasping. A novel approach has been developed for creating motion-adjusted 4D MR images. By incorporating a motion compensation technique into a T2-weighted turbo spin-echo sequence, it's possible to significantly reduce respiratory variations without utilizing respiratory gating. This technique enables high-quality images to be produced in a single breathhold, and subsequent reconstruction methods ensure accurate motion compensation. A proposed reconstruction strategy aims to minimize blurring caused by respiratory motion, and it incorporates a biharmonic model to regularize the solution. To account for variations in scanning position, a task-oriented score matching algorithm is used. Results from abdominal scans of 30 participants demonstrate the technique's effectiveness, and comparative studies with conventional 4D MRI methods reveal its superiority in terms of image clarity and resolution. This unencumbered imaging process allows for the creation of detailed, wide-scale body MR images. A demonstration web platform, at https://mtram.iq.ucla.edu/, provides interactive access to the 4D MR images. This technique has many potential applications, including the enhancement of MR-based imaging methods for quantifying fat mass and metabolic rates. A related patent was filed in 2021. We introduce InDistill, a fast and efficient framework for reducing large models, preserving their key computational elements and data flows through specialized tools, such as FocusDistill for pinpointing key components and FixDistill for repairing inaccuracies. By splitting model training into two distinct phases, one for minimizing disturbances and another for fine-tuning, InDistill effectively condenses the learning process into just a few hours. InDistill's effectiveness is showcased in accelerating model condensation on a diverse range of tasks, including image classification, word prediction, and generative modeling. We found InDistill cuts through noise and reaches near-identical performance to the full-sized model, outperforming other distillation strategies with improved model training speed, higher peak AUC, and lower average loss. Two submersion functions from the plane to the line can be topologically equivalent, implying the topological equivalence of their foliations. However, there is no uniform criterion to assess this relationship. We'll analyze linear-like submotions, a subset of submersions, to understand their role in maintaining or altering topological relationships between foliations. We'll develop a set of necessary and sufficient conditions to ensure the topological equivalence of linear-like submotions and use these principles to establish a new criterion for the topological equivalence of foliations based on submotions' linearity in certain directions. We find that non-homeomorphic linear functions have distinct foliations and that adjusting these functions by constant values doesn't alter the topological equivalence of their foliations. Additionally, we demonstrate that the topological equivalence of linear submotions is a determining factor in the topological equivalence of their foliations and that this relationship is only altered by foliations with isolated singular points. We'll also show that the space of linear submotions with fixed coefficients is compact and that the topological Equivalence of linear submotions is determined by their Residua. Using these principles, we can separate the spaces of linear submotions based on their foliations and show the existence of distinct topological Equivalence of these functions and their foliations. Finally, we begin to explore the implications of introducing nonzero rotation in the plane on the topology of foliations, a topic we will continue to investigate in a forthcoming paper. A plan is presented in the conclusion, outlining a strategy to extend these principles to all submisions in a separate work. Furthermore, the conclusion concludes by highlighting important applications of these principles, which will be explored in depth. The present paper primarily focuses on understanding and establishing a new theory of topological equivalence of linear submotions and their foliations, which lays the groundwork for a broader theory of topological submotions and their foliations. In a long-awaited follow-up project, we will apply these principles to resolve several outstanding enigmas in the fields of topological dynamics and differential equations. The theory of topological equivalence, initially developed for linear systems, is remarkably more complex for nonlinear ones, and in this work, we will make significant progress toward addressing two long-standing puzzles: first, describing the criteria for topological equivalence of nonlinear submotions in plane, and second, clarifying the relationship between the topological equivalence of foliations and the properties of their corresponding submotions. However, these assumptions may not accurately represent systems such as arid landscapes where water scarcity and long-term adaptation influence plant behavior. We developed a detailed plant dynamics model incorporating non-local foraging, competition, and environmental factors like rain and temperature. The model takes into account plants' responses to daily changes and annual adaptation periods and accounts for their spatial behavior through a combination of movement and growth factors. We ran simulations to analyze the model's behavior, utilizing statistical tools to understand the complex interactions within the system. We discovered that non-local foraging can significantly impact arid land ecosystem dynamics, leading to the coexistence of different plant species within these areas. Our approach provides a practical framework for studying complex systems like non-linear, intra-action based plant interactions, and offers insights into understanding intra-action based movement principles. It achieves this by using randomized mappings, known as "sketches," to facilitate fast detection of top-supported vectors. Research into its robustness has been conducted, including studies on its resistance to attackers manipulating the vector distribution. Previous studies have shown that the algorithm is highly susceptible to adaptive attackers who can select and modify vectors based on analysis of previous sketches. In an attempt to strengthen the algorithm's adaptability resilience, we investigate the minimum number of bits required for the binary hyperplane distribution to resist adaptive attackers. Our findings provide tight lower and upper bounds for this resilience metric, and it turns out the non-adaptive minimum required outperforms the current state-of-the-art distribution by a logarithmic factor. It is also shown that the algorithm's adaptability resilience is closely related to the problem of finding the minimum-support vector, and an extension of this problem's well-known lower bound is established. These results offer the first theoretical characterization of the algorithm's adaptability resilience, paving the way for potential practical improvements. We investigate how to maximize income when there are third-party brokers or intermediaries.  Traditionally, economists study situations where transactions involve only the buyer and seller, and when intermediaries are absent, the strategy of offering the best possible terms (price and terms of exchange) is ideal.  However, when intermediaries are involved, implementing such a strategy doesn't always guarantee optimal outcomes.  For example, even if a intermediary adds value by reducing costs to the buyer, they might actually harm the seller, causing overall income to suffer.  To address this challenge, we develop mathematical models that help determine optimal terms of exchange when brokers are involved and propose two specific strategies - the Maximum Income Pricing (MIP) and Maximum Income Pricing via intermediaries (MIP-i), for situations where intermediaries are indispensable and can be bypassed respectively.  We conduct thorough explorations to establish key properties for MIP and MIP-i and also present algorithms to implement them.  Our research further extends to various common scenarios to demonstrate practical applications.  Our theoretical findings are confirmed by a range of experimental tests.  We implement the MIP-i algorithm in Python, a playable version can also be found at https://github.com/NimaiC/dealer-finder/ [accessed: July 2024].  We believe the techniques developed here have potential to help design optimal exchange mechanisms in a wide variety of settings.  Moreover, a related issue concerning finding the best strategy in a competitive environment is also investigated.  While the problem of maximizing income is studied here, our general approach can be applied to related optimization issues in this context.  It is noteworthy that the techniques developed here assume that participants' behavior follows logical and logical principles. A generalized framework for rapidly deploying robust structures utilizes tensioned cables as the fundamental structural component. This basic structure can be adapted to various applications such as supporting loads in three-dimensional spaces, navigating challenging environments, and maintaining stability in unstable conditions. Our robotic system leverages the inherent flexibility and resilience of the structure to effectively recover from disturbances and maintain its configuration. By simultaneously manipulating three robotic arms with grasped objects, our system efficiently transfers forces to effectively move, position, and orient itself to restore the structure's stable state. To achieve these complex tasks, we developed multiple innovative strategies, including a planning algorithm based on a high-level task command that utilizes a new reconfiguration method, a predictive model to improve real-time decision-making, a planning model that accounts for the constraints of grasped objects, and a real-time control strategy integrated with external force control to ensure stability and efficiency. Through extensive simulation tests, the effectiveness and practicality of our planning and control methods were demonstrated. Finally, the effectiveness of our strategy was verified by conducting actual experiments on a physically simulated environment and a real robotic system. Our findings open up opportunities for the widespread application of external force control in structural manipulation. Additionally, our project has potential real-world applications in fields like healthcare, search and rescue, exploration, and other complex situations. One of the main limitations of our strategy is that it may not be suitable for tasks that require precision due to the generation of vibrations caused by external forces. Monocular depth estimation has been used to enhance various computer vision tasks with unsupervised pre-training methods. These approaches have been adopted in tasks such as semantic segmentation, despite the depth estimation itself not directly relating to the segmentation. This work aims to verify the claim that depth pre-training is beneficial for segmentation by examining its actual impact on a popular benchmark, PASCAL VOC. Our study shows that the benefits of depth pre-training are more significant when using outdated segmentation architectures, but become negligible with the deployment of modern, high-performing models. Furthermore, we suggest that depth pre-training can be seen as a signal for selecting the most suitable training objectives and data augmentation techniques to improve segmentation performance. This involves prioritizing objectives and augmentations that induce spatial coherence and regularity. With this altered perspective, we were able to develop a more effective method for choosing objectives and augmentations, which was applied on PASCAL VOC and the Cityscapes benchmark. Our results indicate that this approach yields better outcomes than the traditional depth pre-training technique. The code for our method is written in PyTorch and can be found at https://github.com/alibaba/DemoPyTorch. By complementing the method with additional supervisions, we were able to achieve a significant boost in performance, with the corresponding model submissions made available on https://www.cityscapes-dataset.org/. The statistical property of effective deduction for correlation measures was previously defined to account for the average level of information exchange between pairs of variables with a specific correlation. It was initially demonstrated that a certain variable order measure, van der Waerden's coefficient, exhibits zero effective deduction. This study aims to prove that another well-established measure, Kendall's tau, also has zero effective deduction. To achieve this, we first establish that Kendall's tau can be calculated as a weighted sum of individual binary interaction measures, where the weighting depends on the joint probability distribution of the variables. We further show that each binary interaction measure lacks effective deduction, which ultimately leads to the conclusion that Kendall's tau does not convey any additional information beyond the collective contribution of its underlying binary interactions. This new finding highlights a novel distinction between measures that focus solely on individual binary interactions, such as Pearson's rho, and those that do not, like Kendall's tau. It also facilitates a deeper exploration of the subtle correlations within the data by enabling the evaluation of individual binary interactions in addition to the overall measure. Moreover, our results provide a valuable framework for using Kendall's tau to develop strategies for interpreting statistical information through symmetric measure extensions. This study provides essential guidelines for interpreting Kendall's tau coefficients, which have been widely applied in various fields. We present numerical illustrations to demonstrate how our results can be effectively used in practical scenarios. Moreover, we apply these findings to two real-world datasets, which were previously used in actual study scenarios, to demonstrate their practical implications. The study's conclusions are also extended to another widely employed coefficient, Spearman's rho. While both Kendall's tau and Spearman's rho are considered to capture variable order relationships without ambiguity, our study reveals that Spearman's rho actually has non-zero effective deduction, unlike Kendall's tau. However, we do identify a certain probabilistic dependence structure for which Spearman's rho might appear to convey some information beyond its underlying binary interactions; this distinction further emphasizes the significance of our theoretical findings. The study's conclusions are further extended to another important variable order measure, van der Waerden's coefficient, which was previously known to exhibit zero effective deduction. However, our study provides an alternative characterization of this measure by showing that it lacks effective deduction at both the overall and binary interaction levels. This new understanding leads to the development of a distinct class of measures that share a common property with van der Waerden's coefficient. This study proposes a novel concept for edge cognitive networks in the automotive sector by incorporating the principles of decentralized optimization and game theory. The primary objective is to design a dynamic and adaptive structure for edge cognition that can learn and generalize from data patterns while minimizing sensitivity to individual components. The framework features a decentralized architecture where distinct modules work together to maintain overall system integrity. The training process of these modules is grounded in a general loss function and is robust to the loss of any module without compromising the overall performance. The proposed approach ensures that no sensitive information is exchanged during the training process, thereby maintaining user privacy. The theoretical efficiency of the proposed model is analyzed and validated through empirical testing. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed concept in maintaining privacy and achieving better generalization capabilities compared to existing methods. Furthermore, the computational overhead can be adjusted according to specific computational requirements, thereby providing an additional layer of control for managing edge cognition at the network level. The proposed concept has the potential to address the core challenges of edge cognition, including trade-offs between performance, generalization, privacy, and efficiency. This paper introduces a novel conceptual framework, Euler Significance Surfaces, to analyze three-dimensional geometric shapes with varying significance levels. By extending the one-to-one correspondence between the standard normal distribution and three-dimensional coordinates to a distribution of any type, we derive the ES Scales, a set of axes where the distribution is rendered as a three-dimensional geometric shape, characterized by distinct significant features. We derive a set of universal conditions to identify these significant features, reducing to the conventional ones when dealing with the standard normal distribution. We illustrate the efficacy of ES Scales and Euler Significance Surfaces with real-world data sets, including its application in forensic analytics. Additionally, we outline a potential extension of this work to develop a comprehensive approach to dimensionality reduction across various statistical distributions. The methodology is made accessible through the R package esr. Further methodology and data are also provided as supplementary materials. The work is ultimately aimed at enhancing understanding of data by translating distributions into three-dimensional geometric shapes that are both analytically and computationally defined. The mathematical derivations within this work are intended to stimulate innovative applications in statistics. The computational implementations, in turn, aim to transform practice into a more seamless and effective art. The overarching objective is to harmonize the distinctive approaches of statisticians and data scientists. In our Holling-Tanner predator-prey framework, we incorporate a prey population model that incorporates an Allee effect, specifically a minimum population threshold beyond which growth accelerates. We explore how the predator's olfactory acquisition rate is affected when the predators partially rely on the prey's emitted cues. By analyzing key population values, we have found that when the predators rely entirely on the prey's cues, they always successfully deplete the prey population. In contrast, when the predators partially rely on the prey's cues, several predator population patterns are possible, including nonexistence, fixed points, Bogdanov-Takens bifurcations, homoclinic orbits, double Hopf bifurcations, and periodic orbits. Notably, our findings suggest that when the predators partially rely on the prey's cues, the prey population can avoid being completely depleted. Using numerical simulations, we demonstrate these potential outcomes in a logarithmic parameter space. Lastly, we verify these results using a high-performance computer equipped with Velocity software. Overall, our analysis suggests that when the predators partially rely on the prey's cues, the prey population has a higher likelihood of sustainability. This paper builds upon a previous study, investigating the efficient computation of faces within a convex polytope at its boundary using the Aspect Pivot (AP) method. Initially, the study found that the AP method, when applied to a general simplicial cone, yielded an O(n!) optimal computational complexity in worst-case scenarios. Subsequently, this is followed by an improved analysis under a linear iteration limit, thus demonstrating the feasibility of achieving a manageable computational complexity through reductions of approximately n! with constant factors. To achieve this, the study integrates duality principles from linear optimization, thus facilitating a significant reduction in computational complexity, ultimately resulting in an O(n^2 ^ (d n) ) optimal computational complexity in worst-case scenarios for both dual and primal polytopes. Furthermore, the study illustrates the practicality of the AP method's efficiency through its successful application in computing all indistinguishable pairs of (1, -1)-extremal faces within the coordinate simplex up to a dimension of n = 20. Ultimately, the study proposes future enhancements, potentially yielding a nearly efficient O(n^3) optimal computational complexity in worst-case scenarios. Nevertheless, these optimizations remain theoretical considerations for now, subject to the outcome of forthcoming experiments.  Ultimately, the study culminates with the proposal of a future model allowing for the near real-time computation of face sets across various polytope types using the AP method, thus realizing Professor Nemat-El-Haouze's 2017 challenge to achieve the "instantaneous determination of all faces of a polytope". The measurement of the top quark production cross section in t/tj events at the LHC relies heavily on an accurate determination of the top quark's total cross section in purely hadronic final states. Among the main factors affecting this accuracy are off-shell corrections to the top quark production. To assess their impact, we calculate total hadronic cross sections for the leading quantum corrections affecting top quark production in both t/tt and t/jj events. The application of these corrections to the measurement of the top quark's cross section in t/tj events reveals a necessary modification of the extraction value by about 10% in both leading orders. To facilitate the calculation of these corrections in future studies, we outline the approach using the numerical method of MadGraph5\_aMC@NLO. Additionally, we cross-check our results with an independent calculation based on helicity amplitudes. The interpretation of our findings suggests that, in order to achieve a level of precision of about 10%, the consideration of non-resummed off-shell external corrections to the top quark production in the framework of QCD is necessary. Given the limited theoretical understanding of these corrections, a reliable determination requires the accurate inclusion of next-to-leading order QCD corrections in the framework of parton collinear physics as implemented in the numerical method of MadGraph5\_aMC@NLOSky. With the introduction of these complete next-to-leading order QCD corrections to the top quark production in the framework of the numerical method of MadGraph5\_aMC@NLOSky, the extraction value can then be sufficiently precise, allowing for a contribution analysis of leading quantum corrections to the top quark production in the framework of the numerical method of MadGraph5\_aMC@NLOSky. The application of these corrections to the measurement of the top quark's cross section in the framework of the numerical method of MadGraph5\_aMC@NLOSky reveals a non-significant impact of leading quantum corrections to the top quark production in the leading order and next-to-leading order on the determination value. The application of these corrections to the measurement value also reveals a significant influence of leading quantum corrections to the top quark production in the next-to-next-to-leading order. The calculation of the determination value can also be carried out with the numerical method of MadGraph5\_aMC@NLOSky by including the influence of leading quantum corrections to the top quark production in the framework of the numerical method of MadGraph5\_aMC@N

Our research focuses on the security of facial recognition technologies and their ability to evade detection. We analyzed the resilience of Zero-shot face anti-spoofing models that use a Transformer architecture, particularly those using patch-based input representations. To gauge model performance, we created a comprehensive and varied dataset of artificial spoofing attacks that mimic real-world applications. Our findings indicate that high accuracy in lab settings do not necessarily guarantee robustness in real-world scenarios. We also discovered that incorporating spatial information among patches improves model resilience and overcomes a common limitation of Transformers not being able to effectively recover lost features. With this knowledge, we suggest potential avenues for enhancing the overall efficiency of Transformer-based models in facial anti-spoofing applications. The code and models used in this study have been made publicly available on our GitHub repository. Additionally, we are releasing FAS-T, a large-scale dataset of artificial spoofing attacks, to advance the field of facial recognition and anti-spoofing through thorough and rigorous evaluations. In evolutionary computation, parallel MOP-EAs can benefit from the exploitation of temporal correlations in evaluation processes by employing a parent selection strategy. However, the effectiveness of this approach is hindered by the synchronization challenge. Evaluation time bias may enhance the overall performance of parallel MOP-EAs by prioritizing populations with quicker evaluation times, thereby reducing the impact of asynchronous computations on solution quality. This paper proposes a novel parent selection strategy, freqSPS, centered around the frequency of non-zero fitness values, to mitigate evaluation time bias and show its advantages through comparative simulations with the widely used first-come, first-selected method. Results indicate that the proposed strategy not only minimizes evaluation time bias but also offers better overall performance in solving high-dimensional optimization problems. Examples using the ZDT1, ZDT4, and C2DT6 test functions demonstrate the efficacy of the freqSPS strategy, while a real-world application using a recent optimization problem from the 2021 IEEE CEC competition highlights its practical usefulness in solving multi-objective optimization problems. Frequency-based parent selection has the potential to address evaluation time bias, enhance solution quality, and increase computational efficiency in asynchronous parallel MOP-EAs. However, the proposed solution only alleviates synchronization difficulties and does not completely resolve the synchronization challenge. Further research is needed to explore more effective strategies for populations with varying evaluation times. Additional considerations are also provided to refine the proposed strategy, such as its adaptability to scenarios with a large number of non-zero fitness values and the diversity of solutions in the final population. Frequency-based parent selection offers valuable insights into the exploitation of evaluation time bias in asynchronous parallel MOP-EAs, while its generalizability to diverse computational settings requires further investigation. Ultimately, the employment of a parent selection strategy should depend on an in-depth comprehension of evaluation time bias and the goals of solution quality and computational efficiency. Frequency-based parent selection can be an valuable method in asynchronous parallel MOP-EAs but its effectiveness may differ when dealing with synchronous computations and solution diversity. We investigate the short-time time-evolution of the density matrix $\rho(t)$ when governed by a Lindblad master equation, which describes the dynamics of open quantum systems in the Markovian limit. Given a time-regular perturbation $H_1(t)$ and an unperturbed Hamiltonian $H_0$, with which $H_1(t)$ commutes, we derive an approximate solution for the time-evolved density matrix up to the order of $\epsilon^2$. Our method, which involves expanding the operator $U(t)\rho_0 U^\dagger(t)$ using the Magnus expansion, yields two distinct formulas, differing in their treatment of higher-order terms. One formula holds for arbitrary $H_1(t)$ but features higher-order terms; the other uses a time-averaged expression for $H_1(t)$ in the perturbation expansion, but requires that $H_1(t)$ commutes with both the unperturbed Hamiltonian and the Hamiltonian governing the homogenous evolution $U(t)$. We analyze the accuracy of our approximations in two scenarios: our analysis reveals that the second approximation is generally more accurate, but may exhibit divergence that can be mitigated with the correct choice of time-averaged expression for $H_1(t)$. Utilizing this accuracy criterion, we derive a closed-form expression for the time-evolved density matrix in the presence of von Neumann dynamics, and verify that it aligns with established results. Furthermore, we apply our approximations to the case of spin-$\frac{1}{2}$ systems, where the perturbation takes the form of off-diagonal matrices. Using numerical computations, we investigate how the size of the Hilbert space influences the accuracy of our approximations, finding that the accuracy depends on both the size of the Hilbert space and the duration $t$ but that the accuracy improves as the perturbation tends towards a diagonal matrix. At the end, we offer some suggestions for enhancing the predictive capabilities of our approximations, which can be achieved by introducing a specific time-dependent damping rate into the Lindblad master equation. Using the example of a situation involving a system with generated coherent states, we illustrate that such an approach is feasible. Our findings indicate that the choice of damping rate significantly impacts the accuracy of our approximations and that the optimal rate might be derived from a specific rate of decay for the perturbation. Our study focuses on examining depolarization resulting from both ferromagnetism and site-specific spin immobilization in the Ce-based alloys CePd$_{1-x}$Rh$_x$ through detailed analyses of the isotropic neutron polarization (AMP) technique.  The alloys were grown in three distinct Rh concentrations: $x$ = 0.075, 0.125, and 0.300.  The AMP method is instrumental in detecting small amounts of ferromagnetic or ferro-ordering clusters within paramagnetic and paramagnetic-ordered alloys, respectively.  The alloy samples were examined over a temperature range from 1.4 K to the Curie temperature, $\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{C}}$, for each Rh concentration.  The Rh concentration of 0.075 Rh was found to enhance the temperature dependence of the AMP beyond its existing pure CePd alloy response, indicating a ferromagnetic response.  Conversely, the alloy samples with Rh concentrations of 0.125 and 0.300 were found to exhibit a stable, temperature-independent response, interpreted as site-specific spin immobilization within the alloy samples.  A secondary, temperature-dependent AMP was identified in all alloy samples, requiring analysis of a modified model that incorporates both ferromagnetism and site-specific spin immobilization.  The analysis revealed a unified interpretation of the experimentally measured AMP, incorporating the effects of ferromagnetism, site-specific spin immobilization, and dynamic spin correlations.  The application of the AMP method to the Rh-concentrated alloy samples with a paramagnetization temperature of approximately 150 mK is a first for these alloy systems.  Our model, incorporating the effects of ferromagnetism and site-specific spin immobilization, sufficiently explains the observed AMP for all alloy samples within the measured temperature range.  The dynamics at the lowest temperatures are found to be attributed to a unified set of dynamic spin correlations that are common to all samples within the measured temperature range.  The AMP is shown to be sensitive to detecting low-temperature spin correlations that are identified as reaching their saturation at approximately 20 mK and remaining so to at least 60 mK in the case of the alloy CePd$_{0.85}$Rh$_{0.300}$.  The model and analysis methods developed here may be directly translated to the study of additional rare-earth and transition-metal based alloys, while the lowest-temperature spin correlations observed in these alloy systems may serve as a prototype for similar studies with other alloys.

Our analysis combines VLA and LOFAR data for the giant molecular cloud G176.51+00.20, focused on detecting narrow 21 cm spectral features within the cloud's perimeter. By subtracting broad emissions and using an inverse data cube, we identified numerous narrow self-absorption and broad-outflow features. These include 12 self-absorption lines, primarily associated with C+ roots, and 8 broad lines, indicating outflows. We found that self-absorption lines are concentrated on the cloud's western side, paired with HII regions. We observed that the self-absorption signals often match the shapes of narrow HI lines seen in absorption against the beam's center. However, when in emission, these shapes can be distorted by the effects of Doppler shifts and wide-outflowing components. Our data also indicate that the self-absorption lines tend to be weaker than their absorption counterparts and that their widths are consistent with cloud scales. We suggest that the western HII regions within G176.20+G176.20 contain these narrow-line regions, similar to those seen in other studies, such as G351.12+0.18. We observed that the self-absorption lines are absent on the eastern side of G176.51+00.20, where more abundant radiation would likely destroy the narrow HI regions. However, some of the self-absorption lines may be associated with the cloud's northern protrusion. We believe that the extended LOFAR integration over this protrusion may contain HI narrow-line emissions similar to those seen in other systems, such as G351.12+0.18. A novel low-coupon approach for blind image restoration has been introduced, incorporating the Kernel Mixture model (KMM). By recognizing the density of the noise and signal as distinct kernel components of a Gaussian distribution, the KMM facilitates a flexible decomposition of the noise and signal. This allows for the separation of these components using the EM algorithm, ultimately leading to a simplified procedure for restoring damaged images. Notably, KMM models various types of noise, including non-Gaussian valuations like Laplacian and impulsive noise. Our empirical results demonstrate the KMM's effectiveness in restoring distorted images, especially when little is known about the image contents or noise characteristics. All the code and technical details can be accessed at https://github.com/huihutou/Blind_image_restoration_KMM. That being said, KMM has some inherent limitations: (1) failing to handle cases where kernel components exhibit degenerate symptoms, and (2) struggling to generate realistic images when the signal distribution is significantly complex. All things considered, KMM presents an appealing yet limited solution to the realm of blind image restoration. Future research should aim to build on top of this approach, addressing these existing limitations in the process. Distributed consensus is a fundamental process that allows multiple entities to agree on a common state despite possible network disruptions, device failures, or malicious interventions.  Ongoing research targets improving the efficiency of consensus protocols to facilitate datacenter-scale operations with hundreds of servers.  Previous efforts, such as Helios and Canopus, primarily focused on high-performance consensus protocols; however, these protocols fail to handle concurrent failures or malicious attacks efficiently.  In response to this gap, we introduce RCanopus, an improved failure-resilient version of the Canopus protocol.  RCanopus effectively handles various failure modes and malicious behaviors while maintaining Canopus's high performance characteristics.  We validate the robustness of RCanopus through both simulated and real-world testing, demonstrating its efficiency in scenarios with up to 40 processes across nine data centers.  Notably, RCanopus's performance advantage over other robust protocols, including Raft and PBFT, is substantial, with RCanopus exhibiting speed-ups of 3 to 7.3 times in these scenarios.  Moreover, RCanopus's real-world testing reveals that it is not only robust but also exhibits high reliability, with the probability of failure in Amazon EC2 deployments exceeding the specified threshold in nearly all of the tested scenarios.  Ultimately, we observe that RCanopus's high-performance characteristics make it an attractive solution for a wide variety of distributed system applications.  Specifically, we contend that if Canopus-level performance is acceptable for certain applications, then using such protocols in scenarios with high failure rates could significantly reduce development and maintenance costs.  In addition to its efficiency, we found the distributed system designed with RCanopus to be highly secure, with the risk of failure in EC2 deployments across nine data centers exceeding the specified threshold in only two out of 60,000 simulated test runs.  Consequently, if Canopus-level performance is acceptable for these applications, then using such protocols in scenarios with high failure rates could significantly reduce failure rates and corresponding economic consequences. Recent atomic-scale modeling of lipid membranes, demonstrated in research reports, has provided valuable insights into the impact of cholesterol on bending modulus. This study aims to establish a systematic approach for extracting the modulus from simulated pressure distributions. However, critical factors such as finite-size effects, data resolution, and pressure distribution modeling are overlooked in existing studies. To address these areas, a comprehensive analysis is conducted based on molecular dynamics simulations of pure DOPC lipids and 20:0/22:1 PCs with varying levels of cholesterol. This study offers a standardized method for assessing the bending modulus and highlights significant findings regarding finite-size effects, data resolution, and pressure modeling. A related article published in 2021, attributed by B. O. Diez and M. Deserno, has provided a framework but the results in this current study show a notable discrepancy. As a result of these discoveries, more accurate and reliable estimates of the bending modulus can be obtained, especially in scenarios involving small lipid populations and data sets collected using high-resolution force distributions. Moreover, this research introduces a non-linear relationship model for the pressure distribution, enhancing the accuracy of modulus estimation. All relevant data sets are available on the repository at: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.590444.

Recently, there has been significant interest in object detection for robotic vision and autonomous systems, with a focus on assessing uncertainty in detection outcomes. Current studies primarily concentrate on classifier uncertainty in individual categories and lack a comprehensive approach to object detection uncertainty, which encompasses uncertainty in both location and category. In this research, a Bayesian method for uncertainty assessment in deep object detectors is presented. The proposed approach BayesOD incorporates a predictive model and classifies uncertainty into two categories - shift and generic categories. The generic category category uncertainty can be utilized to estimate shift and directional information. The efficacy of the proposed approach is demonstrated through theoretical analysis and experimental evaluation on the ImageNet database. The results show that BayesOD surpasses conventional object detectors in both accuracy and uncertainty performance. Furthermore, uncertainty information predicted by BayesOD is applied to enhance the robustness and flexibility of deep learning-based object detectors in complex scenarios. Predicting traffic congestion is crucial for city infrastructure and transportation management systems. Accurate forecasting is especially challenging due to the temporal and spatiotemporal complexity of traffic behavior. Most current approaches focus solely on the temporal aspect, disregarding the interdependence of nearby locations and varying speeds. In this paper, a framework for traffic forecasting is introduced by analyzing overlapping regions of multiple road segments. Focusing on spatial and temporal interconnections allows for more effective prediction. A traffic prediction model with temporal dependencies is developed, integrating snippets from multiple roads, and leveraging snapper's spatial dependencies. We tested our approach with real-world data from road snippets in Austin and observed substantial improvements over existing models. Our code is now available online. Our research focuses on understanding the Cosmic Ray Albedo Neutron Decay (CRAND) process that produces seismically-induced lightnings in low Earth orbit spacecraft. We use a Monte Carlo simulation model incorporating OptiBeamo, a comprehensive particle transport code, to study the generation of neutrons and gamma rays from p-p reactions within the atmosphere. By calculating the production and diffusion of neutrons throughout the atmosphere up to 20 GeV, OptiBeamo enables us to investigate neutron detection within satellites. Our simulation reveals significant neutron and gamma-ray production above 10 GeV, alongside a detailed analysis of the energy spectra of neutrons and gamma rays. The findings of our simulation align with experimental data on neutron detection by the CAMEX-5 satellite and gamma-ray detection by the AEOP-2 spacecraft, supporting the validity of our Monte Carlo model. The simulation also yields valuable insights into the seismically-induced lightning phenomenon, emphasizing the necessity to consider atmospheric neutrons in the interpretation of neutron experiments. The results will be utilized in our forthcoming AEOP-2 simulation study. The proposed model holds the potential to be broadly applicable not only for satellites but also for ground-based experiments measuring neutron components, and we intend to investigate this further in the near future. A demonstration of the OptiBeamo code's capability for generating source distributions (in neutrons and gamma rays) at various locations throughout the atmosphere is provided as part of the supplementary materials package for this study. Recent research has established the superiority of Graph Neural Networks in their ability to learn and represent complex graph structures and node attributes. A key aspect of GNNs' success lies in their ability to perform localized learning. Despite extensive studies on the fundamental properties of GNNs, most existing models follow a universal pyramid-like shrinkage skeleton, where each layer progressively reduces graph resolution. Furthermore, research has shown that current models are inadequate in capturing detailed information. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel GNN framework that enhances its design with a Link Rewire module. By reconfiguring the link structure, we are able to improve the accuracy of node classification and generate more precise node representations. To this end, we conduct an in-depth analysis of a large dataset of social networks to understand the characteristics of the link structure. Subsequently, we combine in-depth analysis with unsupervised and semi-supervised learning approaches to design the Link Rewire module. Comprehensive experiments confirm that our model yields superior performance in social media network classification. Moreover, we show that our model generalizes well across various graph types and attributes, as well as in low-resource settings. Notably, our model achieves superior performance despite the minimal modification to the link structure, underscoring the importance of structure in social media networks. Ultimately, we open-source our model to facilitate further research and development. A preliminary version of this paper was published in a conference paper by 2021. This is an extended version of that work, featuring additional empirical validation and comprehensive analysis. We intend for this research to foster Deeper Graph Neural Networks and inspire further exploration of designing more effective GNN models. Protecting sensitive data in machine learning is a primary concern which adopts a differential privacy framework to ensure confidentiality. Methods for secure inference aim to generate predictions while maintaining differential privacy. Although a low-rank matrix completion technique is crucial in many applications, it often conflicts with differential privacy requirements. Since current approaches either sacrifice data confidentiality or achieve incomplete low-rank matrix completion, we treat this problem using Huber loss optimization with a censored cost function. By incorporating Lasso penalization, we obtain a principled solution for low-rank matrix completion that is both differentially private and robust. We further analyze the performance of this solution and validate our approach with supporting experimental results. Moreover, we provide Theorems 1 and 2 to establish the efficacy and privacy of our approach, and Theorem 3 to define robust convergence. Building on a matrix completion algorithm by Candes et al., we obtain a private and robust estimate, and using the Lasso framework, we further obtain a stable solution in the presence of noisy data. Experimental results are presented to demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in concurrent applications, particularly noise removal in images and forecast analysis in time series data. We also compare our approach with established methods at different parameters and evaluate the impact of Huber loss and Log loss using precision and recall metrics. Finally, we validate our approach using the Reuters dataset to determine the reliability of our findings. In summary, our approach offers robust and reliable low-rank matrix completion with proven differential privacy guarantees, complemented by experiments showcasing improved performance in concurrent tasks. We also provide additional theorems, including robust convergence, and apply our method to real-world data, yielding superior results. This force pulls the mirror towards the atom, causing it to oscillate when the system reaches a balance. As a result, both the atom and the mirror produce various forms of electromagnetic radiation, depending on the specific positions and movements involved. The radiation produced by the atom includes shifts in its energy levels as well as changes in its electric and magnetic fields, while the radiation produced by the mirror is produced through changes in its mass distribution and potential energy. In equitable AI development, addressing systemic inequities within used data and utilized models is crucial. Despite progress in understanding and measuring bias in predictive models, there is a research gap when it comes to analyzing bias in graph-based AI applications. Our goal for graph-based data is to measure and highlight localized areas of bias, specifically inequity in representation, within individual nodes and their communities. By using neighborhood-based metrics like the Hubs and Periphery metric, along with Data Generation from Inferred Distribution, a graph dataset can be reconstructed to reflect inherent biases. To facilitate further research, we have created LGIAD, a dataset consisting of 9 datasets with varied characteristics, to serve as a benchmark for studying bias in graph-based data. Using LGIAD, we test the effectiveness of two methods in reducing bias: Model Bias Reduction, which modifies a graph-based model to reduce target attribute-based bias, and Predictive Bias Reduction, which modifies a graph-based model to reduce predictive bias. Our results demonstrate that our two methods, Model Bias Reduction and Predictive Bias Reduction, are successful in graph-based bias reduction, and outperform existing techniques such as redistribution and bias regularization. Our research in graph-based bias reduction is part of a broader effort in software and machine learning ethics, aiming to understand and address systemic inequities within used data and utilized models.  Ultimately, we strive to develop more equitable AI.  In terms of potential practical contributions, our Predictive Bias Reduction method could directly inform the development of equitable AI models, and LGIAD could facilitate the graph-based bias reduction competition in the domain of counterfactual reasoning and causal inference. This research focuses on developing estimative solutions for the spatially nonhomogeneous reversible enzyme reaction: \begin{align*}
S+P_b\rightleftharpoons SP_b\\
A+SP_b\to AS_p+b\,.
\end{align*}Using an approach that combines elementary modes and combinatorial principles, we initially derive an analytical solution for the kinetic equations based on the assumption of initial S and A availability. We then generalize this solution to the scenario where S and A are produced by zero-order reactions, $dS/dt=\alpha_S$ and $dA/dt=\alpha_A$. Since this scenario is relevant in biological systems, we derive new iterative solutions for the spatially nonhomogeneous case with equal diffusion coefficients. We also examine the asymptotic behavior of the solutions as $\epsilon \to 0$ in the internal scaled frame of reference, preserving the combinatorial spirit of the solutions. Furthermore, we prove the existence and uniqueness of the solutions using the Banach principle and show that the obtained solutions satisfy the sum rule and the additivity property. We also conduct numerical operations on the solutions as in the analytical case, confirming our theoretical findings. We conclude that the iterative approach can effectively handle complex biochemical reactions, even those that exceed the combinatorial standard. This method is versatile, applicable to a wide range of nonhomogeneous reversible enzyme reactions with complex spatial and temporal patterns. Recent advances in Recommendation Systems have led to significant performance gains thanks to the extensive use of Evaluation-based Item Recommendation, where user ratings on various evaluation platforms are utilized to provide personalized product or service recommendations. However, the ratings on evaluation platforms suffer from a mix of two properties - heterogeneity and temporality - due to differing sentiment distributions and temporal dynamics, which poses a significant challenge to modeling their correlation. To address this issue, we develop a novel framework called Sentiment-sensitive Interactive Fusion Network (SIFN) that effectively captures the complex interplay between evaluation platform items and user ratings. Specifically, we employ a Temporally Decoupled Language Model to isolate the time dimension from the heterogeneous rating distribution, coupled with an Interactive Fusion Module that fuses the time and rating information using an attention-based mechanism. Comprehensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate the superiority of SIFN over leading models. Notably, our work offers a pioneering approach to modeling diverse evaluation platform item recommendations through the use of explicit rating sentiments. The proposed model achieves improved recommendation performance and is available on GitHub at https://github.com/dataork/SIFN. Our research enables a deeper understanding of the complex relationship between evaluation platform items and user ratings, which has important implications for research in Recommendation Systems and Evaluation-based Item Recommendation. The resulting model can effectively capture the time and sentiment properties of user ratings, thus providing valuable insights for evaluation-based item recommendation. The main contributions of our approach are as follows. Firstly, we develop a unique rating distribution characteristic - the heterogeneity of evaluation platform items - which poses a significant challenge to modeling its correlation. Secondly, we introduce the Temporally Decoupled Language Model to isolate the time dimension from the heterogeneous rating distribution, which demonstrates the importance of explicitly managing the time dimension from the viewpoint of rating distribution. A group of homeomorphisms in a topological space fail the Roelcke precompactness property if any infinite subset of functions, when applied successively to an initial set, covers the entire space only after removing a negligible set from the original subset. The community has developed relatively few, concrete examples of sets that fail this property. Researchers have shown that subsets of the group $Homeo_+(S^1)$ consisting of rotations with irrational angles are such sets. We have proven that any subset of the group $Homeo_+(S^2)$ consisting of orientable surface homeomorphisms is also such a set, thereby providing the first instance of a manifold being involved. This achievement follows from our establishment of the more general result that subsets of the group $O(3)$ consisting of orientations are indeed such sets. Moreover, the given example resolves problem 1422 from the low-dimensional topology research portal in a positive manner. We had initially considered employing Kirchheim's work as the basis for our example but, instead, the given outcome offers an alternative one. Additionally, the provided example is consistent with the known fact that the group $Homeo_+(S^2)$ is not metrizable. We have carefully explored and carefully explain why this property is inherent, unlike other groups such as $Homeo_+(S^1)$, which is metrizable. We have also shown that any subgroup of $Homeo_+(S^2)$ that is topologically closed, yet fails the Seidel property, is not uncountable and that its intersection with the subgroup $Homeo_+(S^2)$ is not a topological abelian subgroup. This achievement is a refinement and, in some cases, a reversal of the known theorem by Wehrheim that identified the properties of the group $Homeo_+(S^1)$, which is metrizable. We have carefully explored and carefully avoid the opposite phenomenon that is observed in the group $O(3)$. In a companion note, the community is presented with an alternative solution to problem 1422 from the research portal, one that is based on Kirchheim's work. In a second companion piece, the community is presented with an alternative to our established result, one that is based on the work of Tymochow, Weir and myself from 2021. In a third companion piece, the community is presented with an additional theorem related to the group $GL_+(3, \mathbb{Z})$
