The Dunkl operators in one dimension have a useful expression in terms of momentum and a singular differential operator that involves a logarithmic factor when the parameter $\nu$ is zero. This expression leads to an alternative representation of the Dunkl operators as regular differential operators on functions by combining the momentum operator with the product of a function and a logarithmic factor, which acts as a non-local operator. Additionally, this expression applies to vector-valued functions and provides a connection to the Riesz potential. With $\nu$ set to zero and considering scalar-valued functions, the expression simplifies and allows for a direct connection between the Dunkl operators and regular differential operators, thereby providing a new perspective on known results. Specifically, it leads to a new proof of the hypergeometric equation's completeness, which results from the regularity of the given expression's range. Furthermore, it allows for a new proof of the hypergeometric equation's hypergeometric function solution, as well as the $\nu=0$ case's connection to Bessel functions through the irregularity of the given expression's range in specific scenarios. Finally, the expression's extension to even-dimensional spaces is also discussed. 

For specific $\nu$ values, the expression's regularity or irregularity in various function spaces can be easily determined, which might be useful in the inversion of the Dunkl operators in certain domains. For instance, if $\nu$ is an integer and the function space involves square-integrable functions, then the expression's regularity on the real line leads to a new representation of the Dunkl intertwining operator, which might be applicable to the construction of Dunkl spherical functions on even-dimensional spaces. 

In contrast, if $\nu$ is zero and the function space is more broadly defined, then the expression's irregularity at point zero results in a new depiction of the Dunkl intertwaking operator in the space of Schwartz functions. This new depiction might be useful in the construction of Dunkl spherical functions in odd-dimensional spaces, which might be relevant to the recent developments in harmonic analysis on the Riemann sphere. 

The expression's last aspect is connected to the representation theory of the symmetry groups by pointing out its easy generalization to the space of sections of vector bundles over compact manifolds, which might be useful in the construction of unitary representations of the groups $O(n)\times O(2)$. Additionally, such an expression might be applicable to other symmetry groups, which might be useful for developing interesting unitary representations in harmonic analysis.

Consequently, this yields the finding that two relatively inductive integer group actions are consistently equivalent exactly when they are orbit equivalent. Furthermore, it is proven that the set of virtually cyclic group actions that are relatively inductive exhibits countable cardinality. A new, explicit orbit equivalence functor is established, derived from the one for induced metrical actions to virtually cyclic group actions, which is found to be surjective for relatively inductive group actions. By exploiting this result and drawing from Rørdam and Worrall's algebraic orbit classification program, it is possible to compute the cardinality of the set of relatively inductive integer group actions, revealing a cardinality of $2^{\aleph_0} $ and thereby confirming a dimension conjecture proposed by Ghosh, Lustig, Rajwade and Stalder. By leveraging techniques from infinite dimensional topology, it is discovered that two relatively inductive group actions corresponding to metrical dynamics possess orbit properties consistent with Rørdam and Worrall's algebraic orbit classification program. Consequently, using Glimm and Wazenberg's methods from the 1970s, it is possible to generate AF subalgebras with AF dimensions from relatively inductive integer group actions, thus confirming another conjecture from Ghosh, Lustig, Rajwade and Stalder. In recent times, a deep understanding of Kerr-lens mode-locking has been developed along with strategies to counter the limitations it imposes on increasing the power of ultrashort pulses. Despite this progress, further enhancements to reach the theoretical limits of Kerr-lens mode-locking may necessitate a more precise analytical description of the phenomenon than is currently available. To fill this need, we present a detailed geometric analysis of Kerr-lens mode-locking that we believe offers a more comprehensive insight into this complex area of photonics than earlier literature. We start by reviewing the foundational elements of Kerr-lens mode-locking and then investigate ring resonators, which offer simplified mathematics but still encompass all the fundamental characteristics of the field. Our analysis reveals, however, that self-phase modulation within the resonator, a critical factor in homogenizing the spectrum in Kerr-lens mode-locking, has not been adequately addressed in previous discussions. We rectify this oversight by examining the role of the Fourier transform and energy distributions involved. We use our insights to explore the challenges of achieving broad-band spectra and high energy densities in Kerr-lens mode-locking and suggest possible ways to overcome these limitations. We also leverage our model to examine the potential for generating frequency-compressed few-cycle pulses with record-breaking properties, providing a clear roadmap to achieving such pulses. We conclude our discussion by considering and evaluating numerical solutions to the combined nonlinear problems we studied. We predict that our geometric analysis will facilitate the development of Kerr-lens mode-locking pulse sources with unparalleled performance. We have tested and validated our model through detailed numerical simulations, and our method is versatile, applicable to a wide variety of ring-resonator designs, including those with multiple channels and complex geometries. We have also explored the feasibility of generating frequency-compressed pulses in free-space and free-space comb generation. Lastly, we have obtained analytical descriptions of the problem in Cartesian geometry, a highly practical and widely employed configuration. We predict that our model will lead to significant breakthroughs in Kerr-lens mode-locking and ultrashort pulse generation and will inspire novel approaches to designing and developing high-performance photonics. Large-scale nonlinear regression tasks are now executed across multiple devices due to their computational intensity. Yet, conventional methods requiring simultaneous model updates from all devices are impractical due to variability in task complexity and power limitations. This paper proposes an asynchronous federated training protocol, where each device updates the model according to its available computation time, also considering unequal tasks to avoid idle waiting states. Furthermore, we integrate a technique that adjusts the model weight adaptation in line with computing device speeds and power status, to enhance convergence efficiency under heterogeneous hardware configurations. Experiments using real-world datasets confirm the proposed method's efficacy in reducing training duration for asynchronous operations, by up to 3.48 times, alongside substantial power consumption savings and computational resource utilization improvement. Meanwhile, the loss in prediction accuracy is minimal at 0.98%. Overall, the results demonstrate a high ROI of the proposed approach. By analyzing a silicon layer of 0.256 $\mu$m and a PBG reflector with air holes, the team discovered that the structure can absorb 60% of sunlight across the entire solar spectrum. Furthermore, the researchers assessed various properties of PBG crystals, including period, hole size, and depth, influencing the stop band's characteristics. Wildfires pose a significant threat to global ecosystems, and efficient visualization tools are crucial for researchers and emergency responders to accurately locate and respond to these fires. Although visible spectra images often capture detailed wildfire patterns, they are frequently obscured by smoke, glinting off water surfaces, or poor lighting conditions. Conversely, thermal images possess higher accuracy in detecting fires, yet smoke glint, water surfaces, and environmental factors can also distort these visuals. Most existing image processing methods fail to seamlessly integrate these wavelengths due to inherent differences in scale, texture, and semantics. Consequently, there is an pressing need for techniques that can effectively fuse combined wavelength visuals in a manner easily interpretable by humans and AI models. Existing techniques primarily rely on image splitting, feature mapping, or coarse-to-fine approaches, which can lead to the preservation of subtle, semantic features in combined wavelength visuals being lost. Inspired by cutting-edge image generation technologies, we developed the Fire Generative Adversarial Network (FIRe-GAN), a groundbreaking, adversarial training system for producing high-quality, multi-spectral wavelength visuals. FIRe-GAN leverages a Custom Hybrid Generator (CHG) and multiple discriminators, which are tailored to capture details from both thermal and visible spectra, as well as their combined semantic features. Through the efficient preservation of semantic information, the model achieves superior results in the preservation of semantic features. Experiments reveal that FIRe-GAN produces high-quality, multi-spectral wavelength visuals with superior performance across multiple evaluation metrics. Moreover, FIRe-GAN's generated visuals facilitate semantic segmentation by a ResNet-50 network, enhancing its accuracy by nearly 20%. Similar advancements are observed in Local Binary Hashing accuracy, with FIRe-GAN providing a boost of up to 16%. Our technique offers great potential in computational imaging, computational photography, emergency response, and other related fields. As social media use becomes a ubiquitous part of daily life for numerous individuals, the necessity to harness its potential in addressing mental health concerns grows.  Research into machine learning-based detection of mental health from social media data is an actively researched area, yet a major obstacle lies in amassing sufficient data for various categories of mental health.  In this paper, we explore two data collection techniques and evaluate their application in training a BERT model to identify depression indicators from social media posts.  Our results enable us to compare the efficacy of two distinct data collection strategies and provide empirical validation of their effectiveness.  Furthermore, considering that data collection is a time-consuming and costly process, we selectively apply techniques such as data augmentation and model fine-tuning to enhance performance.  Ultimately, using our trained model, we contribute 71 unique depression indicators, thereby enriching the existing body of knowledge in this field.  Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/aaryan0001/SocialMediaMML Depression Detection.  For demonstration purposes, a live deployment of our model can be accessed at http://socialmedia.mechanicalsinger.xyz.  We plan to expand our model to other mental health conditions and explore its applicability in related domains.  Furthermore, we intend to establish an annotation platform for social media content and provide detailed guidelines to facilitate future research in this area.  In the long run, we aim to establish a collaborative project involving the mechanicalsinger and users, where the latter can draw insights from the former's social media presence.  Such a project has the potential to pave the way for a groundbreaking social media-based research paradigm in the medical and psychological fields.  In addition, we aim to extend our scope to include other mental health disorders and conduct an in-depth analysis of psychological disorders using emerging technologies like AR, VR, and mobile-powered games.  Ultimately, we aim to establish a network of psychological experts, social scientists, and technologists to collaborate on cutting-edge projects at mechanicalsinger.xyz.  In the process, we will also utilize NLP to gather relevant literature and facilitate discussions on various mental health topics across multiple platforms.  In the near future, we will initiate a series of surveys, interviews, and focus groups to better comprehend the psychological impact on individuals, including those affected by depression, PTSD, anxiety, and other relevant psychological disorders.  Subsequently, we aim to leverage AI-driven medical technology to identify and predict mental health patterns in individuals, thereby fostering a better understanding among team members and the general public.

Our theoretical results demonstrate the influence of bellman matrix off-diagonal structure risk on Q-function gradient estimators in model-free reinforcement learning and provide an empirical validation of our novel Bellman matrix construction methods in both simple environment settings and complex environment scenarios. Statistical analysis, including data science, extensively utilizes matrix calculations. Matrix inequalities such as Hadamard, Schur, and Lyapunov hold significant importance in this context, with numerous applications in various scientific fields. These inequalities have extensive implications in the realm of nonnegative matrix decomposition, to name a few. From a theoretical standpoint, these matrix inequalities can be regarded as an extension of fundamental constraints observing random matrices. Recently, we have derived constraints defining the fundamental limitations of rank-one matrix evaluation with groupwise heterogeneity. Moreover, we have derived the sharpest multivariate generalizations of fundamental constraints in the form of Schur, Hadamard, and Lyapunov theorems. These constraints can be used to optimize various matrix valuations, such as trace, expectation, or majorization, subject to certain matrix evaluation methods. In addition, we have demonstrated that the hadamard inequality is essentially equivalent to the Lyapunov inequality, with hadamard providing stronger constraints in certain scenarios. Moreover, we have derived the sharpest multivariate generalizations of the Lyapunov inequality, showing that the Lyapunov and Schur inequalities have no further strengthening to offer. Finally, through numerical simulations, we have verified the efficacy of our derived constraints in various scalar matrix evaluation methods. The use of our derived constraints is illustrated in the form of a Python code available at the GitHub repository https://github.com/kutila1/FundConRankOne. This work is, in part, an extension of previous research on fundamental constraints for homogeneous rank-one matrix evaluation, as published in a doctoral dissertation by Kutila (2022), with a related PhD thesis addressing additional topics available at https://doi.org/10.25876/tou-3657. Additionally, we have obtained related results in the form of fundamental constraints for nonnegative matrix decomposition, as presented at https://arxiv.org/2103.10435. We present C19Cat, a COVID-19 categorization model that uses two phases with BERT attributes to improve accuracy and adaptability. The first stage, also known as the immunization stage, utilizes vaccinated patients' data to enhance model performance. By initial modeling, both unvaccinated and vaccinated patients' data are combined. Subsequently, a reverse-differential encoding technique is applied to distinguish between vaccinated and unvaccinated patients' labels. The second stage, or vaccinated patients' fine-tuning stage, fine-tunes models with vaccinated patients' data, thereby flipping the reverse-differential encoded labels and flipping it back. By doing so, the models can accurately determine patients' COVID-19 labels while considering their vaccination status. By means of our experimentation, we show that C19Cat is capable of outperforming existing models in all categories of vaccinated patients with various vaccination timing scenarios. For instance, when the timing of vaccination is 7 days apart from the patients' data collection, our model performs better than existing models with an impressive 1-2% accuracy boost across all categories. Our model performs even better when the timing of vaccination is 14 days apart from the patients' data collection, resulting in further improved results. The integration of vaccinated patients' data into two-phase COVID19 categorization models using BERT attributes seems very promising and should be further studied in future research. Researchers are becoming increasingly interested in the antagonistic susceptibility (AS) phenomenon in machine learning, where overfitting models consistently perform better than those trained with a conventional approach.  Despite the growing body of AS research focused on image recognition, the concept remains underrepresented in the field of Natural Language Processing (NLP).  To address this gap, this study investigates the AS principle in the context of speech education.  By leveraging the LibriSpeech dataset and utilizing two self-supervised models, the team evaluates the efficacy of AS training in improving model performance.  Through an analysis of the results, the authors demonstrate that AS training can be an effective tool for achieving superior model performance and provide insights that can guide the development of more efficient NLP speech education techniques using contrastive learning methods.  Importantly, the study reveals that a higher contrastive learning noise level is associated with better model performance, thus suggesting that AS and self-supervised learning may have complementary roles in the development of more robust NLP speech models.  Furthermore, the study highlights a number of theoretical explanations for the AS phenomenon, including the concept of 'easy' and 'hard' examples and the potential trade-off between model bias and accuracy.  Ultimately, the study suggests that further exploration of the AS principle is warranted in order to optimize NLP model performance.  Code implementation is available on GitHub at https://github.com/stergios-papoulias/antagonistic_susceptibility_speech_self_supervised_learning. Researchers frequently encounter the challenge of working with incomplete data, and dealing with missing data is an integral part of many scientific studies, often analyzed using various techniques. In the context of this paper, we explore the application of the E-value metric, initially proposed by Cohen, in the Bayesian framework for handling missing data. By employing various models, we demonstrate how the E-value can be utilized to assess the impact of data gaps on study findings. Furthermore, we provide practical implementation examples, including a case based on real-world ice disc experiment data and an unrelated application involving face recognition systems. The accompanying software is freely available on our GitHub repository for public access. Using the supplied code, researchers can easily compute E-values for their own data, regardless of the study's field or data availability. Lastly, we elaborate on the implicit assumptions associated with the E-value metric and discuss potential extensions to the measure's original formulation. One such potential extension could involve incorporating partial data, and we illustrate this approach with a numerical example. Nevertheless, we argue that the original E-value model is generally more suitable for missing data analysis. Ultimately, we provide an understanding of the underlying relationship between the E-value and frequentist p-values, showing that E-values can serve as an optimal version of p-values. Consequently, E-values provide a means of expressing results that remain unaffected by the type of data or experimental design employed. Furthermore, E-values offer a unique way of comparing or combining results, and researchers can accurately determine whether their findings are significantly different from one another. In fact, a notable portion of Bayesian studies, including many published findings in the field of computer vision, have employed E-values as an indicator of reliability. Consequently, E-values pose a distinct variation of p-values, and their interpretation is grounded in frequentist theory. In other words, while Bayesian reasoning is utilized to estimate an E-value, its actual meaning and interpretation are rooted in the realm of frequentist theory. The blockchain technology, renowned for its data integrity and impenetrable transparency, is gaining traction in the learning and transportation sectors. The (semi)centralized approach of typical blockchain systems, however, fails to align with the decentralized principles of the Internet of Vehicles and learning environments. Fortunately, a variety of blockchain extensions has been developed to overcome these limitations. This paper offers a comprehensive survey of cutting-edge blockchain-enabled learning systems and federations that support the core values of autonomy, data security, and user anonymity, specifically in the context of the Internet of Vehicles. The survey discusses the underlying frameworks, algorithms, and validations for blockchain extensions as well as the diverse applications of blockchain-enabled learning systems and federations, evaluating their potential and challenges. The discussion also explores potential avenues for future research and development in this field. The paper conducts a systematic analysis of 131 relevant publications from 2018 to 2021, offering a comprehensive overview of this topic with embedded contextual information and graphical aids to enhance readability and usability. The paper is available under a liberal license to permit liberal use and modification. The corresponding GitHub repository stores the data and hyperlinks referenced in this paper for easy access. The primary objective of this paper is to facilitate further research and development in this field by providing a thorough understanding of the current state of knowledge and the various aspects of blockchain-enabled learning systems and federations. The LHCb collaboration has measured the time variation of the decay processes $D^0 \to K^+ \pi^-$, $D^+ \to K^+ \pi^+ \pi^-$, $D^0 \to K^- \pi^+ \pi^+$, $D_s^{\pm} \to \phi \pi^{\pm}$, $\Lambda^0_b \to p \pi^+$, $\Xi^0_b^{\ast+} \to \Xi^0 \pi^+$ and $\Omega^0_b^{\ast+} \to \Omega^{\ast 0} \pi^+$, where the particles are not produced directly but instead through various intermediate processes. These measurements are based on data obtained from proton-proton collisions at 5.02 TeV, recorded over 5 years with high statistical accuracy. 
Data analysis at different time intervals has identified prominent oscillations in several decay channels, indicating the occurrence of beauty and charm quark rehadronisation. 
Data collected at different times also show differences in momentary trends in several decay channels, implying that there is no uniform rehadronisation pattern across all measurements. 
These results provide valuable experimental input for a detailed theoretical study on the evolution of heavy flavour particle lifetimes. 
Moreover, these measurements have also determined the current average lifetimes of several baryon and meson particles and have thus refined previous estimates. 
These experimental findings also provide crucial inputs to a detailed theoretical study on the decay processes. 
Data also shows that there are noticeable differences in several decay channels that require further theoretical analysis to understand their underlying physics mechanisms. 
These experimental results also provide valuable insights not only for a detailed theoretical study on heavy flavour particle oscillations but also for a comparison with theoretical model predictions. (102 words) \end{abstract}

Valuable linguistic insights can be obtained from ancient texts but those written before the age of printing are scarce and difficult to annotate. Existing automatic annotation methods are often tailored to modern languages and fail to account for the textual nuances of historical documents. In this paper, we explore the use of Set-Valued Forecasting techniques to annotate historical part-of-speech datasets, such as the catalog of annotated Old English texts. Old English poses particular challenges due to its sparse vocabulary, irregular grammar, and syntax that has been significantly altered since the Anglo-Saxon period. To address these issues, we have developed an innovative technique for old English part-of-speech annotation by incorporating the analysis of historical texts, impact of vowel mutation and syllable division into the annotation process. Our proposed approach has generated competitive results in part-of-speech annotation for single and grouped tokens in two datasets, demonstrating its efficiency in reliable annotation. Furthermore, we have also successfully applied the technique to a set of unlabeled Middle English text from the codex V. C. 5. 15, allowing us to produce a highly accurate part-of-speech catalog that surpasses existing annotation methods. These novel findings and data have been made publicly available to the linguistic community on GitHub. By leveraging machine learning technology, we can analyze a wide range of user input regarding their expectations from a revized city neighborhood. Initially, we develop an entity recognition model to extract essential data from user-generated texts, such as the types of facilities and services mentioned. Next, we establish a specification model that categorizes and quantifies each type of expectation (e.g., the expected speed of internet access). To demonstrate its effectiveness, we tested our approach using a dataset comprising 698 user-generated expectations and demonstrated its practical application in an interactive prototype. Furthermore, we collected further user feedback to validate the accuracy and usability of our generated specifications. Our evaluation showed that the generated specifications align with the original user inputs, providing high-quality expectations that urban planners can utilize as a foundation for planning and decision-making. Consequently, multiple gate operations in a sequence frequently cancel each other out due to frequent measurement mishaps, especially within the realm of superconducting quantum circuits. However, this occurring fault can be rectified by employing a distinct control method known as the concealed inverses protocol. This approach involves introducing a hidden inverse gate that reverses the effects of a previously executed faulty gate without being aware that it was faulty, and it does so by ensuring patient waits between operations. Research into the CIP has previously been conducted with magnetic resonance systems but has not been implemented in superconducting quantum devices. For the CIP to successfully operate in a superconducting quantum circuit, certain conditions must be fulfilled - the faulty gate must be reversibly executed and one must remain informed of all gate results. Although CIP is capable of rectifying any type of error inducing phase flip, it does so by extending the duration of gate operations, which may make CIP more suitable for applications requiring accuracy over speed, a characteristic commonly seen in density measurements. A unified Lie-Poisson framework is developed to describe various nonlinear field theories and their associated symmetries. This framework, encompassing both infinite- and finite-dimensional systems, requires a dual representation of Lie algebras and their adjoint actions. We derive a general method for implementing Clebsch maps within this framework, and subsequently, obtain novel integrability conditions for the resulting first-order nonlinear systems in terms of Lie-Poisson structures on the duals of Lie algebras. These conditions naturally reveal the critical role that Poisson-Lie groups and their representation theory play in the construction of these field theories. Many well-known examples, including Maxwell's equations, the Born-Infeld equations, the SU(2) Euler equations, the Camassa-Holm equation, and surface water waves, are shown to fit within this unified framework, with specific computations of adjoint actions and Clebsch conjugations presented for specific Lie algebras and their representations. Additionally, new applications to geometric systems, such as surface wave equations on Lie algebras, are discussed with the majority of such field theories likely falling under this new unified classification. This unified classification also allows for the exploration of new nonlinear systems that were previously unknown. First-order nonlinear systems are considered to be superintegrable within this framework if they maintain two independent integrability conditions, and three degrees of freedom are achieved. Various examples of such superintegrable systems are presented, including a system that converges to the SU(2) Euler equations. In a related context, NLS and LD equations are shown to be superintegrable when considered in one spatial dimension. Moreover, first-order nonlinear systems are shown to be application candidates derived from Krylov module theory, which could lead to new, previously uncharacterized systems of partial differential equations. Lastly, a series of open problems are proposed to further the understanding of this framework in the study of differential equations. They include extending the Clebsch conjugation to the full nonlinear setting, determining admissibility conditions for Lie-Poisson structures, investigating whether surface wave equations can be extended to higher dimensions, and whether the Euler equations can be extended to generalized KdV equations. A demonstration of how Lie-Poisson structures of types A, B, and C arise in the context of Krylov module theory and the Lie algebra gl(∞) is also provided. They relate to equations of partial integration, the tetrahedron equation, the Toda equation, TLL, and the spin Sine-Gamma

This paper builds upon a previous finding by Bony Estier et al. [arXiv:2103.05095], demonstrating the broad importance of conservation principles in mathematical modeling. Specifically, it shows that for a detailed Navier-Stokes model of a conservative flow, the principle of energy conservation has a profound effect on the existence of solutions under various conditions of regularity and potential well-regularity. In this work, the authors prove that an essential component of this model - the mass conservation principle - automatically follows from the standard incompressible flow assumptions, despite the system being inherently non-linear. They further demonstrate that while non-conservative models lack this crucial mass conservation property, it significantly influences the properties and existence of solutions within those models as well. Combining these findings with those of Bony Estier et al., the authors show that both the existence of conservative and non-conservative flows share crucial parallels and can be extensively characterized using the same conserved integral estimates. These estimates not only explain the monotonicity formulae and conservation principles in conservative flows but also provide powerful interventions capable of stabilizing non-conservative models and thereby guaranteeing the existence of those models. Moreover, the authors' work on non-conservative models notably resolves two longstanding open problems: the Baker-Ebin problem and the Nirenberg problem, both of which revolve around the existence of regular solutions. It is hoped that this collective finding will effectively disseminate the crucial insights gained from the conservation principle to various areas of geometric analysis and partial differential equations, thereby empowering researchers to harness its power in their individual disciplines. Lastly, the authors take a step further by broadening the application of their theory to encompass a diverse range of partial differential equations while also suggesting two novel problems for future inquiry. For the sake of clarity and accessibility, an accompanying note is provided by Bony Estier, first setting out the theory of conservation principles in a pedagogical framework and subsequently formalizing the underlying assumptions and findings of the primary paper. Moreover, a supplementary document, provided by Vasseur, delves into the themes of geometric Navier-Stokes equations and the role of conservation principles within them. However, manual analysis of these scans by radiologists is a time-consuming process. Previous studies have shown that capsule networks can improve the accuracy of infection detection compared to other scanning methods, such as X-rays. Building on this insight, we developed a two-stage Time-distributed Capsule Network model that can accurately identify COVID-19 from lung CT images. Our system consists of two parts: a capsule network module that converts input into feature vectors, and a classification module that uses these vectors for infection detection. The sample correlation's mean, standard deviation, and distribution are key elements in understanding its behavior. Mathematical expressions were developed for the correlation's moment properties using a specific representation of its distribution, and these expressions are considered the first of their kind. In order to make these expressions practical, the distribution of the sample correlation was approximated using a normal distribution, and a weighted average of normal distributions was used to account for edge cases. The accuracy of this model was verified through comparison with Monte Carlo simulations, and consideration was given to incorporating sampling distributions into statistical tests of correlation coefficients. Furthermore, a practical application of these expressions was demonstrated in the context of analyzing arrangements of data. It was discovered that normality plays a crucial role in the distribution of the sample correlation, with a key transition occurring at a sample size of 8. In arrangements featuring balanced data, the distribution of the sample correlation is symmetric and exhibits minimal deviation from normality. In contrast, the distribution of the sample correlation is asymmetric and exhibits substantial deviation from normality in cases involving non-balanced data, regardless of data arrangement type. This highlights the sample correlation's inherent properties and serves as a foundation for its discussion and interpretation, with implications extending to the development of statistical procedures involving arrangements of data. Furthermore, a similar approach was employed in examining the distribution of Fisher's combination of correlations. In addition to discussing theoretical topics, a comprehensive overview of mathematical and conceptual tools for discussing sampling distributions was developed and is presented in the paper's supplementary materials. These tools encompass a range of distribution properties, including Derivative Change of Distribution, and enable the derivation of various sampling distribution properties. Moreover, a number of commonly employed statistical tests, including t-tests, χ² tests, correlation analysis, factor analysis, and others, were analyzed and explained from a distinct perspective, and key concepts were identified as enabling the derivation of many sampling distribution properties. It is anticipated that this foundational approach may facilitate more efficient and in-depth discussions of statistical concepts and tests in scientific publications. The provided Supplementary materials include a number of pedagogical derivatives designed to facilitate statistical procedure explanations. These derivatives demonstrate the application of the Domain Model and Derivative Change of Distribution concepts to various statistical procedures. Consequently, the discussion of statistical concepts and tests is condensed into two primary pillars: the Domain Model and Derivative Change of Distribution. This foundational simplicity enables more efficient and in-depth discussions of statistical concepts and tests. Furthermore, the derived materials may prove useful in educating and informing readers about statistical procedures. A general approach to deriving quantum gravitational effects in scattering amplitudes is outlined, and its implications for observable, physical phenomena. To set the framework, Einstein's general relativity is re-imagined within the "S-matrix" formalism. This involves reinterpreting the gravitational field as a mere perturbation and leveraging the underlying symmetry of the theory, which yields a well-defined and renormalizable framework. Building on this foundation, the methodology is used to estimate the gravitational influence on high-energy collisions between two particles. Specifically, the scattering of two photons is considered as a means of extracting purely gravitational effects. Furthermore, the principles underlying this technique are adaptable and can be generalized to study more complex systems, including those governed by loop quantum gravity and string theory. The simplicity and versatility of the S-matrix formalism make it an attractive tool for exploring a wide range of quantum gravitational phenomena. Several promising research directions are highlighted, including the potential for experimental verification of quantum gravitational effects in high-energy particle collisions and cosmic rays. To arrive at concrete, testable predictions, the calculations must be based on a suitable quantum gravity model that partitions the gravitational effects into "intrinsic" and "extrinsic" components, with the latter accounting for the underlying non-perturbative structure of the gravity loop integral. With a predictable and controllable formulation of this kind, the S-matrix approach can be a powerful vehicle for linking theoretical frameworks to observable consequences. The given paper provides an introduction to this research program and presents a concrete case study of Einstein's gravity. Other submissions explore more advanced applications, such as loop quantum gravity and string theory, and propose an experiment to verify the phenomenon of quantum gravitational "intrinsic" energy. The accompanying thesis offers a comprehensive review of the underlying literature on quantum gravitational scattering amplitudes and serves as a detailed guide to the derivation of the described methods and results. We investigate the uniform stabilization of incompressible Navier-Stokes equations in finite-dimensional subspaces of critical Lq spaces in dimensions three and four. Our study encompasses both smooth and non-smooth initial data within Besov spaces matching the embedding properties of the targeted energy spaces. To achieve this, we employ a distance-to-ellipse method in a control scheme with an elliptical reference set to derive a unified, local feedback stabilization strategy for the Navier-Stokes system. Our approach provides the first proof of uniform boundedness of the Navier-Stokes flow in three-dimensional half-spaces for all non-negative times, as well as explicit distance estimates between the system's solutions and the stable manifold of the truncated extended system. Our results extend the scope of previous work in this area, encompassing a broader range of initial data and covering various combinations of q values between one and infinity. Our numerical simulations in this work are based on an augmented Lagrangian differential evolution method, which successfully converges to the optimal feedback regulator in a few seconds. Our study further demonstrates the derivation of the stable manifold and the construction of a local finite-dimensional feedback stabilizer using a distance-to-ellipse approach in a general Banach space setting. This contributes new methods in optimal control theory and linearized stability analysis in a general context, which can be applied independently of the Navier-Stokes system in a symbolic algebraic framework. Our work is intended to address a long-standing open question in this area, posed by Kazhikhov in 1998, regarding the finite-dimensional local stabilization of the three-dimensional Navier-Stokes system in a wide variety of function spaces, including the critical Lq energies in dimensions three and four. Our study provides a partial answer to this question, focusing on the context of finite-dimensional interior localized feedback regulations in a unified, distance-sensitive framework. Our work is designed to be versatile, allowing for the derivation of decay rates and uniform bounds for solutions in a wide range of function spaces through a distance-sensitive approach. Our study encompasses the limit cases where q approaches one or infinity in a natural manner. Our work is intended to extend the existing body of research in this area, including the work of Temam and Ziane in 1999, as well as the work of Glangetas and Lutz in 1990, particularly in the context of weak or strong solutions in low-dimensional systems. Language serves as the primary means of communication, enabling connections and understanding between individuals. Mastering language requires thorough knowledge of words and their associated meanings. The development of computational techniques for language analysis has been driven by advances in dictionaries. Traditionally, dictionaries have been compiled by lexicographers, but with the rise of the internet, online resources have become a valuable alternative. The LitMind Lexicon, a web-based dictionary, is one such resource, offering a data set and tools for language analysis. With over 1.3 million entries, it provides definitions and example sentences for word research and meaning interpretation. With over 700 million words in its corpus, it enables frequency and part-of-speech analyses, making it a valuable tool for computational language studies. This paper introduces the LitMind Lexicon and outlines its methodologies for compiling definitions, example sentences, and word frequency data. In addition, it examines the characteristics of the lexicon and showcases six practical applications using the litmind dict -- text classification, word segmentation, machine translation, named entity recognition, part-of-speech tagging, and semantic feature calculation --, demonstrating the lexicon's vast capabilities in computational language studies. Comparative studies revealed that the litmind dict excels the Xinxi Wang Lexicon and the HowNet, surpassing them in definition coverage and example sentence diversity. Ultimately, we conclude that the litmind dict emerges as a reliable data set and useful tool for language analysis. The lexicon and associated tools are available for download at https://www.litmind.cn/. Additionally, an interactive interface for dictionary usage can be accessed at https://dict.litmind.cn/. In order to achieve robust learning even in the presence of imbalanced or unevenly distributed data, researchers have explored the effectiveness of combining global and local information with synthetic data. This technique involves training neural networks on a centrally located global dataset while also using selected regional datasets to adjust the global decision boundaries. Although prior studies have studied the impact of sample count and number of regional datasets on performance, they simultaneously modified both the global and regional classifiers, leading to conflicting results. This has resulted in a lack of clarity in understanding the relationship between the number of regional queries and achieved accuracy. We establish that the optimal number of regional queries depends on the distribution of class data within the regional space and introduce a method for determining the optimal number of queries for applied regions. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach using comprehensive evaluations of prior techniques, our proposed optimal query method, and a novel strategy for selecting applied regions on multiple datasets from the UCI Machine Learning Repository, achieving an average 6.3% improvement in accuracy. We further highlight the advantages of our approach by comparing it to prior work. The second iteration of our fast algorithm for optimal transport, initially presented in arXiv:1809.10395, is the subject of this investigation. The previous version, arXiv:1809.10395, had an time complexity of O(n^1.5), which was substantially faster than the traditional O(n^2) methods. In this study, a novel computational technique, referred to as Linear TC-TCP, for computing optimal transport is proposed. The proposed technique employs a novel triangular array for handling evaluations and leverages the unique properties of block-wise euclidean distance to calculate pairwise distances in O(n), thereby facilitating the application of the Bregman Variational Gradient algorithm, a renowned efficient method for optimal transport, to attain a linear time complexity of O(n). It is worth noting that the proposed TC-TCP method requires special handling of diagonal entries, which is a critical factor for its efficacy. Furthermore, the computational complexity of the proposed method is conditional, contingent upon the level of subdiagonal data's accuracy. In cases where high-accuracy data is ensured, the proposed method is characterized by the complexity of O(0.69*n), a sublinear efficiency. In order to enhance the computational stability, a precise renormalization method, referred to as Precise-Renormalization, for calculating projective matrices is proposed. The proposed technique is accompanied by a detailed proof of convergence. The proposed methods are rigorously tested using real-world datasets, and our tests confirm that they are effective and reliable. Notably, our fast algorithms have been successfully applied in various fields, including computer vision, gene regulation, and other domains. When exposed to intense nuclear radiation, the sample's environment undergoes a significant transformation, which in turn affects the measurement of the sample's properties and can even induce the phenomenon of drag. This is particularly evident in the context of the liquid-metal halide solutions that comprise the halogen-penetration-depth drag experiment. To model the effect of radiation on such environments, we propose an approach based on the principle of energy minimization, drawing analogies to the study of liquid mercury. We apply this model to the specific case of GPDD in liquid EILH-Fe, and find that it aligns with historical experimental data. We also utilize this model to explore the long-term behaviors of GPDD in various systems following different types of radiation exposures, including the potential for a stable, regular oscillatory behavior. Ultimately, this work serves as a starting point for developing more sophisticated coevolutionary models of the interactive behavior of radiation, the substance, and the experimentally observed drag phenomenon. By utilizing radio-frequency detection, we examine the influence of various interstitial regions on the system, namely a quantum point adjacent to an insulating gate, a normally conducting gate, and a gate that induces multiple islands. In the case of the insulating gate, the quantum point's tunneling rate is shown to be predominantly driven by multi-electron collisions between the quantum point and the insulating gate. For the case involving a normally conducting gate, the quantum point's tunneling behavior can be described by both single-electron collisions with the nearby island and multi-electron collisions with the insulating gate. Lastly, the quantum point's tunneling dynamics is fully attributed to single-electron collisions with the multiple islands that are induced by the conducting gate. These experimental findings are particularly valuable in the context of ultra-low background cavity Penning traps, a field in which single events can be identified with high sensitivity. Such an environment necessitates a thorough comprehension of the underlying charge-tunneling mechanisms at the low-temperature regime. Ultimately, our results present a choice for optimizing the design of future quantum devices: the quantum point could be designed as an island, or alternatively, the insulating gate could be employed as a barrier. Furthermore, the charge-tunneling mechanisms are also modeled using a multi-level density of states approach, thus offering an essential tool for device design in the quantum domain. In the realm of scalar conservation laws, a notable example of an entropic contraction in the L1 norm can be found in Kruzhkov's work in 1977. For systems of conservation laws, Kruzhkov and Lusk in 1994 demonstrated an entropic contraction in the so-called Kruzhkov's norm, but a well-established standard in the context of scalar conservation laws has proven challenging to replicate. In a new work titled "Some new entropic contractors for systems of preservation laws", the concept of Kruzhkov's norm is modified and applied to derive new entropic contractors for certain conservation laws. These contractors are then utilized to establish a variety of standards for entropic discontinuities in the L1 data class. In the current research, a combination of Kruzhkov-Lusk's contraction and the generalization of Kruzhkov's norm concept introduced in our previous study is applied to demonstrate a comprehensive set of entropic contractors for potential use in generic systems of one-space-dimensional conservation laws. Our analysis, in contrast to Kruzhkov-Lusk's and the new norm concept, does not involve an exponential function, making it more suitable for potential one-space-dimensional systems of conservation laws. In the course of our discussion, a particular example is provided in the context of the Euler equations for barotropic fluid dynamics, where a contracted L1 ball is established for entropic shock wave solutions, subject to specific small data conditions and in the absence of a pressure function exponent equal to one. The Hunter-Saxton equation has significant ties to the rotation group's $SO(2)$, and it appears in various contexts with connection to the Euler-Poisson equations and surface dynamics.
In the past, research on the Hunter-Saxton equation has focused mainly on its solution properties, and only a limited number of studies, such as those by Liu and Liu or Liu and Liu again, have explored the equation's robustness.
We build upon their findings in this research by demonstrating the robustness of the Hunter-Saxton equation under a specific metric, and we extend their outcomes by showing the equation's Lipschitz robustness, utilizing a novel technical approach. 
We also reveal that more detailed information can be derived from the metric's properties in the reduced phase space. 
Finally, we illustrate through examples the importance of considering these robustness properties in the context of least action principles and phase space geometry. 
It is our hope that this study contributes a piece of mathematical insight in the continued efforts to grasp the Hunter-Saxton equation's intricate geometry.

Evaluating scoliosis using ultrasound imaging requires experienced professionals to measure the spinal curve manually. A proposed more reliable method involves employing an robotic system to increase consistency in measurements. However, using ultrasound imaging with robotic technology comes with its own reliability issues. The goal of our study was to compare the dependability of robotic ultrasound imaging technology for scoliosis assessment with that of traditional manual measurement. To achieve this, we examined the measurement errors associated with ultrasound imaging on robotic and manual setups. The results showed that robotic ultrasound imaging is as trustworthy as manual measurement, with only marginal differences between the two in terms of reliability. The findings indicate that robotic ultrasound imaging is a viable option for scoliosis assessment, offering the advantage of being less fatiguing and capable of producing consistent results over extended periods of time. Further research is necessary to explore the feasibility of ultrasound imaging in clinical scoliosis diagnosis. A key factor behind their success lies in their ability to effectively merge low and high-level information through concatenation or feature exchange.  For multi-input, multi-output (MIMO) tasks, DCNNs typically employ feature exchange as a means of sharing knowledge between different inputs.  Nevertheless, conventional feature exchange methods fail to account for the shared nature of MIMO inputs, thereby hindering their performance in such scenarios.  In this paper, we introduce a novel semi-supervised feature exchange (SSFE) technique designed for MIMO networks, primarily to facilitate the sharing of knowledge among MIMO inputs through a cross-patient low-dimensional embedding space.  Initially, SSFE generates a low-dimensional patient embedding to facilitate knowledge sharing among MIMO inputs.  Next, SSFE integrates a multi-input, wide-depth DCNN with multiple outputs, designed to extract robust low-dimensional patient and input feature representations that are then combined through a symmetric classifier to produce a unified output.  In addition to performing feature exchange, SSFE incorporates a novel multi-input, multi-output dataset to generate robust low-dimensional patient embeddings.  In doing, SSFE achieves higher accuracy than the current best performance in multi-view breast cancer diagnosis tasks. The unstructured environment that industrial robots operate in poses a constant threat to their stability, and the possibility of colliding with fixed boundaries or other obstacles is always present. In order to safely enable robots to execute tasks outside of controlled manufacturing settings, it is essential to implement sophisticated control systems. This research presents a method for utilizing supplementary sensors to regulate the movement of an industrial robot through assessing its dynamic movement and utilizing feedback control to prevent erratic behavior. An elastostatic model-based controller was developed and tested on a six-axis Denso robotic arm using experimental data, resulting in notable improvements in motion smoothness and efficiency, as evidenced by a 50% reduction in oscillations and optimized trajectory execution. The effectiveness of this system in mitigating external disturbances and facilitating accurate and efficient task completion was demonstrated through various experiments. This research marks the first implementation of a similar technology on an industrial robot and contributes significantly to the field of industrial robotics. Results were also reported through an experimental competition focused on smooth motion. Additional information, including related videos and data, is available online at https://ofset.github.io/2022/#3d-printing-robot-kinematics-visualization. The supplementary material includes a customized PointCloud3D Jupyter widget for visualizing three-dimensional data. The source code for this project, as well as an associated processing application for generating three-dimensional motion plots, can be found on the OFSET GitHub repository. A novel approach to analyzing extensive health records is suggested, centered on the concept of life history. By creating a dimensional framework evaluating multiple health states, researchers can craft a map illustrating the progression of a patient's health over time. This concept is applied through a quantitative map, plotting the probability of specific health conditions against each other, against time, and based on various health markers. A statistical method is developed to estimate these probabilities from available data. As part of this approach, a technique is introduced to identify patterns in these probabilities, allowing researchers to better comprehend the health patterns and significant factors involved. The approach is demonstrated using a large dataset of people who experienced a myocardial infarction in Turin, Italy between 1990 and 2013, along with a discussion of its potential to guide clinical decisions and inform public health initiatives. All related data and code can be accessed online. This innovative strategy aims to unlock new insights from the wealth of data collected in modern healthcare systems. It leverages cutting-edge tools, including data visualization and mapping techniques, to create interactive and dynamic health journey representations for patients, focusing on the myocardial infarction perspective. A related tool, the Life Course Health Pathway Analyzer, is developed to facilitate this approach, showcasing its potential in the context of cardiovascular diseases. Moreover, a comparison is made with similar approaches, highlighting the unique characteristics of this methodology and setting a foundation for its advancement in the field of life history analysis. This research is made available for public use with the aim of spurring further development and expansion in this direction. One promising strategy for modeling complex solutes in water involves projecting the solute's electron density onto a structured grid system, known as quadrature points. Several studies have already explored this approach, although most have focused on individual sets of quadrature points. Our proposed method involves generating a unified set of quadrature points capable of accurately capturing the behavior of all types of solutes by extrapolating the optimal quadrature points from a reference set derived from hydrogen atoms through a Bessel function scaling procedure. Our scaled quadrature points maintain the symmetry and rotational invariance characteristic of real-space approaches, while outperforming existing methods in terms of accuracy for a range of solutes with moderate atom pairs. Our findings indicate that projecting electron density onto a 256-point grid, achieved in under 10 megabytes, is sufficient to produce highly accurate results. Our method enables solute modeling with improved efficiency, effectiveness, and flexibility compared to existing approaches. Our associated Python software is publicly available at github.com/ atomicmatrix/molecular-continuum. Using this software, we have achieved a significant reduction in computational error for a wide range of solutes when compared to the standard approach involving six quadrature points per heavy atom. Our results show that by extrapolating the optimal quadrature points from a reference set, it is possible to achieve a high-fidelity solution at a lower computational cost. Our method involves two procedures: extrapolation of the reference set of quadrature points and linear combinations of Bessel functions, allowing for unified quadrature points that can model any type of solute, including charged, non-uniform, or diatomic molecules. Our method does not rely on the polarizability of the solvent but instead phonon-like properties of the quadrature points, leading to enhanced performance. Our method involves pre-calculating a reference set of quadrature points for each type of solute and storing these sets, enabling rapid application to a wide range of solutes. Our method does not involve any modifications to the source code of the water simulation, as it is achieved through a pre-processing step, and it is compatible with existing public code repositories. Our method can handle solutes with a highly variable electron density distribution, including charged states. Our method is not limited to the specific grid size used in this work and can be applied to larger or smaller grids, enabling accurate modeling of solutes at a reduced computational cost. This paper introduces a formal structure called the power framework $\mathcal{P}\mathcal{W}\mathcal{R}\mathcal{O}\mathcal{E}$ comprising directed regions, and explores its mathematical attributes. For instance, any partition of a directed region results in a power framework, and the power framework obtained from a directed region is unique up to a specific transformation. Additionally, the power framework is related to harmonic functions. Our findings also lead to the definition of harmonic functions, their maximum and minimum values, Green's identities, and Hilbert's sytem within directed regions. We further extend the power framework to directed areas, and define a notion of potential within it. Potentials derived from continuous functions within a directed area exhibit specific properties, and our work enables the formulation of Hilbert's method within this context. Conversely, any potential within a directed area can be expressed as the difference of two harmonic functions. Moreover, the power framework has an intrinsic connection to the work of Clairaut and Legendre, and our method allows the interpretation of their findings as a specific instance of our general approach. Lastly, the power framework provides a novel perspective on duality, and our work shows that Green's identities reveal the nature of potentials as a specific type of commutative operation within directed areas. Based on these insights, we further explore the power framework and its various applications in monogenic functions, extreme problems, and partial differential equations, as well as the geometric properties of potentials and harmonic functions. One common challenge in medical image categorization tasks is the presence of noisy labels. Deep neural networks can produce noisy labels during training, either intentionally assigned by humans or generated by the data preparation process. Various methods, such as robust loss functions and clean up procedures, have been employed to counter label noise. However, these traditional approaches are limited by high computational demands or ineffective removal of noise. To address these issues, a novel method known as the Bayesian Label Restoration Mechanism (BLRM) is proposed. BLMRn utilizes a specific posterior probability P(L|F) to distinguish between erroneous and accurate labels, differentiating itself from other noise countermeasures by leveraging a well-known statistical framework, the Bayesian framework. By combining a custom-built loss function and a parameter adjustment strategy, BLRM facilitates effective cleanup of noisy labels with minimal computational requirements. Our experimental results demonstrate that BLRM outperforms other noise countermeasures in various scenarios involving different types of label noise and data distributions. Furthermore, BLRM is applied to a real-world problem in the field of gastrointestinal disease image categorization, with the goal of developing a practical tool for practicing clinicians. Our code is publicly available on the computational repository GitHub at the address https://github.com/liuq81/BLRM. In addition to this, BLRM is applicable to a broad range of tasks beyond medical image categorization. In summary, BLRM is intended to mitigate label noise in image processing tasks. Evaluation of BLRM on a large open-source cancer image classification data set using 35 different types of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) reveals that the method achieves consistent and superior performance to other noise countermeasures with a very low additional computational cost. Our results demonstrate that the method successfully removes noisy labels with very little extra computational cost. To further assess the generalization capabilities of BLRM, a series of experiments were conducted using the ENOEN data set, a large, noisy dataset for image categorization with 20 different types of label noise and multiple CNN architectures. Our findings indicate that the method effectively cleans up noisy labels in a wide variety of situations. Ultimately, when compared to other noise countermeasures, BLRM yields superior performance at a very low additional computational cost in a large-scale evaluation conducted across a variety of CNN architectures. To further authenticate the results, two additional experiments were performed. One study confirmed that the underlying probability model of BLRM is effective in distinguishing between noisy and clean labels, while a 2nd investigation revealed that the method's performance on real-world datasets is consistent

This paper introduces and studies a novel interpolation operator $I^{\varphi}_n$ associated with a function $\varphi$, and derives an accurate estimate of its norm in terms of the degree of interpolation $n$, and the $\BMO$-norm of $\varphi$. The findings are then applied to establish the interpolation error for various space-time interpolation scenarios, including the interpolation from the space of Holder continuous functions with negative exponent $\alpha$ to the space of Holder continuous functions with exponent $\beta$, under the condition that $\alpha < \frac{3}{2}+\beta$. The obtained estimates are versatile enough to encompass situations with non-uniform mesh sizes and diverse interpolation domains. Moreover, the dependence of the estimates on $\varphi$ and $n$ allows the choice of an appropriate $\varphi$ to ensure the estimates' tightness. The results are showcased with the specific example of interpolating from the BMO space to the Holder continuous space with exponent $\frac{3}{2}$ and the modified BMO space $\BMO_c^{\ast}(\Omega)$. The proof of the main estimates relies on a combination of the interpolation technique for quasi-norms and the combination-composition method, and provides a novel and practical approach to estimating the norm of the interpolation operator $I^{\varphi}_n$ without assuming the existence of a fundamental tensor for the space. This distinct method offers a local and explicit way to estimate the interpolation error, and is applicable to diverse interpolation scenarios, even those involving complex or unexplored functions. The method's exploration of the properties of the interpolation operator enables a deeper and more precise understanding of its behavior. Furthermore, the approach can be extended to other unexamined functions, and is expected to yield similar results for other space-time interpolation scenarios. Ultimately, the research reveals that the choice of $\varphi$ plays a pivotal role in determining the accuracy of the interpolation error, and demonstrates the significant potential of the combination-composition method in addressing challenging problems in functional analysis and partial differential equations. The work is expected to inspire the development of new and general interpolation techniques and provide a foundation for future advancements in this area. Furthermore, the approach can be applied to address other complex functional analysis and partial differential equations-related problems. A related random walk on a graph with non-negative weights and a connected transition matrix performs a stochastic process. Given two distinct vertices in the graph, the transition probabilities between them are unique and depend on the vertices themselves. When we calculate the transition probabilities between these vertices over time, we obtain a matrix whose elements are polynomials. Notably, the features of this polynomial determine the transition dynamics, and a specific root reveals the long-term likelihood of transitioning between these vertices. In our work, we identify a root that is independent of the vertices in question, as well as a condition that ensures this root is distinct from the transition matrix's eigenvalues. We develop a related random walk theory that encompasses this root and provide an alternative method for calculating it. Our approach is versatile and allows us to adapt it to various scenarios, such as multiple related random walks and graphs with blocking factors. By applying this root to a red protein-degradation model in biology, we are able to simplify the model's stochastic process and observe that this simplification aligns with existing theoretical knowledge. In particular, we are able to derive a closed-form solution for the model's likelihood matrix featuring this root. Our method significantly reduces the computational time needed to calculate the transition matrix, and we are able to verify our theoretical findings using simulated data. Ultimately, we are able to use our proposed statistical method for multiple-degradation protein models to extract the total number of individual degradation proteins from a given protein. Specifically, when dealing with three related random walks in a graph, we are able to calculate a combined transition likelihood independent of the vertices in question and obtain a closed-form solution for the likelihood matrix featuring this root. Notably, our approach is distinct from previous stochastic methods for multi-degradation protein models. In formal tolls like PVS, an assertion language separate from the code's type system is used for specifications. We propose a new way to define a timed type, which PVS lacks, by employing an existing concept called clock restrictions. These restrictions, incorporated into PVS's assertion language, serve as a prototype for defining states with temporally related attributes. We discuss the advantages of using this approach, particularly its balance between the expressiveness of standard PVS definitions and the precision of timed definitions. The integration of timed definitions into PVS's framework involves two primary components: the definition of a timed type and its associated axioms, along with a reflection principle for utilizing PVS's definition mechanisms within a typical PVS development environment. The text presents the formal definition, along with a brief overview of its underlying principles, and demonstrates its applicability through a range of meaningful definitions. We reflect on the potential implications of this definition technique and outline future research directions. A separate appendix provides step-by-step model checker inputs to illustrate the definition's correctness. 

Formally defining what constitutes a valid timed state, especially when incorporating complex system dynamics, can be a substantial challenge. To mitigate this difficulty, PVS's definition mechanism allows for skipping the explicit definition of certain validity axioms when using the definition's universal instantiation property. However, this definition's usefulness is constrained by its one-to-one correspondence between timed states and PVS states, thus limiting its applicability to contexts explicitly defining these validity axioms. To overcome this shortcoming, we employed a unique approach, mixing static and dynamic timing concepts. For instance, we defined a function parameterized by a PVS state and a time to return a timed state, along with a function that takes a PVS state and returns its associated PVS state. This approach, though distinct from the standard definition's universal instantiation property, allows for a useful combination of its uses, thus making the definition more practical in a wider range of situations. 

A significant benefit of our definition technique is its potential for a useful intersection with PVS's refinement mechanism. To illustrate this point, we defined a timed state with a maximum speed of one unit per time unit. To implement this constraint within PVS, we defined a relation capturing the definition's intent and incorporated it into PVS's definition framework. The resulting definition provides a useful illustration of how PVS's definition mechanisms work in conjunction with this particular definition. Building on previous work, a study aimed to refine further the potential of the coherent structure model in predicting instantaneous boundary turbulence. By combining data analysis techniques, researchers were able to develop a detailed model accounting for all significant factors contributing to turbulent fluctuations in a boundary layer. The first step involved categorizing turbulent velocity components into different coherent structures and then comparing this classification to information from experimental experiments to fine-tune a model's calculations. The model was also adjusted to incorporate the interactions between different structures and the effects of energy transfer within them. As a result, a theoretically sound framework was established, providing a foundation for investigating the complexities of turbulent processes. Furthermore, this study's approaches can be applied to other coherent structure models to advance the prediction of turbulent fluctuations. When put into practice, however, it became clear that accurately categorizing turbulent structures and modeling their interactions at the boundary layer is a computationally complex task, often requiring advanced simulations or significant electrical memory. Nonetheless, by incorporating some of these approaches, researchers were able to slightly enhance the predictions of turbulent fluctuations, revealing that significant predictions could be made for some of the turbulent structures that were previously beyond the reach of earlier models. The revised model's predictions of turbulent fluctuations were found to be somewhat improved, although the total error in the predictions remains high, suggesting that further refinements are needed to realize the full potential of this study's approaches. In terms of future research, one of the key considerations will be to refine numerical methods to incorporate the complexities of turbulent processes in a more detailed and precise way. By combining advanced simulations with the techniques described in this study, there may be a path towards a more complete and detailed understanding of turbulent processes. As such, future research may be oriented towards further refining both the theoretical foundations and computational methodologies of this study in order to optimize the prediction of turbulent fluctuations. We investigate the additive anomaly between gauge theories and the infant Skyrme model to develop a Born-Infeld infant Skyrme (BIIS) theory. The vacuum of this theory is characterized by a non-trivial constant 3-form field $H_0$. At its core, the BIIS Toda system emerges, describing motion within an AdS space. Additionally, the theory features self-dual solutions representing the solitons of interest. These solitons are linked with a non-trivial homotopy group $\pi_2(SO(3))$. The solution has implications for the Skyrme model's $B\wedge J$ term when $J$ is not zero, and it predicts the appearance of instantons in the BIIS theory's Euclideanized path-integral formalism. We also derive the one-loop effective action of the theory and observe that its action functional is topologically modified. Moreover, the BIIS Toda system's soliton field is found to display quasi-topological behavior. A specific mathematical condition is derived to ensure the theory's one-loop effective action remains finite. Consequently, under this condition, which involves the Wronskian of two hyperbolic functions, the one-loop effective action does not depend on the 3-form field $H$ but rather the dimension $d$ of spacetime instead. Ultimately, the condition is satisfied in spacetime dimensions $d\geq 5$. To complete our analysis, the BIIS theory's central charge is calculated, depending on $d$; interestingly, under the specified condition, it remains constant in spacetime dimensions $d\geq 5$. Furthermore, the charge is found to display quasi-topological behavior. A physical interpretation of these results is also provided. In particular, we demonstrate that the one-loop effective action's mass spectrum corresponds with the additive anomaly between gauge theories and the infant Skyrme model itself. The BIIS theory's spectral properties are found to be distinct from those exhibited by gauge theories with fermions. In addition, we derive the Euclidean action for the three-dimensional BIIS theory and show that it is characterized by zonal spherical harmonics. Consequently, the theory's spectral properties are found to be distinct from those exhibited by three-dimensional Yang-Mills theory with a Chern-Simons term. Electric current can be generated and directed within a granular material by external magnetic fields, provided that it undergoes specific mechanical transformations such as bending, stretching, and twisting. In this study, numerical simulations based on the discrete element method confirmed a previously hypothesized phenomenon - that magnetic fields can penetrate certain areas within the material while creating an induced current on its surface. To further explore this phenomenon, a coil is wrapped around a core comprised of highly ferromagnetic granules. When exposed to a changing external magnetic field, the coil acts as a magnet, producing an induced electromotive force and current. Notably, the direction and magnitude of this current are closely related to the mechanical deformations experienced by the core. A theoretical model developed for ferromagnetic granular materials successfully explains the results, demonstrating that the electromagnetic properties are largely determined by the core's structural state. This unique property presents considerable opportunities for harnessing electromagnetic energy and may shed light on the intricate electrical properties observed in solid materials. It has also been discovered that the material can exert an anomalous shielding effect, suppressing external electromagnetic fields within specific parameter ranges and mechanically induced deformities have minimal influence on these phenomena. A thorough numerical calculations were carried out to map out the material currents induced by varying magnetic fields and mechanical deformations, thus facilitating an understanding of the mechanics governing these electromagnetic properties. In multi-category text classification, the order of features often has a significant impact on performance, but many machine learning algorithms are unable to utilize this information effectively due to their reliance on a single output or the bagging technique, which distributes data across various outputs without considering relationships between them. Three synthetic oversampling algorithms for multi-category text classification have been proposed, involving the simulation of negative words from positive categories and the simulation of negative categories to accommodate cases where the majority of data belongs to the negative class. The proposed methods were evaluated using text datasets with multiple categories in both bagging and boosting environments and demonstrated superior performance to traditional oversampling techniques. Ultimately, the results suggest that synthetic oversampling can be an effective tool in multi-category text classification.
