Advanced machine learning models can set high standards for performance on specialized tasks, yet frequently struggle with broader applications of related concepts. To enhance model versatility, researchers focus on developing algorithms that can learn from diverse data, but this approach can be resource-intensive and may not be feasible for projects with limited budgets. An alternative solution involves utilizing additional training data specifically designed to improve model versatility, which can be created using techniques such as generating fixed-template text or acid-based mutation on existing examples. We introduce a data enhancement method known as TextFusion, which combines two existing techniques to maximize performance in application fields lacking comprehensive training data: 1) a text insertion technique that places guidance phrases into base examples to convey their core meaning, and 2) a keyword insertion method that replaces guidance phrases in a controlled manner. We apply TextFusion to three classification projects and achieve notable results: our approach surpasses current standards in classification performance on all three datasets we used, without requiring any data augmentation. TextFusion was also found to perform comparably to a leading data augmentation method in a related experiment, but our specific adaptation of the keyword insertion concept surpasses current standards in classification performance in our own study. We further found that our modified text insertion concept with guidance phrases surpasses current standards in classification performance in comparison to the baseline method in our own study. Ultimately, our approach demonstrates the value of leveraging existing models effectively training more general AI models through the use of a dedicated software tool. Our work builds on previous research, complementing Gurevich, Chakravarti, and Osserman's findings from 2019, which established a link between the configuration of primitive lattice points within a parallelogram formed by mapping $\mathbb Z^2 \to \mathbb Z[1/n]$ and the characteristics of a Jacobian variety. Specifically, the research defined a Jacobian variety as primitive, with primitiveity defined as the absence of lattices that map the original Jacobian variety to a smaller one of the same dimension. In our study, we identify necessary conditions for a K3 surface to have a primitive Jacobian variety and, through the K3 Action Theory, we define parallelism for pairs of Jacobian varieties. We establish that each fixed point of the identity component of the automorphism group's action on a K3 parallelism class corresponds to a unique lattice that maps the original K3 surface to a smaller one of dimension two within that class. We identify the possible lattices and evaluate the necessary conditions for a K3 surface to have a primitive Jacobian variety based on its Markovian spectrum. This work generates new constraints on the counts of rational points and the Markovian spectrum of K3 surfaces, thereby expanding the existing constraints identified by Gurevich, Chakravarti, and Osserman. Ultimately, we outline specific parameters within parallelism classes and lattice maps that could potentially yield primitive surfaces, thereby contributing to the ongoing Search for Primitive K3 Surfaces. In the process, we establish a complex Siegel domain that represents all possible lattices in a given K3 parallelism class, thereby complementing existing complex moduli spaces. A related numerical computation has also been conducted, detailed in the accompanying arXiv:2204.11911 document. We have also demonstrated an algorithm for independently evolving the clusters in the $\mathbb H^2$ part of a Siegel domain, which represents a given K3 surface. A novel algorithm has been developed to compute the genus of a complex graph within a polynomial time complexity. This achievement builds upon the existing SPQR tree construction algorithm initially designed by Snoeyink for planar graphs, which we've adapted to handle non-planar graphs through the use of a planarity test. This additional planarity test step, while incrementing the computational time by a polynomial factor, does not violate the overall polynomial time complexity of the overall algorithm. Furthermore, we outline an alternative strategy rooted in a random sampling approach first proposed by Moore and Voigt for estimating the genus of a graph, which samples edges less frequently as the graph size grows larger. We contrast this with our own algorithm, which ensures accurate results for graphs of up to two connected components, while leveraging sampling: (i) to handle graphs of two or more connected components; (ii) to handle graphs lacking specific sub-structures (i.e. K5 and non-articulation points); (iii) to handle graph embeddings that violate certain conditions (i.e. face boundary violations and Euler's formula). We analyze and illustrate the underlying principles of our algorithm through five theoretical cases and a comprehensive real-world testing scenario involving graphs of up to 1000 nodes. According to our findings, our approach consistently outperforms existing algorithms in highly complex graph scenarios. However, our method shows a polynomial increase in computational time in best-case scenarios, which we attribute to the necessity of the planarity test. Notwithstanding this limitation, our algorithm proves to be a valuable addition to the existing arsenal of genus estimation methods due to its superior performance in real-world testing scenarios. Ultimately, our research reveals that random sampling may yield more desirable results than our approach in ideal graph scenarios with the potential to outperform existing methods across the board. Consequently, further research is warranted to explore the feasibility of integrating sampling and planarity testing for accurate and efficient genus estimates. Based on our real-world testing findings, the biggest advantages of our approach can be summarized as follows: (i) uniqueness-to-genus-metric property; (ii) faster runtime compared to existing algorithms in real-world testing scenarios; (ii) accurate results for graphs of up to two connected components; (iv) ability to handle graph components and sub-structures effectively; (v) ability to handle graph embeddings that violate critical conditions. Notwithstanding these achievements, further research is required to optimize existing sampling methods for accurate and efficient genus estimates in all graph scenarios. This paper presents a decentralized algorithm, designed for large-scale convex optimization problems that can be segmented into individual, independently manageable components across a network of interconnected nodes. A novel solution, the Randomized Newton method, leverages personalized computational resources and network connectivity to iteratively refine solutions and achieve optimized performance. By combining elements of stochastic gradient descent, its faster convergence rate, and the robustness to abnormal node behaviors found in distributed gradient descent approaches, the proposed method demonstrates strong convergence and fault-tolerant properties. Through mathematical proof and simulation-based validation, the Randomized Newton method demonstrates significant performance improvements, surpassing current best practices in distributed optimization techniques. Additionally, the approach offers a new framework for creating resilient network control algorithms that can operate effectively in diverse complex environments. Finally, the method's applicability is further illustrated through its successful application in a real-world scenario involving distributed network flow optimization. Our research involves investigating the use of neural networks to identify hate-speech in two Indian languages, Hindi and Bengali. Given the significant harm caused by hate-speech on minority groups, our aim is to develop a comprehensive study that explores the possibilities of identifying hate-speech in these languages. Alongside our main contribution, which is an annotated corpus tagged as hate-speech in Hindi and Bengali, and a related classification task, we also compare the predictive capabilities of several neural network architectures based on features such as graphs, word and character-based sequences, and deep networks. By examining the effectiveness of transfer learning (using a model fine-tuned from a related task) and a one-shot approach, our study reveals that hate-speech classification in less resourced languages can be successfully achieved with Indo-European language-based pre-trained models. Furthermore, we highlight the importance of considering linguistic properties and developing novel neural architectures for improved hate-speech identification. Our findings also stress the need for a better understanding of hate-speech, particularly in the context of Indian subcontinent relations, and for label-balanced training to enhance the predictive capabilities of hate-speech models. Through a thorough analysis of experimental results, we explore challenges faced by models, providing a deeper understanding of the task and its limitations. Ultimately, our study highlights the potential of hate-speech identification in promoting social well-being through advanced machine learning advancements. In space exploration, reliable nuclear energy is essential, and this requires advanced radiation detection tools that can operate in severe environments and accurately distinguish between various gamma rays. To meet these demands, scientists are developing high-tech gas time-projection chambers that can pinpoint nuclear events with precision, even taking into account the recoil of interaction particles. Since nuclear recoil frequently corresponds with neutron radiation, accurately measuring recoil detection is vital for evaluating the effectiveness of neutron area detectors. To facilitate direct measurements of recoil detection, we introduce two new metrics: the recoil light yield and the recoil signal size. These measures provide a transparent way of considering recoil particles participating in interactions that have left signal traces in detectors. We will illustrate the application of these metrics using data from SIM-PTC, a state-of-the-art gas time-projection chamber at CEA-Saclay. Moreover, we will investigate and compare these methods with other conventional techniques used to estimate recoil detection, such as the use of mapping-uncertainty analysis. By using simulations of elastic-scatter events and actual data from SIM-PTC experiments, we will evaluate the sensitivity of each method. It has been determined that simulated elastic-scatter events can be detected by the SIM-PTC detector with an 80% efficiency. The GUIDES project seeks to enhance smart city development, specifically by improving management of urban infrastructure. This focus on infrastructure, which underpins all other aspects of a smart city, allows for more efficient governance and service delivery to citizens. The project aims to achieve this through the semantic annotation of city infrastructure systems, which will be shared via the Open Data Platform to support decision-making and service offering. The project has developed a set of common concepts for defining infrastructure, as well as a knowledge engine to provide COMPARE, a classifier capable of identifying users' geographical areas and suggested settings for data sharing. The project has also developed the Data Browser, a tool for discovering and visualizing data based on users' interests. The project's findings will be shared through GUIDES City, a knowledge base and platform for exchanging best practices and future research directions. The project will evaluate its performance using metrics such as data quality, energy consumption, and cost, which will be evaluated in four initial cities - Bari, Bologna, Reggio Calabria, and Rome - with plans for the expansion to Brescia, L'Aquila, and other cities across Italy. The project's performance will be continuously monitored, with the evaluation of external factors, such as the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic. The project's source code, as well as all technical documentation, will be publicly available on GUIDES City. The project will maintain regular communication with the research and development communities through regular meetings and conferences, including the submission of papers at key events, such as the 2020 Workshop on Dataset and Semantics at ISWC. TERS is an advanced technique for analyzing the properties of materials at a nanoscale, which uses electromagnetic signals to gather information about samples. However, the complex electromagnetic signal's interaction with the sample also provides valuable data. Theoretical simulations are necessary to fully comprehend the relationship between this interaction and sample characteristics, and to distinguish non-sample components of the signal from the sample's unique properties. These simulations are necessary for interpreting TERS images, as the technique measures the sample's varying properties in addition to its spatial distribution. The price of this insight is the loss of control over the influence of the probe and sample-probe interactions, which hampers the capability to accurately predict the sample's distribution of electromagnetic properties. To rectify this, we developed a full quantum mechanical model of the probe and sample, which is the first of its kind for TERS. The results show that the probe's influence is more substantial than previously thought and that correcting for it is essential for accurate assessments of electromagnetic properties within samples. The probe's effect is particularly noticeable in scenarios involving samples with covalent bonds or those with electrostatically or thermally driven variations. The proposed approach is not only applicable to TERS but can also be applied to other techniques, such as SNOM and STM, to greatly expand the scope and understanding of nano-scale electromagnetic property mapping. Reconciling the benefits of centralized and decentralized control structures is the focus of our paper, where we introduce a framework that reconciles the drawbacks of pure decentralization and the inflexibility of pure centralization. Key aspects of our approach are highlighted through a simulator built with the Three Amigos framework. By achieving collective autonomy, our method allows the coordination of local decisions made by individual agents within a multi-agent system, striking a balance between the unpredictability of fully decentralized models and the rigidity of fully centralized models. The simplicity of our approach enables the seamless integration of new agents within such systems, making it adaptable to a wide range of applications. Furthermore, our method does not necessitate detailed knowledge of all agents' objectives, making it applicable to situations where goal information is unavailable. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through a series of evolutionary simulations that show its capacity for rapid adaptation and its robustness in diverse scenarios. In contextual named entity extraction, we're dealing with a complex problem of identifying words related to specific entities. Unlike overall text, our focus is on individual words' connections to entities. We've found that word importance varies greatly depending on the class it belongs to and the number of entities it's associated with. By considering this term importance, which can be obtained through context-free models like BERT or ELMo, we're enhancing the ability of contextual NER models to identify words crucial to specific entities. Experimental results from both fine-grained and coarse NER tasks demonstrate the significant improvement achieved. Furthermore, our method is highly scalable and can be seamlessly integrated into existing researchers' and practitioners' contextual NER workflows. We've made our code and training data available for download. After thorough evaluation, we conducted ablation tests to validate the effectiveness of our term importance approach and verified that it's particularly effective even when the dataset in question is small. What's more, our method is particularly beneficial in English text but showed promising performance with limited success in six languages with fewer than 10,000 entities. Ultimately, our experiments have shown that providing term importance is a viable approach to enhance the ability of contextual NER models to identify words related to specific entities. We believe this strategy could be applied to various natural language processing tasks, not just NER. Users interact more effectively with data visualization than with raw numbers; however, certain types of analysis require scrutiny. Although properties of univariate datasets are well understood, those of multivariate datasets are still under research. This paper focuses on how to interact with multivariate temporal data (MTD) consisting of multiple series that simultaneously describe a phenomenon. Current methods involve displaying individual channels individually and comparing them in separate plots, but these approaches has drawbacks. To address this, the ISee platform enables users to interact with MTD using a continuous, one-screen display. This research is part of a larger effort to develop a comprehensive theory of interaction with MTD. In this study, the MTD is represented as a four-dimensional temporal display (three dimensions for context and one for observation), and users are given two interactive tools: selection of interest areas, and scrolling. To facilitate understanding and navigation, the MTD is represented as a linear combination of simpler datasets called channels. This concept is formalized in a mathematical model called the MTD-Linear Combination (MTLC) model. The study demonstrates that MTLC is versatile, applicable to various real-world datasets. Key findings from our study include the discovery of five common patterns in multidimensional temporal data and the development of strategies for efficiently exploring such datasets. In addition to the theoretical contributions, our study demonstrates the practical value of the ISee platform and its potential in fields like healthcare. For example, it can be used by clinical researchers to analyze the complex interplay between a patient's blood levels and clinical markers during a clinical trial. Following our user study, we identified areas for further improvement of the ISee platform, laying the groundwork for future research. Ultimately, our research aims to contribute to a deeper understanding of interaction models for multidimensional temporal data and to inspire the development of new visual interfaces. The theoretical model is validated by comparing it to a system comprising a superconducting interface and an electrolyte, where the interfacial charge arises from a complex order parameter describing the phase ordering of the interface. Additionally, the theory allows for the prediction of capacitance in various scenarios and reveals that capacitance is largely unaffected by the solvent polarization parameter when the electrolyte contains a monovalent ion but exhibits a substantial dependence on the solvent polarization parameter when the electrolyte contains multivalent ions. By integrating the Dirac equation with a specified electronic structure of Nb, the calculated electronic density of a magnetically isolated impurity aligns with experimental ySR state density measurements, and the calculated ySR state energy dependencies on the magnetization direction are consistent with predicted quantum oscillations. Furthermore, the calculated electronic properties of magnetically coupled dimers and coupled impurities demonstrate sufficient accuracy for qualitative interpretation of experimental results, and the calculated phase shift and magnetic properties are comparable with those of surface and bulk transition metals. The calculated ySR state energies and magnetic properties are used to determine spin-diffusion length and other parameters, and the calculated current properties of magnetically coupled impurities are in agreement with predicted oscillatory behavior. The goal of distribution-to-distribution scan alignment is to match a training distribution with a testing distribution by learning representation methods that ignore irrelevant variations and emphasize meaningful similarities.  Although method extensions have successfully overcome many distribution variations, some have led to biased models, causing poor performance on other datasets.  Our primary goal is to identify and eliminate prejudice in improved model extensions.  To achieve this, we introduce a novel approach called 2DD2D-PF, combining a general approach with a specific algorithm based on a deep neural network.  By testing 2DD2D-PF on various extensions and datasets, we demonstrate its effectiveness in eliminating prejudice in extended distribution-to-distribution scan alignment model extensions.  Furthermore, 2DD2D-PF's general filter can be applied to other types of extensions beyond its current implementations, allowing for effortless adaptation.  Moreover, 2DD2D-PF's deep neural network component can be adapted for other filtering methods, making the development of bias-free extended model extensions a practical reality.  Lastly, 2DD2D-PF's ability to balance relevance and robustness is an important step towards eliminating prejudice in future extension performance evaluations. In the field of electromagnetic signal processing, machine learning has been a key player for centuries, providing optimized signal recognition and categorization algorithms. Despite this, the primary approach of training a model from scratch using labeled data is inherently flawed, as it leaves the model vulnerable to attacks that manipulate the clean signal training library. This adverse effect is particularly concerning for the military, where the compromise of classified datasets could jeopardize national security. To mitigate this risk, various techniques such as adversarial training, feature masking, and dataset disguising methods have been employed to safeguard against hostile attacks on the training host. This research introduces novel techniques to combine multiple strategies for an enhanced training protocol, specifically focusing on categorizing radio frequency modulation schemes. To this end, an archive of six modulation scheme variants was created, along with the corresponding disjoint datasets, to simulate an adversarial scenario where the model is trained with multiple datasets simultaneously. This approach is distinct from previous research, which mainly focused on manipulating the training dataset itself to resist attacks. Additionally, we describe an innovative technique for detecting and assessing the level of host disruption, based on the concept of cross-entropy. This method is capable of identifying the degree of host disruption after an attack has occurred. Segmentation of Multiple Sclerosis lesions in brain MR images plays a crucial role in diagnosing and evaluating MS treatment effectiveness. Recent advances in machine learning have led to the creation of MS segmentation models, but these models are often tailored to specific datasets and work optimally when trained from scratch using a large amount of labeled data. A recent approach called online continuum learning allows for the adaptive training of models without needing to retrain from scratch, without compromising performance. We conducted an experiment comparing an online continuum learning model with a large pre-trained MS segmentation model and a model trained from scratch using limited annotated data. The results show that the online continuum learning model maintained its high accuracy while avoiding performance degradation commonly experienced by models trained without it. This approach has the potential to reduce costs associated with collecting extensive labeled datasets and improve the efficiency of medical image segmentation tasks. Code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/alexk165/MS_Seg_OL. Our study's outcomes suggest promising avenues for future research in the field of continuous learning in the medical imaging domain. Considering the success of this study, we recommend applying online continuum learning to other medical image segmentation tasks to achieve comparable results. An extended version of this article is also published at arXiv:2101.06459. Please see the related paper for a more detailed analysis. 

Please note that a version of this work was presented at the Medical Imaging Learning with Less Data (MIL2D) 2020 challenge hosted by CBMI. The competition link is https://mil2d2020.cbmi.it/ (running between March May 2020) where we secured the 1st place. The data used for this study was obtained from the MIL2D2020 challenge dataset which consists of 30 patients, each with two MRI scans, along with manually annotated lesions for training and validation purposes. We implemented and compared three models as described in the abstract. The code for the MIL2D2020 challenge can be accessed at https://github.com/alexk165/MIL2D2020_solution_Alexandre_Kowal. Our study's outcomes suggest that decreasing the number of optimization steps in the online continuum learning process can help maintain the model's performance on a particular dataset. Conversely, extending the number of optimization steps may lead the model to converge better in a low-data setting. Consequently, we recommend fine-tuning models with large pre-trained counterparts for better MS segmentation results, while adjusting the number of optimization steps for other datasets to achieve optimal performance.

A system consisting of rigid wedges composed of spheres was experimentally studied through observation in both static and dynamic conditions. The objective of the study was to detect the states of idleness and dynamic stability within the system. The experiment involved the systematic placement of two 6-mm diameter spheres between two fixed points on a horizontal surface. The third sphere, of different colors, was placed at varying distances from the line connecting the first two spheres to assess its stability. The results revealed a well-established state of splay variation in the two-sphere system and an approximate expression was derived to describe this state. However, it was found that the three-sphere system exhibits different states of splay variation and dynamic stability, characterized by complex and non-repetitive motion, as well as states marked by quasi-periodic and chaotic behavior. The results also demonstrate that the three-sphere system is capable of producing a new state of splay variation. The approximations and descriptions obtained through the study have notable limitations in terms of practical applicability, as they are derived under the assumption of rigid contact between the spheres, an assumption that is inherently opposed to the stable states of splay variation. The study concludes with the suggestion that future research involving lyapunov exponents could be used to analyze in greater detail the dynamic behavior of the three-sphere system through the application of methods such as Poincare sections and the FFT method. The study contributes to the development of more accurate and dynamic models describing these stable states of splay variation. The methods described in the study have the potential to be applied to a wider range of complex mechanical systems. The associated movie depicts an animation of the dynamic behavior of the three-sphere system composed of 6-mm diameter spheres using the methods described in the study. The animation shows the distinct states of splay variation and dynamic stability characterized by the system. The movie requires the insertion of a username and password for access due to copyright restrictions. The required information can be provided upon request. The primary data used to conduct the study is contained within the attached Microsoft Excel spreadsheet. The spread sheet is titled "Dinamika-lyagkiesfer". The study was based on findings presented at the 25th Conference on Technical and Physical Problems in Ground Transport, held in St. Petersburg, Russia in 2019. The resulting contribution was awarded the prize for the best scientific report at the conference. The study was also selected as the winner of the scientific competition "The Best Research in Transport" in the Mathematical Modeling category in 2020

This new framework enables us to unravel the intricate relationships between thermodynamic properties and dynamic behavior in glass-forming polymer liquids. Therefore, applying the TDCs to these systems is a natural next step. In this work, we systematically explore the connection between slow dynamics and thermodynamic properties in glass-forming polymers. From weak to strong deviations from random mixability, we establish unique dynamic invariants for various configurations of the systems. In particular, we demonstrate that the dynamics can be effectively characterized by combining Zeros of Density Autocorrelation Functions and Standard Deviations of Relaxation Times with appropriate combinations of thermodynamic variables. In order to test the validity of this approach, we conducted simulations on different polymers, such as Bjerrum, Mean-Shift, and Soft-Sphere models, covering a wide range of temperatures and densities. In addition, we also performed experiments on Poly(alloyate) and Poly(ethylene carbonate)-co(-L-lactide) to verify the applicability of this method. Comprehensive simulations across various parameter spaces in the weak and strong deviation regimes of TDCs have proven the existence and controllability of the predicted invariants. Consequently, we obtained a dynamic map that can be modified to accommodate diverse scenarios by adjusting the thermodynamic variables. This approach effectively facilitates the exploration of the complex energy landscape in glass-forming polymer liquids and establishes dynamic invariants that can be used to optimize material compositions and processing conditions. Ultimately, the dynamic maps can be utilized to identify suitable configurations for numerous applications, such as soft matter, drugs, and functional polymers. On a larger scale, the underlying strategy of characterizing complex systems through universal geometric patterns in the configuration space could also be generally applicable to solve real-world problems. In response, this research introduces two new architectures from the Transformer family that directly account for rejection handling in language models.  Each approach is grounded in theories from developmental psychology and cognitive science, suggesting that children initially process acceptance more readily than rejection.  As a result, the rejection rate in these models should mirror the lower acceptance rate observed in children, according to psychological theories.  We evaluate these models against standard transformer architecture and find significant improvements in response generation, with particular gains in accuracy for rejection scenarios.  In addition, the results of this research are consistent with existing psychological theories on rejection processing.  Furthermore, the research also examines the influence of vocabulary size on model performance and finds that smaller vocabularies can hinder both normal and rejection-specific response generation.  Ultimately, the research highlights the value of integrating psychological and neurological insights into the development of artificial general intelligence. Cutting-edge systems for natural language processing lack the ability to explain their decisions, making it difficult for artists and designers working with these models to fully understand the underlying creative processes. By applying the concept of "forward thinking" from the field of psychology, we developed an innovative method, incorporating a specific type of attention mechanism, called the Look-ahead Focus attention, with an eye on understanding the internal workings of neural language models. This approach effectively reveals the sequence of events in a language generation process, uncovering novel insights into the nature of creative computations in the brain. Through computational modeling and a user study, we investigated the Look-ahead Focus method, uncovering new psychological phenomena associated with these processes. The results suggest that understanding neural language models requires not only examining their internal operations but also considering the sequence of events driving their generative processes. Ultimately, we believe that developing creative machine interpretation systems that cater to the needs of artists and designers can have far-reaching benefits, while also shedding light on the complex nature of human creativity. With this goal in mind, we aim to establish a collaboration between artists, designers, and researchers to tackle the various dimensions of this shared area of investigation.

This article develops a method for calculating Kontsevich weights precisely in the context of symplectic-Poisson systems, utilizing a multi-form expansion that is easily derived through the double commutant method. It then applies this procedure to find the curvature graph weights, and in doing so it obtains previously unknown results for a class of Poisson structures defined on the cotangent space of a Lie algebra, including the Lie-Poisson system itself. Additionally, this procedure yields simple expressions for the weight of graphs featuring edges of odd multiplicity on semisimple Lie algebras, which are derived in a basis that is not necessarily standard. It also obtains a multi-form expansion for the edge weight that is universally applicable, and in doing so it yields symmetric results. Finally, this procedure is extended to certain groups, including SU(3), and the associated graph weights are computed. It should be noted that the calculated weights are specifically defined by the context of symplectic-Poisson systems, and do not generally apply in arbitrary Poisson systems. Moreover, the weights are known only to be semiquantitative approximations to the precise weights, as derived in this article. Conversely, the calculated weights may serve as an expedient means of computing the precise weights through the unwinding of the multi-form expansions. In this spirit, the calculated edge weight for a line is specifically demonstrated to converge to the precise edge weight as the multiplicity approaches infinity. It then follows from the calculated multi-form expansions that the precise edge weight for a Lie-Poisson system on the cotangent space of a semisimple Lie algebra, defined in a basis that is not necessarily standard, is simply one-half the multiplicity-odd term of the calculated multi-form expansion for the edge weight on a standard basis. Xie et al's  structure is a useful combination of Galerkin and weak formulation approaches that enable efficient computation and high valuation accuracy for Asian options. We provide evidence that their method is inherently prone to errors in traditional least-squares implementation, leading to underestimation of option values when using finite elemental bases. We offer an alternative formulation based on weak formulation and Galerkin decomposition to rectify these issues, along with a novel weighting scheme that improves accuracy and stability. Simulated data reveal that incorporating the correct boundary conditions and adjusting the weighting parameter can significantly enhance the valuation precision of Asian options. We also observe that dual weighted Galerkin decomposition is an effective method for valuing options with fine details and complex price structures. Furthermore, our analysis for a multi-geometric Brownian motion model illustrates that the valuation results are equally applicable to a variety of Markov processes. We provide concrete justification for the correctness of Xie et al's original formulation, attributing the numerical underperformance to the absence of dual mass matrix in traditional least-squares implementation in the context of Galerkin methods. We prove that adding the dual mass matrix can rectify these issues, in line with the numerical results obtained from our simulation study. We also prove that the valuation method can be extended to a more comprehensive setting, encompassing option-to-share and option-to-future valuations with option-dependent strike prices, frictions and other features. However, even with the advanced dual mass matrix formulation, accurately capturing the numerical underperformance observed in the simulation study appears to be beyond its capability. We eventually attribute this issue to an incorrect elemental decomposition in traditional least-squares implementation in the context of Galerkin methods, resulting from a failure to decompose correctly across spatial and temporal dimensions, especially when dealing with non-linear partial differential equations. We ultimately consider the numerical underperformance a manifestation of the interplay between the structural issue of incorrect decomposition, lacking dual mass matrix in traditional least-squares setting and the associated accuracy loss, implying the need to integrate dual mass matrix and correct elemental decomposition in Galerkin methods in order to achieve high valuation precision in the context of partial differential equations governing option pricing. In particular, a novel discovery was made on a large scale - a gamma-ray halo - that - has a temperature in the millions of degrees Kelvin and is tens of thousands of light years wide. This type of feature has also been found in the areas surrounding over a hundred groups and clusters of galaxies. In some cases, the shape of these features is sinuous and resembles the pattern of a chicken wing, earning them the name 'Fermi Bubbles.' Interpreting convolutional neural network (CNN) vision models has proven challenging despite their impressive performance across various image tasks. Visualizing feature representations and their relationships helps to understand how CNNs operate internally. Although existing methods have made progress in explaining CNN behaviors, they still fail to offer a holistic view of a network's visual dependencies. Moreover, many approaches are plagued by inconsistencies between proposed explanations and actual network behaviors. To address these limitations, we introduce the concept of Latent Visual-Semantic Filter Attention (LVSA), a proposed connectionist interpreter that can reconstruct image datasets from latent codes, while adding semantic details through image manipulation. By proposing this interpreter, we challenge the notion that visual explanations should only mimic network behaviors. Our findings indicate that LVSA can explain GANs and other CNNs with high accuracy and suggest that an overly strict fidelity metric may hinder human understanding of these models. We support our analysis with experiments on multiple datasets, including CIFAR10, ImageNet, STC, and Fashion2012. The project's source code is available for public access at https://github.com/asharakeh/vsemo. Moreover, to the best of our knowledge, this work presents a unique approach to revealing the internal workings of CNNs through visual explanations derived from latent semantic structures. By leveraging LVSA, we can better comprehend the internal workings of CNNs, thereby fostering a deeper understanding of these models' visual reasoning capabilities. Ultimately, this interpretation enables us to evaluate the accuracy of visual explanations and validate the efficacy of LVSA. Our analysis provides a range of potential applications for this approach, encompassing tasks such as evaluating the accuracy of iconic image classification models, discovering new image categories, and revealing the internal workings of state-of-the-art models like ImageNet. To verify the generalizability of LVSA, we successfully apply it to explain a variety of CNN vision models, including different architectures and datasets. Moreover, to the best of our analysis, this approach presents a groundbreaking framework for reconnecting human vision and machine vision through the use of LVSA. Ultimately, this interpretation enables us to evaluate the efficacy of LVSA on various state-of-the-art datasets, thereby solidifying its potential applications and generalizability. This study showcases the varying outcomes of Architectural Effective Cause research, which attempts to identify the causal component of a system without a discernible outcome. By adapting this concept to the evaluation of hidden information in the MPHIA personal dataset, researchers explored its potential applications in the realm of legal proceedings in Japan. Despite the absence of a clear definition of hidden information, the investigation is marked by a persistent query of whether such information exists and what it entails. A particular focus of this study is on architectural components - consisting of hardware, software, and physical spaces - and its causal connections. In this context, the research question is tailored to pinpoint the causal architectural factor contributing to the disclosure of hidden information, with the ultimate aim of developing a system that learns and comprehends human intentions and emotions. A novel approach for unknown hidden information is introduced, utilizing a survey instead of definitional questions to establish the survey's validity. A data-driven approach for hidden information is also presented, leveraging the survey results and a complex dataset to define and induce causal architectural factors. These factors are integrated into a knowledge graph for effective cause analysis, highlighting its practical applications in the real-world use case. A comparative analysis of the results demonstrates the feasibility of induced causal architectural factors in understanding and explaining unknown hidden information on the MPHIA personal dataset. In addition to its practical implications, the research contributes theoretically by integrating structural learning methods with graph clustering and knowledge graph analysis for multi-table structures. A particular method - the Transitivity Inference for Uncovered Knowledge Graphs (TIU-KG) - is introduced, along with its capabilities in node clustering and its extensive applications in diverse domains. A publicly available implementation of the research approach is disclosed, along with its application in the evaluation of architectural effective causes on the MPHIA personal dataset. Furthermore, the research assesses and interprets the causal architectural factors from both qualitative and quantitative perspectives, with a notable recommendation for their practical implementation in the evaluation of architectural effective causes. In terms of social implications, the research has significant consequences for the evaluation of architectural effective causes, with potential applications in various domains, with particular attention to its use in the case of unknown hidden information on the MPHIA personal dataset. Moreover, the research makes a substantial contribution to theoretical understanding of the concept of hidden information and its application in the evaluation of architectural effective causes. With a diverse range of results, the research showcases its uniqueness and originality. Lastly, the research reaches out to diverse communities, with particular attention to its use in the legal profession in Japan and its potential applications in various domains

The second-order Accidental Perturbation method and its variants have been found successful in solving the central equation of classical two-body motion, yielding accurate results. Building upon this foundation, we explored the application of this method to investigate the balance issue of static points in both Saisana and Lidov types of quasi-periodic orbits. Our analysis, however, revealed a peculiar balancing phenomenon, where the application of Accidental Perturbation to static points results in a double degeneracy of the 1:1 resonance divisor. A novel extension of the Accidental Perturbation method has been proposed to tackle this challenge, enabling the identification of resonant arguments and capture curves even when the 1:1 resonance divisor is doubly degenerate. Furthermore, our modified method allows for the characterization of two types of pseudo-balancing static points, as well as balancing for a broader category of quasi-periodic orbits. Our findings confirm that the modified Accidental Perturbation method can efficiently investigate the balance issue of static points with high accuracy. We have computationally validated our results for a few chosen scenarios, and they are consistent with the actual numerical calculations, demonstrating the method's effectiveness and reliability. Our research offers insights into the mechanisms of the second-order Accidental Perturbation method for tackling the balance issue of static points, providing a valuable reference for similar investigations in the field of Hamiltonian mechanics and proper oscillator. Additionally, we have identified four forms of Accidental Perturbation, which can be potentially applied to various proper oscillators and resonant objects, and we have theoretically verified their validity and applicability in the context of a one-dimensional Hamiltonian system. Our method involves iterative calculations to derive the correct equations, and our computational results for a test case show promising accuracy, even with a relatively large perturbation. A major advantage of our approach is that it rectifies a critical shortcoming of the second-order Accidental Perturbation method, where it fails to investigate the balance issue of static points due to a complex equation. Computing the first-order perturbation is a crucial step in the process, and it necessitates the solution of a first-order Accidental Perturbation equation. Due to its nature, the equation's solution depends on the location of the object, and it poses an intricate integral divisor. Some specific scenarios can be solved, such as the Saisana type of quasi-periodic orbits, but a critical challenge arises with the Lidov type of orbits. Our study utilizes a mean-field framework and solves the dynamo equation across its entire frequency spectrum, incorporating complex and non-local interactions that go beyond traditional frameworks. By incorporating a broad range of turbulent influences, we show that the mean magnetic field in a convective dynamo has multiple characteristic patterns, affecting its alignment and orientation in relation to the convective velocity. These turbulent interactions are essential for generating and sustaining the mean magnetic field and have a significant impact at certain scales that are currently overlooked in traditional mean-field theories. We demonstrate that these complex turbulent interactions can be represented by a set of standardized, harmonic coefficients that describe the relationships between the convective velocity and magnetic field across their entire frequency spectrum. These coefficients can then be used to develop a comprehensive and dynamic mean-field dynamo model, allowing for its quantitative application in various complex geophysical and astrophysical contexts. Additionally, we demonstrate that the dynamo equation's solutions exhibit scale-dependent properties and become stationary and isotropic at larger scales, aligning with the expectations of the traditional mean-field frameworks. Nonetheless, at smaller scales, any attempts at simplification will lead to inaccurately low-frequency equations that fail to effectively capture the complexity of the dynamo process across its entire frequency spectrum. By incorporating the complete spectrum of turbulent influences, we have significantly advanced the development of the mean-field dynamo theory and have accurately modeled the intricate relationships between the convective velocity and magnetic field across different scales. Furthermore, we show that the dynamo's ability to generate and sustain the mean magnetic field is primarily influenced by complex interactions at smaller scales, while its orientation is heavily dependent on processes occurring at higher frequencies. This novel mean-field dynamo model, built on a rich frequency-domain framework, is prepared for further development and can be used to develop a highly accurate simulation model, taking into account the intricate properties of the dynamo process and applying them to diverse astrophysical and geophysical settings. Such a model is particularly essential for accurately modeling and analyzing the magnetic field in solar convection, Earth's mantle and core, and other complex convective systems where realistic mean magnetic fields need to be simulated. A novel conservative approximation is developed for Lagrangian finite elements, specifically designed for quasi-linear parabolic PDEs applied to magnetized plasmas' density description. This approach starts by converting the quasi-linear diffusion equation into an equivalent stochastic process, utilizing a finite basis system to transform the equation into a nonlinear problem with initial data based on the inverse of the diffusion matrix's inverse, scaled by a time step and surface area. A suitable numerical method is developed, conserving mass and involving the discretization of the stochastic process via Lagrangian finite elements, defining a random field representing the density distribution and employing time-stepping and surface splitting to approximate the nonlinear problem while ensuring mass conservation and a dimensionally consistent structure. This approach's efficiency is demonstrated with tests of linear and nonlinear diffusion in 2D and 3D environments, as well as an adaptation for use in the quasilinear Boltzmann equation. Additional research reveals the method's potential for broader PDE systems, offering a valuable tool for studying magnetized plasmas. This method is further explored in the arXiv paper "Finite Element Schemes for Stochastic Kinetic Boltzmann Systems with Regularization," which develops schemes for the Boltzmann equation and kinetic equations, building on the framework established here. This article provides a definition of exponential stability for abstract semigroups in Banach spaces and introduces a relationship between exponential stability, input-to-state stability, and a Lyapunov equation. It also establishes connections among these concepts, considering various measures of robustness. What's more, it demonstrates that these concepts of robustness are interrelated via the input-to-state stability theorem. To facilitate these relationships, a notion of multi-step Lyapunov function is defined and its definition and key properties are outlined. Furthermore, a theorem is presented that demonstrates the relationship between the multi-step Lyapunov function and the robustness of the semigroup. Examples are given to illustrate the relationship between the multi-step Lyapunov function and the robustness of the semigroup in the presence of inputs and perturbations. Finally, a practical application of this theoretical framework is demonstrated using a boundary value problem in the field of population dynamics. The research reveals that the notion of multi-step Lyapunov function can be used to derive concrete Lyapunov equations that can be effectively computed using ordinary differential equation solvers, thereby providing a practical computational method for assessing the robustness of the semigroup. The proposed approach has a range of potential applications in the fields of population dynamics, population and population ecology, among others. The corresponding MATLAB code is provided in the supplementary materials. The work is part of a larger research project focused on the practical applications of mathematical modeling, and specifically on the scientific and technological domains of population dynamics, population and population ecology. The model used in the population dynamics population and population ecology is a typical example of a multistable system, and the work presented here focuses on the finer details of its internal dynamics. This paper introduces MuMuPy, a computational software and web-based tool that determines the interaction between muonium molecules and materials. MuMuPy offers the ability to calculate atomic multipole moments and electronic polarizabilities via first-principles methods, in addition to providing a simple way to calculate interaction energies between muonium and various substances through a provided online interface. MuMuPy leverages established methods for calculating condensate-matter interactions, including ab-initio approximation of Born interactions, M\"oller-Plesset many-body perturbation theory, and self-consistent field time-dependent Hartree-Fock theory. This software serves as a useful means to predict and will predict various physical characteristics associated with muonium in different materials. Furthermore, MuMuPy can be employed for designing and analyzing experiments involving muonium, thus showcasing its utility. The software is available at https://stamopoulos.chem.uoc.gr/mumupy/. MuMuPy supports the calculation of interactions for the first 98 elements. For example, MuMuPy can calculate energy levels associated with transitions in hydrogen and helium droplets, providing relevant data. Furthermore, MuMuPy was used to identify promising targets for experimental observation of muonium-nucleus spin-flip oscillations. These targets include osmium, iridium, and tungsten, which due to large corresponding interaction energies, are within current experimental capabilities for observation. This research formalizes a theoretical framework for optimal portfolio management in terms of absolute and relative wealth using power utilities, thereby expanding on existing Stochastic Differential Utility theory. Our research emphasizes the importance of viewing the process of identifying summaries as a combined human-crowdsourced and machine-driven effort. Graph isomorphism problem resolution involves various approaches, among which checking for eigenvalue multiplicities has proven particularly successful. This strategy has been effectively applied to different sub-classes of graphs. Generally, determining whether a graph is isomorphic to another requires computing the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the graph's Laplacian matrix, a common approach adopted in such cases. Research has demonstrated that certain families of graphs, comprising unitary regular graphs, symmetric graphs, and those invariant under rotations, can be identified using the multiplicity of specific eigenvalues. Furthermore, special cases of these families enable determination through the simplest method - checking degeneracies. This work introduces a unified framework where we identify the necessary and sufficient conditions under which graphs can be isomorphic by calculating the multiplicity of a specific eigenvalue. We introduce a group that encompasses various previously studied families and establish that the absolute value of this group's element's order can serve as a criterion for graph isomorphism, particularly for those corresponding to this group. We introduce a set of graphs that correspond to this group but are not covered by the unitary regular graphs family. We provide a computational tool to work with the Laplacian matrix elements and use it to develop an efficient algorithm that checks whether a graph belongs to our defined family. We also explore the characteristics of the family's sub-sets and discuss possible directions for further research. We illustrate the applicability of our approach using known examples as well as artificially generated data. We also compare our results with those obtained using TensorFlow's implementation of the Spectral Embedding Keras model. We conclude by outlining the advantages of our approach and its potential adaptations in graph theory and other domains. The complete source code of our model, along with the computational data, is available at https://github.com/constantin-gundersen/graph-isomorphism. Using our approach, we successfully checked over 13 million graph pairs (without considering symmetry) and nearly 3.7 million graph pairs (with consideration of symmetry), each corresponding to the (20,5) parameters. This study examines various strategic approaches to reduce beam-induced electromagnetic interference in large muon collider rings. We focus on ring designs with low beta sections and high intensity beams, characteristic of next-generation colliders. We develop and compare two strategic initiatives aimed at minimizing wall impact, utilizing PVI systems adjusted according to beta function. The first strategy involves adjusting PVI phases relative to the RF station to minimize impact on low beta sections. The second strategy involves adjusting PVI phases relative to the muon production target, using a matched beam profile at the production point as a reference. We assess the efficacy of each strategy in suppressing beam-induced effects, including halo development, beam loss, and direct beam-pipe interaction background. Based on an analysis of these factors, we recommend the second strategy and plan to further develop this idea for potential implementation in the FCC-muon and CLIC detectors. An additional initiative is intended to prevent PVI phases from drifting as a result of machine errors or other factors, using a beam current control system. We have begun developing the BCC concept and are currently assessing its feasibility. The BCC is designed to maintain precise control over PVI phases, optimize beam distribution, intervene in beam halos, and introduce deliberate beam piping effects for detector purposes, potentially allowing for beam piping background yields comparable to beam-induced background yields in optimal muon collider operations. We plan to establish whether this concept is viable and to identify areas for potential integration into the FCC-muon design. The results of these studies will be published in a joint FCC muon report. Furthermore, the principles underlying these concepts and ideas can be widely applicable to various collider designs incorporating beam-induced effects, thus potentially advancing multiple scientific and engineering projects. The methods used in these studies involve a detailed analysis of muon collider design specifications, even when the designs themselves are not publicly disclosed. Additionally, the results and recommendations generated from these concepts and ideas are intended for use in designing and optimizing various particle beam systems, drawing from prior work in beam-induced effects, particularly from CLIC and ILC studies. The results and recommendations are structured in a format that identifies best practices, points of interest, and open inquiries, thus enabling various scientific and engineering projects to partake in and benefit from this research. The results and recommendations also serve as the foundation for an upcoming publication in the Journal of Physics: Accelerators and Beams. Making neural networks more efficient by reducing computation can be done by limiting the data instead of processing it fully.  However, since the data doesn't change, simply omitting some data at random won't work because the training method would learn to rely on that omitted data.  This requires an intelligent way to selectively choose which data to include.  An innovative method has been created where a separate network decides which data to use and the main network only processes the selected data.  This method can be used in any neural network, allowing for both the decision and data processing networks to be designed.  It uses a unique training method where the decision network tries to mimic the data distribution and the main network tries to achieve perfect results with the limited data.  An even more efficient version uses a decision network that is constrained.  It uses a unique training method where the decision network tries to mimic the data distribution while the main network tries to minimize loss.  This method was tested on image recognition and language tasks and was able of speed up training and reach the same results with just a quarter of the data.  Additionally, the decision network can be used to automatically detect and exclude irrelevant data.  It was also tested on GPU training, speeding up training time four times in the process.  It was found that using this method on already efficient modern architectures like ResNet and Transformer did not result in significant additional computational overhead.  This method was found to be particularly effective for large data sets because the decision network can identify and exclude irrelevant data.  It was found to be particularly bad for tasks with very little data because the decision network has no guidance to follow. It was found that using more complex decision methods like Mixture of Experts did not lead to better results in terms of saving data.  It was found that using more complex decision methods could lead to higher computational overhead.  It was found that using more complex decision methods could lead to better results in terms of saving time.  It was found that using more complex decision methods could lead to better results in terms of reaching the same results with less data. The presence of unpleasant smells in code, also known as code smells, can be very
difficult to detect, especially when developers themselves are to identify them.
Previous studies have shown that introducing reviewers to bad code smells does not
necessarily result in their detection, and it's also challenging for reviewers to
assess the difficulty of detecting smells as compared to the actual detection
itself. The goal of this study is to investigate how developers perceive the
difficulty of identifying smells in actual practice. The study conducted a survey
of 1,444 software developers from eight different programming backgrounds and
asked about their experiences with detectable smells in real-world projects.
Results showed that developers themselves are not always consistent in identifying
smells and also tend to overestimate the difficulty of detecting them compared
to their actual detection. The study suggests that one main reason for this disparity
is that developers themselves are often the ones writing bad code smells without
even realizing it. The study offers several potential solutions to improve the
detection of smells, including proper education on smell identification and
encouraging open source collaboration. The study data can be accessed through

We have developed a stochastic algorithm for approximating tensor singular value decomposition. This method involves factorizing a decomposed tensor into a lower-rank tensor product of three smaller tensors. By analyzing the expected error in approximation, we have determined the relationship between the number of passes through the tensor data and the estimated error. Based on this analysis, we have shown that increasing the number of passes reduces the estimated error. Our algorithm is both batch and out-of-core capable, making it suitable for larger datasets by processing batches or portions of the data at once. We have also determined the optimal inner iteration number for the strongest decay rate of the stochastic objective function. Our algorithm was tested on various tensors derived from image data and singular value decomposition of matrices converted from CSV format. The results confirm that the algorithm can effectively factorize large tensors, even those from four-dimensional video data, despite limited passes. By applying this method, we were able to successfully factorize tensors with 400 million entries using 100 passes, although optimal results required 200 passes. Furthermore, we have successfully applied tensor singular value decomposition to the entire US census 2000 dataset. In our research, we investigate methods for representing sequences of dynamic networks at varying levels of detail, focusing on operations for embedding graphs that have undergone changes over time and for utilizing these embeddings within machine learning frameworks. We evaluate multiple techniques for representing the evolution of graphs in different settings and explore their effectiveness in different contexts. Our study reveals the best approaches for representing these dynamic networks and showcases their applicability in different applications. We observe, however, that the state-of-the-art node embedding algorithms perform poorly when handling large amounts of temporal information, leading us to suggest the use of hybrid strategies that take into account both network structure and temporal characteristics. We hope our findings provide a basis for the development of more informed, complex models of evolving graphs in the future. The implementation of our methods can be found on the GitHub repository https://github.com/fg958/j temporal. We expect that the insights presented in this work will contribute meaningful insights to the field of temporal network analysis. Additionally, we outline the possible avenues for further research mentioned in this document. 

Embedded temporal networks hold immense value in numerous sectors, and their study is closely linked to the field of graph theory. In general terms, embedded temporal networks can be defined as a combination of a undirected graph and a temporal function, representing time, that assigns a timeline to the graph's edges and vertices. This model is versatile enough to accommodate a wide range of temporal data, enabling the representation of surfaces with varying complexities, such as the two-dimensional embedding of a tetrahedron, a three-dimensional object. In our study, we examined various types of temporal data, including general graph embeddings, a particular type known as simple graph Isomorphism testers, and neural networks specifically designed for temporal data. In terms of the model's simplicity versus its level of detail, we found that the more simplistic models performed better when dealing with large datasets, while the more detailed models excelled in more challenging tasks, such as those involving multiple attributes. Another key aspect of our research was the duration of time needed to process the data - we discovered that the more concise models could learn from shorter sequences of temporal data, whereas the more detailed models required longer sequences. Ultimately, our study is intended to inspire further research into the development of more informed, complex models of evolving graphs and their potential applications. The European Space Agency's GAIA mission will create a detailed 3D chart of over a billion stars near our galaxy, accurately measuring their positions, motions, and luminosities to an unprecedented degree of accuracy. By observing stars across multiple lines of sight, GAIA will reveal their true positions, motions, and internal structures. However, complications arise from the need to contend with various observational errors and noise levels. To demonstrate the feasibility and efficiency of the mission's data processing pipeline, a series of evaluations are presented, focusing on determining precise star positions from optical data, an essential component of the assessment. By developing and implementing novel algorithms, such as those based on Dyadics Integrators for Astrometry (DIA) and Random Sampling Importance Sampling (RSIS), this study compares their performance with traditional methods like Mean Area Variance (MAV) and Random Sampling Variance (RSV) based on Astrometric Multi-typer Estimator (AMYE). In particular, this investigation involves modeling and simulating the observation process for select demonstration zones using Real-Time Data Assimilation Framework for Astrometry (RADAMAS), generating synthetic data based on a precise mathematical representation of the observations, then processing these data with various astrometric data processing channels to yield accurate final state estimates of the stars being observed. Our analysis and findings, based on extensive numerical evaluations, show that the new algorithms perform just as well as, if not better than, established methods like MAVERIC, by demonstrating a high level of accuracy in mapping positions of the observed stars, with some improvements observed in performance metrics such as mean absolute error, total absolute error distribution, and 3-sigma parity errors in various demonstration areas across the galaxy, where the noise levels change from relatively simple to more complex levels in more advanced scenarios. Moreover, this study demonstrates the potential of the new algorithms to further reduce errors in positions, like a 26% improvement achievable with a 3 sigma parity error in more complex demonstration area scenarios, to name one such potential improvement, where the noise levels do indeed become increasingly more intricate. In conclusion, we assert that these new algorithms are worthy of inclusion in the assessment, where they will undoubtedly exhibit comparable, if not better performance in the actual mission data processing pipeline. Such an assessment would further solidify their potential to generate highly accurate 3D chart representations of our galaxy's stars, where the degree of accuracy in position mapping demonstrated here, across the various mission demonstration area scenarios, would clearly translate to their overall distribution as well.

Deep learning methods, in the form of physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), have proven successful in extending analytical solvers to complex partial differential equations (PDEs). However, the lack of a systematic approach to evaluating the reliability of PINNs raises concerns about their credibility. We've found that a portion of the model's uncertainty can be attributed to an error associated with the data, which can be mitigated through a process called a posteriori theory. By utilizing this theory, known as the discrete norm, we can quantify the data-related error and establish a lower bound for the expected PINN outcome. We've successfully applied this technique to two numerical methods: the finite difference method and the finite element method. Furthermore, we've developed methods for constructing upper and lower bounds for the PINN solution without relying on model parameters. We've conducted a detailed analysis of the theoretical bounds, evaluated their practical implications, and examined various numerical examples to demonstrate how the technique can be effectively used. This method is expected to enhance the use of physics-informed neural networks in fields requiring rigorous reliability, such as risk assessment, engineering, and computational physics. We've also made available open-source code enabling the PINN-based a posteriori analysis described in our research. The goal is for this tool to facilitate the widespread adoption of physics-informed neural networks in the validation and verification process. Importantly, our proposed approach can be used not only for verifying PINNs but also for deriving rigorous, model-dependent confidence intervals for any numerical method capable of being formalized. Such procedures are typically found in fields such as finite element and finite volume methods used for solving PDEs and are widely applied across various areas. Furthermore, the idea is not limited to PINNs but can be applied to a broader range of machine learning methods aimed at solving physical systems. In the future, we plan to extend this idea to incorporate experimental data and make the corresponding code open-source. The resulting tool enables the a posteriori analysis of any machine learning model used to simulate physical systems, whether or not the underlying governing laws are known. Importantly, our approach is limited to situations where the underlying governing laws are known and we rely heavily on the existing theory developed for the validation and verification process. This idea is not meant to handle cases where the data-driven model lacks a closed-form expression but is instead based on a collection of observed data points. In such cases, the concept of posterior error estimation is typically employed and is found in fields such as function approximation, low-resource speech recognition, or computer vision.

Several key factors influence the spread of airborne pathogens, 
such as SARS-CoV-2, and other airborne viruses and bacteria. 
The characteristics of air contamination, the presence of suspended particles, the type of atmospheric moisture, and the operation of indoor heating and ventilation systems all play a significant role in spreading respiratory diseases. 
To evaluate the impact of these variables on transmission, we propose a unique machine learning model in the form of a spatial regression analysis. 
The first part of this study reviews existing literature on techniques for modeling atmospheric contamination, pathogen transmission, and the influence of humidity and indoor ventilation systems on disease spread. 
Air quality models have used geostatistical methods, the random field model, and machine learning approaches such as KNN and GBRT to analyze spatial data. 
However, few studies have explored the relationship between atmospheric moisture and disease transmission, and existing research on AI-driven pathogen transmission models has focused on system dynamics and reinforcement learning. 
The second part of this study involves developing a machine learning-based spatial regression model to analyze air samples taken in public spaces, such as train stations, and predict the geometric distribution of aerosols based on the composition of atmospheric moisture and the performance of ventilation systems. 
The model's efficacy was assessed through multiple evaluations, and its potential as a diagnostic tool was demonstrated through a case study of AI-driven air quality management in Chile. 
The third part of this research involves investigating the influence of atmospheric moisture and ventilation systems on the geometric distribution of aerosols using AI-powered spatial regression analysis. 
Fourth, we investigated the impact of atmospheric moisture and ventilation systems on the respiratory transmission of airborne pathogens such as SARS-CoV-2, Influenza A and B, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis using AI-driven spatial regression analysis. 
Lastly, we analyzed the impact of individual health behaviors, such as smoking, diet, and physical activity, on influenza transmission, and the effect of atmospheric moisture and ventilation systems on airborne pathogens using AI-driven spatial regression analysis. 
Due to limited data availability and specific requirements, we conducted an in-depth case study instead of a broader investigation. 
The model's results reveal that atmospheric moisture and ventilation systems have a significant impact on the geometric distribution of aerosols, and respiratory diseases. 
AI-driven methods for modeling atmospheric moisture and ventilation systems show promising results, and their use in epidemiological studies provides valuable insights for policymakers and public health experts. 
It is our hope that future research will expand on these models through a more comprehensive investigation.

In this paper, we establish key findings related to minimal vertex sets within infinite hypergraphs. A hypergraph is considered minimal if its vertex sets cannot be broken down further, and we show that a subhypergraph formed by combining several hypergraphs contains a minimal vertex set for every k-element subset of its vertex set V_k. Additionally, for every finite hypergraph, a unique minimal vertex set exists for each subset of its vertex set. Moreover, we show that a hypergraph is minimal if and only if its only subhypergraphs are the hypergraph itself and the hypergraph formed by combining it with every one of its vertex sets. This leads to the conclusion that a hypergraph is minimal, but not necessarily simple, and that simplicity and minimality are distinct, non-interchangeable properties. We also derive a sufficient condition under which a hypergraph's minimal vertex sets for every k-element subset of its vertex set V_k are contained within a subset of its vertex set V_k. In addition, we provide a characterization of weakly $n$-partite hypergraphs, and define and examine the properties of fractional hypercliques, leading to a characterization of minimal vertex sets within them. However, the open problem remains whether a hypergraph's minimal vertex sets for every k-element subset of its vertex set V_k are contained within a subset of its vertex set V_k or not. Since the 1960s, researchers have used the concept of binding energy from electron spectroscopy to study intermolecular forces and astrochemistry. Each molecule has its unique binding energy distribution, and referencing accurate datasets is crucial in validating theoretical frameworks and models. Existing datasets were previously inaccessible, and new experiments face challenges due to the lack of a standardized approach to collect and present results. We introduce the binding energy assessment platform (BEAP) to organize and provide access to binding energy distributions. With support from the astrochemical community, BEAP aims to become a database for various quantum chemical binding energy models. We was initiated with six initial datasets for hydrogen-bonded complexes, and BEAP allows users to access, download, fit, or compare distributions along with related analytical tools. We demonstrate BEAP's functionality with binding energy distributions for the water dimer and dicarbon, and we discuss the opportunities for collaboration and feedback within the community to expand BEAP's resources and scope. Feedback and participation are welcome at [beap@rice.edu](mailto:beap@rice.edu). The platform is accessible at https://beap.rice.edu/.
