Our goal is to develop quick methods to assess and criticize the effectiveness of quantum algorithms by projecting real quantum states onto specific, typically straightforward, objectives. We've found that low-depth, randomly constructed Clifford circuits effectively approximate optimal targets, enabling us't to evaluate their worth without extensive computation. Through a study of multi-qubit circuits produced by Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) creation and the Shimony-Hughes-Rieca (SHR) protocol, we demonstrate the viability of our approach. We also show that these circuits can be utilized cross-functionally, thereby minimizing the resources required to project a quantum state and find its appraisable, target-simulating shades. We observe that these circuits not only assist in evaluating quantum algorithms but also hold potential as building blocks for creating complex, parametric quantum circuits. Furthermore, we illustrate their application in analyzing the security of quantum key distribution protocols using numerical simulations. We plan to make the source code for our projects available on GitHub with the intention of contributing positively to the quantum computing community. Ultimately, through numerical simulations, we assess the practical costs associated with our approach and determine that while shallow circuits may not completely replicate optimal targets, they are highly effective, especially when working within realistic, batch-processing scenarios. In fact, based on current technical capabilities, we find that shallow circuits may be nearly perfect, with errors measured in thousands of parts per million (ppm) that can be recovered through subsequent, more complex circuit layers. Consequently, these circuits have promising applications as a fast and efficient tool for projecting and appraising the effectiveness of quantum algorithms. What's more, we've shown that implementing post-processing layers is a more feasible task than entirely rewriting the circuit when seeking increased precision in our results. In summary, our work provides a range of applications for shallow circuits starting from evaluation and criticism of quantum algorithms to potential future uses in quantum computing itself. We have chosen to work within the well-established and tested framework of Clifford circuits, thereby ensuring the development of these applications is both theoretically and practically sound. We are eager to see the community adopt and expand upon our work as we have intentionally left many aspects of these concepts open to future research and development. In the future, we could potentially apply similar ideas to broader classes of quantum systems, thereby advancing the field of quantum computing itself. Ultimately, our goal is to make quantum computing a more efficient and cost-effective process. The source code for our project can be found at https://github.com/kevinincelly/Shallow-Shades-on-Quantum-C

The global solvability of the Davey-Stewartson II equations is demonstrated for initial data pairs $(u, v)$ in specific $L^2$ subspaces, subject to the constraint $|k|u(v)$ with certain growth restrictions. Under these conditions, the resulting equations for $u$ and $v$ separate and exhibit the form of a Schrödinger equation in $x$, coupled with a Riemann equation in the variable $k$, whose well-posedness is proven. Furthermore, the existence of solutions is established for the Riemann equation through the application of a nonlinear variation of the parameter integral operator and by invoking the properties of Fourier transforms. Additionally, the behavior of the resulting transform of the singular integral operator is analyzed, drawing on previous work described in [Koch and Kaucha\v{c}i, 2015, J. Math. Anal. Appl. 422(2), 1145-1162]. In turn, this allows us to construct a variation of the parameter integral operator for the Schrödinger equation and establish its connection to the properties of the Fourier transform. Finally, through the application of energy estimates, the solutions' behavior as $t$ approaches infinity are found to be within specific $L^2$ subspaces, and unifying unbounded operator theory and energy estimates are used to establish the Fredholm property of the resulting operator for the time-dependent equations. It is found that the solutions' behavior is determined by the properties of a Riemann equation in the variable $k$, whose solutions' behavior is investigated separately. Large language models like T5 and BART are now widely used in various NLP tasks. Notably, in text classification tasks, we discovered that a substantial number of these models' variants, comprising just 1-10% of all models in a given class, are responsible for 90% of performance scores. This phenomenon, where models' performance varies greatly even within the same class, raises questions about reliance on model diversity in metrics such as Leaderboard. This issue could have far-reaching consequences, particularly in applications where higher model performance scores lead to increased confidence and trust. We propose the Sibyl Index to measure model diversity, which is found to be highly correlated with NLP evaluation benchmarks. We also introduce a method to intentionally reduce model diversity during development, aiming to create more trustworthy and robust benchmarks. Our results indicate that our approach successfully decreases the variation in model performance while leaving overall performance intact. Furthermore, models trained with our scheme exhibit improved resilience to unsatisfactory, high-performing models when evaluating cross-domain NLP tasks. Overall, our research demonstrates the importance of model diversity in NLP performance metrics and encourages the establishment of more reliable and robust evaluation standards that account for this factor. The code for our approach can be found at https://github.com/dhelleu/sibyl. Our dataset of NLP performance scores for 33 Leaderboards is available at https://huggingface.org/datasets/treehopper. As an additional contribution, we also examined the impact of model size, architecture, data, and objectives on model diversity, which may be of separate interest to researchers. These findings are available at https://github.com/dhelleu/sibyl/variance. We analyzed a total of 2,853 models and uncovered several intriguing patterns, which may inspire further research. Ultimately, our investigation shows that simply reporting higher performance scores on NLP evaluation benchmarks does not guarantee a reliable and robust model. To remedy this issue, we aim to encourage the NLP community to adopt more robust evaluation standards. We believe that our research presents an opportunity for future investigations. If you find our work valuable, we would appreciate your support to continue this research journey. The primary aim of our research is to assist NLP practitioners in making more informed decisions when utilizing and evaluating large language models. Utilizing multilingual Convolutional Neural Network-based Machine Translation models results in uniform feature extraction for multiple languages from the same model. By leveraging knowledge sharing and reducing the model's size, models created through knowledge distillation and quantization are seen as a promising way to translate languages with limited available data. We focus particularly on developing low-resource German-English translation models. Compared to distillation, quantization is less common in translating languages with limited available data, however it's more cost-effective and efficient in reducing model size. In this research, we used the Transformer model architecture, created variously sized models by applying different quantization techniques such as unfolding and folding, and computed metrics such as BLEU scores for evaluating our results. We found that while distillation-produced models outperformed quantization-produced models in terms of translation quality, particularly on high-resource languages, they showed no notable difference on low-resource languages. This implies that translating languages with limited available data using distillation may be too resource-intensive and that quantization could be a more cost-effective and efficient method. Additionally, we discovered that reducing the number of attention heads in a model has a negative impact on translation quality, suggesting that translating languages with limited available data using few heads may be too fragile. In summary, this research validated the effectiveness of distillation in creating smaller but not lighter models while reducing the model's size with quantization proved challenging. Ultimately, we found that translating languages with limited available data using distillation is too resource-intensive and translating languages with limited available data using few heads is too fragile, leaving room for further research to develop more efficient methods. The detection of pulmonary abnormalities via automated segmentation of lung boundaries from CT scans is crucial in diagnosing prostate, breast, and other cancers linked to high pneumonia mortality rates. However, detecting pneumonia often involves time-consuming and costly manual assessment of lung opacity levels. In our study, we investigate whether image processing techniques can significantly reduce the need for ground truth labels in annotating pneumonia for deep learning models. By using an unsupervised representation learning approach, we train a model to generate enhanced images highlighting pneumonia manifestations before refining it using disease masks. Another model is trained in a standard supervised manner, and we compare the performance of both models in detecting pneumonia in an actual clinical setting. Our experiments yield promising results, indicating that our approach can indeed decrease the necessity for ground truth labels in deep learning models without compromising their accuracy in detecting pneumonia. When combined with full segmentation masks, our method significantly outperforms standard approaches. Moreover, when using limited disease masks, our method performs comparably to existing standard approaches while requiring merely 1% of the usual amount of ground truth labels to train the model, making the annotation process far more efficient. Therefore, this method has the potential to be utilized effectively in various clinical settings. Furthermore, in terms of segmentation performance, our method surpasses existing standard approaches in many aspects and is comparable in a few others, even requiring only 3% of the usual amount of ground truth labels to train the model. Ultimately, when using full disease masks, our method significantly outperforms standard approaches in many aspects, reducing the gap between performance metrics by as much as 15%. In summary, our method successfully applies unsupervised image processing enhancements to reduce the necessity for ground truth labels in detecting pneumonia with high accuracy and reliability. Image description generation, a key challenge in computer vision, requires natural language skills to produce accurate and coherent descriptions of images, even for complex scenes. Current models face difficulties with image description complexity, particularly in generating detailed and sequential descriptions, even when large datasets like Imagscope are considered. To address these limitations, we introduce Manageable Image Descriptions (MIDs), a set of prompts designed to simplify image description complexity, facilitating the ability of large language models like GPT-2 and BERT to produce more detailed and coherent descriptions. We evaluate MID's effectiveness on the Imagscope dataset and reveal that our multi-step approach to develop these prompts, combining prompt-based learning with self-supervised learning, is crucial in achieving promptability. We also examine mid-level descriptions in greater detail, evaluating the impact of our description strategy on the integration of mid-level descriptions into high-level descriptions and their increased coherence. Importantly, we uncover that our description strategy is generalizable to other image description datasets, notably the COCO dataset, with potential applications in other computer vision domains. Moreover, we show that our model can produce coherent and detailed descriptions of novel images not previously seen during training, known as "out-of-distribution" descriptions. Ultimately, our approach demonstrates the ability of large language models to describe complex image content in a manner similar to human-level performance. Autonomous driving sector is facing numerous challenges due to recurring accidents resulting in damage to property. The application of causal models can facilitate the comparison of causes of damage, such as auto-collisions or roof damage, in relation to their causes of death, like a fatal head-on collision. Nevertheless, existing causal models may not adequately address questions like "What would happen if my car's front wheel was damaged?" due to limitations in path-condition specificity. A novel causal model presented in this work effectively addresses such queries by integrating mixed-level factors, encompassing low-level details like tire wear and high-level path variations. Through leveraging existing geometric models, this approach enables the breakdown of causes into their constituent components, aligning with the principles of Bayesian Inverse Problems. A demonstration of our approach is showcased on the Data2Tree platform utilizing tree damage data, where we evaluate cause similarity against expert-annotated labels and establish that the model is capable of accurately distinguishing between causes of death and causes of damage. Additionally, we develop and release OpenTAP, an open-source tuning and assessment protocol for tuning and testing causal models, including domain-agnostic metrics like PCPC and domain-specific metrics like Multiscale Hausdorff Distance. Utilizing this protocol, we demonstrate that our model is capable of modeling death causes as well as damage causes and their respective interconnections. Ultimately, these causal insights derived from our model can benefit the autonomous driving industry in identifying and mitigating causes of damage.

Although numerous advancements have been made in voice recognition technologies, they typically necessitate significant training based on existing models or categories, limiting their applicability to specialized domains or uncommon words. In this research, we present ZVI, a framework designed to analyze spoken inputs without requiring them to be categorized or trained on specific terms. Unlike conventional approaches, ZVI can identify words without needing word-level labels and also tolerate minor inaccuracies in speech segmentation while producing clean word-level outputs. As such, ZVI can be utilized for tasks involving spoken language understanding across various domains without needing to retrain or coming across unlisted words during deployment. In our experiments, ZVI consistently outperformed competing methods in two distinct scenarios: automatic medical diagnosis and cooking recipe comprehension. In the case of automatic medical diagnosis, our error correction technique proved particularly effective in improving the performance of traditionally-designed medical diagnosis models by achieving comparable results with the current state-of-the-art as well as a notable 9.8% improvement over the existing best performance without error correction, while also facilitating more general-purpose medical diagnosis models that can be deployed without requiring retraining. Furthermore, our analysis of the characteristics of our clean speech dataset, CleanSpeech-1, has shown its value in improving the performance of speech-to-text models, leading to higher user satisfaction. Our proposed framework, word-level outputs, and clean speech dataset have the potential to significantly contribute to various applications in spoken language processing. Accurate forecasting of residential energy consumption is essential for managing low-voltage grids effectively, helping to minimize peak demand and avoid distribution system overloading. Despite the considerable research into predicting consumption at higher voltage levels, accurately predicting load peaks and variability remains a challenge for low-voltage grids due to the unique characteristics of residential energy consumption during peak hours. This paper investigates a novel forecasting method for low-voltage grids that combines point forecasts with probability distributions, focusing specifically on predicting daily peak load and the likelihood of peak demand. By combining set-point forecasts with time-series data models, our approach enables the transformation of forecasts into normalized probability distributions, ensuring spatial transferability and intuitive understanding. In our study, we demonstrated the advantages of this method by evaluating its performance on actual consumption data from Dutch low-voltage grid nodes, comparing it to more conventional forecasting techniques that rely on time series data. Our results indicate that the proposed probabilistic forecasting approach allows for more effective peak load prediction and offers improved understanding of low-voltage grid consumption patterns. Furthermore, our technique has the potential to be adapted for use in energy trading and asset management, facilitating optimal low-voltage grid operations. In line with the increasing focus on distribution system management, our work contributes to the development of advanced distributed energy systems by identifying promising avenues for smart distribution and grid operations. This research was supported by an agreement between the University of Amsterdam and Hollandse Kust Zuid, and the data utilized in this study were kindly provided by the University of Amsterdam and the Dutch grid operator, Stedin. Finally, our findings demonstrate that the proposed probabilistic forecasting method can effectively address peak demand prediction challenges in low-voltage grids, and it is available on GitHub under the open-source license. Subsequent analyses have revealed that the characteristics of low-voltage grid consumption are largely unaffected by the local characteristics, suggesting the existence of common patterns in residential energy consumption. This implies that the proposed method can be applied across a wide range of grids while adhering to the principles of local energy production and consumption. In addition to improving forecasting, our approach has the potential to support more effective asset management and distribution planning. In the future, we intend to expand on these findings by incorporating the proposed method into the decision-making process, ultimately leading to more efficient energy management. Detecting COVID-19 with chest CT scans is critical, but it's hampered by a lack of sufficiently annotated data. Most existing methods depend on pixel-level annotated images, yet these are costly to obtain and time-consuming to collect. Given the high costs, mass production is difficult, which restricts the availability of training data. A novel, unbiased detection framework overcomes this data annotation issue by utilizing point-level labels instead of full images. Leveraging these labels, it's possible to not only detect lesions but also improve the accuracy of lesion segmentation due to its attention to relevant areas. We tested our framework on a COVID-19 dataset, comparing its performance to other existing methods like Cranialfrat and U-Net. The results show that the Weakly-Labeled Learning-based Cranialfrat-WL and Patch-Based Cranialfrat-WL models are superior to the original Cranialfrat and U-Net. While the U-Net is currently considered one of the best methods for COVID-19 lesion detection, our modified versions outperformed it by a significant margin. A combination of our Cranialfrat-WL and Patch-Based Cranialfrat-WL models achieved an impressive 0.072 and 0.070 higher IoU scores, respectively, demonstrating the efficacy of weakly labelled learning in COVID-19 detection and lesion extraction. Accurate vertebrae identification is crucial in various medical applications linked to spinal column related disorders and treatments. However, the complexity of CT images, resulting from limitations of imaging technology and physical constraints, poses challenges to automated recognition. Moreover, the varied postures of individuals presents an issue. This paper aims to address the positioning challenge by first correcting the spinal column using rectification techniques, labeled as S-rectification, and incorporating C-rectification if necessary. Additionally, vertebrae identification is enhanced through anatomically inspired constraints. In experiments, our proposed method outperformed competing approaches, demonstrating superior adaptability to different spinal positions through S-rectification, and showed significant resistance to rotation challenges. Furthermore, the use of C-rectification and anatomically-inspired constraints demonstrated substantial improvement over existing state-of-the-art methods. In summary, the proposed technique successfully identifies the correct vertebrae and accurately determines their position. This method facilitates the extraction of meaningful medical data, crucial for analysis and decision-making. Such a technique has far-reaching applications in various medical procedures and examinations. With rapid advancements in medical imaging technology, the use of these scans will only become more vital in medical and surgical practices. Relevant code for this paper is accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/ChenDing2018/ARV.

In this high-electron-density environment, a collective oscillation triggered by the vacuum fluctuation is expected to arise, connected to the plasmon frequency, as predicted by the London-Bloch equations. This research explores the capabilities of elastic actuators in quadrupedal locomotion, utilizing learning-based methods to optimize elastic actuator-based mobility. By replacing traditional motor actuators with elastic actuators, system weights can be reduced, with the latter functioning as springs. However, the feasibility of using these actuators in mobility has yet been established. This key insight empowers the application of various existing control algorithms developed for traditional motor actuators to elastic actuator-based systems. A fundamental challenge in fashion image retrieval involves categorizing images into their respective styles, with a key factor being consistency within a given brand's aesthetic appeal. Unlike other retail industries, the fashion market is distinguished by a high level of subjectivity in image evaluation, necessitating the use of image manipulation techniques to fill the gap between the objective and subjective realms. Existing methods focus primarily on manipulating images at the global feature level, which often leads to discrepancies between the visual characteristics of manipulated images and human-perceived fashion styles. Furthermore, global feature manipulation may result in features that are irrelevant to a particular brand, thus reducing its retrieval effectiveness. Conversely, our proposed semi-supervised Feature-Level Trait Manipulation model is designed to perform feature-level image manipulation while ensuring consistency in a brand's distinctive visual attributes. Utilizing a fashion dataset comprising over 200 brands, we evaluated our model's retrieval capability against leading baselines and demonstrated its superiority through retrieval score enhancements of up to 12.19%. Moreover, our model was found to be robust in handling brands with limited training data, thus exhibiting compelling cross-brand generalization properties. Evaluating the light field's depth properties is crucial for understanding its visual qualities, yet measuring the depth of a specific point within a scene is a challenge due to occlusion and residual depth uncertainty. We address this issue by introducing the Occlusion-Responsive Expense Creator (ORC), a novel method that dynamically allocates computing resources based on patch similarity to optimize overall image quality. By ORC's design, each patch's contribution to the overall image is tailored to reach an optimal trade-off between overall image clarity and overall depth accuracy. We demonstrate ORC's effectiveness through its compatibility with diverse optimization techniques, including both deep learning-based and traditional optimization methods. Furthermore, we showcase its ability to excel in situations with heavy occlusions and low-contrast scenes, outperforming state-of-the-art approaches such as Code-Depth and Disparity-Aware Depth (DAD). We also showcase its compatibility with other leading depth estimation methods, significantly enhancing their performance in situations with heavy occlusions. The resulting model is based on our experiments' suggestions for an ideal ORC parameter setting, suggesting a future direction of developing performance metrics that incorporate occlusion prevalence for more precise parameter tuning.
